descs.en: She nearly ran him over at a street race and jumped off her bike to fight him. He complimented her intake manifold.

synopsis.title: Synopsis
synopsis.content:
Raiden Lin plays the cheerful, slightly useless Lin son so well that the Syndicate and the police both ignore him. In fact he draws the family’s safe rooms and knows the weak point of every building in the city.

One night he’s kneeling in the middle of an illegal race on the old shipyard road, sketching a warehouse, when a motorbike stops two metres from him. Jinx gets off to beat some sense into him. He looks up and tells her that her intake manifold is beautiful.

She grew up in a chop shop under the flyover and swore she’d never be owned by anyone, least of all a Lin. He would like to marry her. He asks on a napkin, drawn to scale. She says not yet. He keeps asking.

He falls first · Sunshine and grump · Mechanic heroine · Complete in four volumes, plus six side stories

authorNote.title: Author Note
authorNote.content:
Raiden is the Lin who talks. In every other book he’s in the background, cheerful, drawing something, being an idiot on purpose. I wanted to know who he was when he stopped pretending, and who he would stop for. It had to be someone who could see through him at a hundred and ninety kilometres an hour.

This is the lightest book in the series, with the most kissing. They’re together by chapter three. The trouble isn’t whether they’ll fall in love. It’s her father’s debts, his father’s name, and two people who were each hidden as children learning not to hide each other.

He spoils her: a building, a dyno, a lathe, a hill. She pays half. She insisted.

contentWarn.title: Content Warning
contentWarn.content:
21+ · For adult readers.

A warm, funny book, with some hard moments:

• A man hit by a van

• A child hidden in a freezer for eleven hours, and a ten-year-old crossing a border alone

• Threats, a knife and an armed crew

• An attempted assault on a teenage girl, remembered, which she fought off

• A workshop fire

• Love scenes on the page

glossary.title: Names & Terms
glossary.content:
The black door — Jinx's first garage, near the Iron Docks, under an old sign that says TAI HING ROPE & CANVAS.
The shipyard road — Two kilometres of cracked concrete between the dead shipyard and the cranes. Illegal races at one in the morning.
Mrs. Tong's — The noodle place on the corner that only serves men off the container ships. The table by the fridge, back to the wall.
The Meridian — Raiden's glass tower in the Symmetrical Ward. Thirty-one floors. The desk man calls the pale green bike “the tram”.
The pale green bike — The one Jinx built him. Twenty kilometres an hour, lights like a train, a drawing board on the tank, a bell.
The steel room — Behind her tool wall. A light that comes on by itself, air, a line out, a warm lamp she added, and a tin of peaches.
The napkins — Thirty-one proposals, each drawn to scale, kept in his wallet where other people keep photographs.
Under the flyover — The Slums of the Industry, where the sun never gets in. Her father's shop, CAO MOTOR REPAIR.
The gap — Behind the scrap heap, between the wall and the pillar. On the archive drawings from 1974.
The triple — A 1973 two-stroke, three cylinders, a widowmaker. Seized for seven years. Ran at 5:40 a.m.
Oh-three-one-one — The day she left. The code to everything she owns.
JINX — The shop in the old chandler's warehouse three doors down, with a long low window anyone can see into. The sign she cut herself.
The stair — Behind the third shelf on the mezzanine. Two hours of fire board. Used once.
The driveway — One point two kilometres on the hill above the reservoir road. It is a racetrack.
The monkey — The passenger in a racing sidecar, who hangs off the side. Raiden says navigator.
Dyno — A rolling road that measures a bike's power at the back wheel.
Intake manifold — The pipes that carry air and fuel into the engine. Hers are all the same length, by hand.

chapters.title: Sketching in the Middle of a Race Track
chapters.desc: She nearly ran him over at a street race and jumped off her bike to fight him. He complimented her intake manifold.
chapters.epigraph: “I didn’t hit him. Write that down. I want it on record that I didn’t hit him.”
chapters.content:
Jinx didn’t race. She tested.

Men in leather jackets never understood the difference, so she’d stopped explaining. A race was when you wanted to beat somebody. A test was when you wanted to know something. On Saturday night, the fifteenth of May, she wanted to know whether the new intake would hold past nine thousand revs.

She’d finished it on Tuesday after three nights at the bench. Four runners, each the same length to the millimetre, curving down into the head like fingers, every port matched by hand with a file and a lamp, and a good deal of swearing. She’d made the mounting bracket herself and spent the better part of Friday arguing with a mechanic down the road who said her sums were wrong. One runner a hair too long and that cylinder would breathe wrong, and the whole engine would feel it, like a stone in a shoe.

The only straight in the city long enough to find out was the old shipyard road: two kilometres of cracked concrete between the dead yard and the cranes, rusted containers on one side and warehouses with their windows out on the other, and a streetlamp every hundred metres that flickered as if it were thinking about retiring. Nobody ran it until the last security van had gone past the Iron Docks gates and not come back. There were no barriers and no lights and nobody with a stretcher. There were bikes worth more than flats, men who’d made poor decisions about their lives, and so much petrol in the air that breathing was optional. Jinx loved it.

“JINX! You racing or knitting?” Big Hon had a voice like a ship’s horn.

“Testing.”

“Same thing!”

“It isn’t. I’ll go last.”

“Why last?”

“Clean road.”

He went back up the line to wave his flag at somebody else. She sat at the back under the last working lamp with her visor up and listened. She didn’t talk to engines. People who talked to engines weren’t listening to them.

When it was her turn the road was empty. She rolled her wrist, and the bike went.

The front settled as she leaned into the long curve past the dry dock. The engine climbed and the note climbed with it, clean and hard, no flat spot, no cough at the top, and she grinned inside her helmet. A hundred and seventy. A hundred and eighty. A hundred and ninety, past the cranes, nine thousand and climbing, and the intake was singing.

And then there was a man in the road.

Kneeling. Right in the middle of it. With a sketchbook.

She was on the brakes before she’d finished seeing him. The rear stepped out and shrieked and the bike slewed and she held it, held it, held it, and it stopped, rocking, with its front tyre a little over two metres from his knee.

For one long second nobody moved.

Then the man looked up. Black hair falling in his eyes. Round glasses. A white shirt with the sleeves rolled to the elbow, a pencil behind his ear, and an expression so calm she wondered whether he’d already hit his head on something.

He looked at her. He looked down at his sketchbook. He looked back up.

“That was close,” he said.

She killed the engine, kicked the stand down, tore off her helmet and went for him.

He stood up just as she got there, which was when she found out he was a good deal taller than she’d expected. It didn’t help him. She took two fistfuls of his white shirt and shook him.

“What is wrong with you?”

“Good evening,” he said, being shaken.

“Good evening?”

“Technically. It’s still before midnight.”

“Are you trying to die?”

“Not tonight.”

“Then why are you kneeling in the middle of a racetrack?”

“Road. It’s an abandoned shipyard road. People use it as a racetrack, I suppose. I was drawing the warehouse. The light’s better from the middle,” he said. He glanced round as if checking.

“You were drawing.”

“Yes.”

“In the road.”

“Yes.”

“At night.”

“Your observations are very accurate.”

She nearly strangled him. Behind her, boots came pounding down the concrete, and Big Hon arrived out of breath with his flag in one hand and half the line behind him.

“Jinx! Jinx, put him down—”

“I didn’t hit him. Write that down. I want it on record that I didn’t hit him,” she said, without letting go.

“You’re holding him off the ground.”

She looked. She was. She lowered him an inch.

“Do you know how fast I was going?” she said to the man.

“About a hundred and ninety. Your braking was very good, considering the surface. Your rear locked for a moment. May I?” He said it the way other people mentioned the weather. He looked past her shoulder at the bike.

“No.”

“I’d like to look at something.”

“I’d like you out of my sight.”

He smiled. It was an annoyingly pleasant smile. Not sorry, not nervous, not in the least bit frightened. Just warm. Then his eyes went back to the bike and stayed there.

“Your intake. You made that,” he said.

Her hands stopped.

He said, “The runners curve in like fingers. Like a hand holding on to something. You could hear it all the way down the road. It doesn’t cough anywhere. You must have spent days matching the lengths.”

She was still holding his shirt. She looked at her fists, and at him, and let go.

He didn’t step back. He didn’t touch the bike either. He crouched beside it with his hands on his knees and looked at the intake for a long quiet moment, the way some people look at paintings.

“Beautiful,” he said.

People called her work excessive. Expensive. Pointless. Reckless. Her father used to call it a waste of time. Nobody had ever crouched on a road at midnight and called it beautiful.

“What else do you know about engines?” she said.

“Enough to know you shouldn’t do a hundred and ninety on this road.”

She immediately regretted not running him over.

“You’re annoying.”

“I’ve been told.”

“By everyone?”

“Mostly women.”

She snorted. It got out before she could stop it. He looked up, and she saw him see it, and she put her helmet back on.

“What’s your name?” he said.

“Why?”

“So I can introduce myself properly.”

“Don’t.”

“All right. Then can I ask something else? Can I buy you dinner?” He shut the sketchbook. She waited for him to ask again, the way men at the Docks always did. He didn’t.

“No.”

“Coffee?”

“No.”

“Breakfast?”

“Do you have a hearing problem?”

“Not that I know of.”

“Find somewhere else to draw, sketchbook boy.”

“Raiden. Raiden Lin,” he said.

“Good for you.”

She swung onto the bike. The engine caught at once, clean as you like. He stepped well back to give her room, and as she rolled forward he called after her, “Be careful, Jinx.”

She turned her head. He was smiling. He pointed up the road at Big Hon, who’d been shouting her name for ten minutes. Of course. She revved it at him on purpose, hard, and heard him laugh, and then she was gone.

✦ ✦ ✦

He stayed by the warehouse wall for another twenty minutes, after the line had broken up and the last bike had gone. Not because the drawing wasn’t finished. It was. Her bike on its stand in the middle of the empty road, the front wheel turned a little, the long shadow of the streetlamp across the concrete, the helmet where she’d thrown it, and the short distance between the tyre and the place his knee had been.

The space beside the bike was empty. He hadn’t drawn her.

He tried. A jaw. A pair of eyes narrowed at him. The line of her mouth when she’d snorted. He rubbed it out. Tried again. Rubbed it out again. He’d drawn hundreds of faces. Hands. People on stairs. He’d spent years learning to see what other people walked past. And he couldn’t get her right.

Finally he leaned his head against the wall and laughed at himself. “Ridiculous.”

His phone buzzed.

Eliana: Where are you?

Raiden: Iron Docks.

Eliana: Why?

Raiden: Drawing.

Eliana: At midnight. Have you eaten?

Raiden: Not yet.

Eliana: You’re impossible. Baba asked where you were and I said the library.

Raiden: Thank you.

Raiden: I think I met someone interesting.

Three dots. Gone. Three dots again.

Eliana: Oh?

Raiden: She nearly killed me.

Eliana: Then I hope you had a lovely evening.

He laughed out loud in the empty road, and walked home, and found he was looking forward to something he hadn’t planned, which hadn’t happened to him in a long time.

✦ ✦ ✦

Jinx got back to the garage behind the rope shop at nearly two. She parked the bike and pulled off her gloves and stood looking at the intake in the light from the bench lamp.

Then she picked up a marker and wrote on the wall by the bench, in small neat figures, 2.11. She’d paced it out on the way back. Two metres and eleven centimetres from his knee. In case she ever forgot.

“Beautiful. Idiot,” she said, in his voice, to nobody. Then she scowled.

She wiped the grease off her hands and went upstairs.

✦ ✦ ✦

At 2:17 Raiden sat at his dining table with somebody else’s elevations on one side of it and a half-made model of somebody else’s building on the other, and didn’t work. His sketchbook was open in front of him. The bike was still there. So was the empty space.

He turned to a clean page, and this time he didn’t try for her face at all. He drew a woman standing beside a motorbike with a helmet on her hip as if she might use it as a weapon. The tilt of her head. The stubborn set of her shoulders. The way she seemed permanently ready to argue with the whole world. Under it, because he didn’t have anything else, he wrote Jinx.

He’d drawn other people’s buildings that would stand a hundred years. He’d spent his whole life learning to make something beautiful out of measurements and lines. And a woman who’d nearly run him over had left him with a blank page.

He shut the sketchbook. Then he opened it again, just to look at the bike.

He was already in trouble. And he hadn’t even bought her a coffee.

chapters.title: “Nice Intake Manifold” Is Not a Pick-Up Line
chapters.desc: He turns up at the black door with three coffees because he didn’t know how she took it. She drinks all three.
chapters.epigraph: “I brought three because I didn’t know how you took it. Now I know. You take all three.”
chapters.content:
Nobody found the black door by accident. That was the point of it.

Her garage sat in a street of ship chandlers and rope shops a few minutes from the Iron Docks, marine paint on one side, anchors on the other. Over the roll-up door it still said TAI HING ROPE & CANVAS in faded white letters. She’d never painted it out. It put people off. Two rooms upstairs, a hot plate, and a shower that worked if you hit the pipe. Downstairs, the only part that mattered: long and high and cool, bikes on stands, bikes on the floor, bikes hanging from the ceiling on chains.

Just after nine on Sunday morning she was on her back on the creeper under a little red bike when somebody knocked. She ignored it. It came again, three times, patient.

“If you’re selling something, I’m not buying.”

“It’s coffee.”

She lay perfectly still. No. Absolutely not.

She rolled out and sat up with grease to the elbows, and there he was in the doorway with the sun behind him: a cardboard tray in one hand, a paper bag in the other, a sketchbook under his arm, a pencil behind his ear, a clean white shirt, and grey trousers that had cost more than her lathe. He looked about twenty-three and pleased with himself and wrong for the street in every possible way.

“Good morning!”

“How did you find me?”

“I asked the man with the flag. He said you’d kill me if I came. Then I asked the boy with the wrong fairing, who told me the street, because he wanted me dead. Then I asked the lady who sells anchors. She looked at me for a long time and said, the black door. I brought three. I didn’t know how you took it. Black. One with milk. One with condensed milk from the man on the corner, who says nobody under sixty drinks it but you might.” He seemed cheerful about it. He held out the tray.

She looked at the coffees. She looked at the bag. Two egg sandwiches and a box of pineapple buns, still warm.

“Are you trying to bribe me?”

“I was hoping to.”

“I said no to dinner. And coffee. And breakfast.”

“I remember. You didn’t say I couldn’t try again on Sunday,” he said.

She stared at him. Then she laughed, not because he was funny but because she couldn’t work out what kind of man did this. “You’re unbelievable.”

“I’ve heard that too.”

“Do you always bother women at work?”

“Only the ones who nearly run me over.”

“That’s a very small category.”

“It is.”

She took the tray. She drank the black one standing up, in four swallows, because she’d been up since six. Then she tried the milk one. Then the condensed milk one, which was thick and sweet and exactly what she wanted and would never have asked for. Then she went back to the black. He watched with a perfectly straight face.

“You’re drinking all three.”

“Did I say you could have one?”

“No. I drink tea. Coffee makes my hands shake. I can’t draw.” He took a battered flask out of his bag to prove it.

“Then why buy three?”

“I didn’t know which you’d like. I brought three because I didn’t know how you took it. Now I know. You take all three.” He watched her finish the condensed milk.

“Should’ve brought twelve.”

“I’ll remember.”

“Don’t.”

“All right,” he said, and she found she’d sat down on the bench with the last cup, and he’d found a crate to sit on, and somehow she hadn’t told him to leave yet.

✦ ✦ ✦

He looked round the garage properly while she ate an egg sandwich. It was cramped and absolutely ordered. Tools on a pegboard, each one in its outline. Spares in labelled tins. A dismantled engine laid out on a low table in the order it had come apart. An old standing fan in the corner, oil on the concrete, and pinned by the bench a hand-drawn diagram covered in measurements in three colours of ink, with revisions crossed out and replaced.

“That’s your intake.”

“Yes.”

“You drew it?”

“Who else?”

“May I?”

“Don’t touch anything.”

He stood in front of it with his hands behind his back. “You changed the diameter here.”

“The original had a restriction at the bend.”

“So you widened it?”

“No. I changed the taper. Widen it without thinking about the air speed and you lose the response.”

He turned and looked at her.

“What?”

“Nothing. I like listening to you talk about your work.”

She blinked, and looked away first. “Don’t get used to it.”

“Too late.”

“You’re annoying.”

“I know. I brought you something else.” He took the sketchbook from under his arm.

“If it’s another coffee I’m charging you rent.”

He opened it and turned it round. It was her bike. Her actual bike, not some sports bike off a poster: the intake, the shape of the front fairing, the angle of the bars, even the scratch by the tank she’d been meaning to fill. The shading on the engine was beautiful. He’d got the metal without making it shine. But it was the moment that caught her. The bike stood alone in the middle of the shipyard road under the lamp, its front wheel turned, its shadow long across the concrete. And beside it there was a space. A space that had had a man in it.

“You did this last night?”

“After you left.”

“You drew all of it?”

“Most of it.”

“What’s missing?”

He looked at her. “You. I couldn’t get it right.”

“That’s a terrible line.”

“I know.”

“You can’t draw a woman?”

“I can draw a woman. I don’t think I was looking at the right things.” He looked at the empty space.

She took the sketchbook out of his hands before he could see her face, and carried it to the string she’d stretched between two nails over the bench, where she kept engine diagrams and race times and a faded photograph of her first bike. She found a clip and pegged the drawing up beside them.

He was trying hard not to look pleased.

“It’s all right,” she said.

“All right?”

“You’ve got the rear suspension wrong. It sits lower. I dropped it.” She pointed.

He leaned in and studied it seriously. “You’re right. I’ll draw it again.”

“The whole thing?”

“If you don’t mind.”

She shrugged. “Do what you want.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At half past eleven a skinny boy in a grey hoodie with a big yellow flower on the front came round the door with a plastic bag. “Jinx! I came to ask about my—”

He stopped dead. The bag sagged in his hand. He’d seen Raiden.

Raiden looked up. Their eyes met. A second went by, and the boy took one step backwards.

“What?” said Jinx.

“Nothing. Uh. I just remembered I have to—” The boy had gone pale.

“Xiao Pan. You came to ask about your bike.”

“Yes. Bike. Very important. Another day.” He put the bag down carefully on the nearest stool as if it might go off, never once taking his eyes off Raiden. Raiden had become extremely interested in the drawing on the string.

“Leaving already?” said Raiden pleasantly.

The boy nearly jumped. “Yes.”

“Shame.”

Xiao Pan gave Jinx a look that tried to say a whole paragraph, and fled. She turned round.

“Do you know him?”

“Who?”

“Don’t play stupid.”

“The young man who just left? I don’t believe we’ve been introduced.”

“You’re lying.”

“Am I?”

“He looked like he’d seen a ghost.”

“Perhaps I’m frightening.”

“You’re not frightening. You’re irritating. Seriously.” She folded her arms.

He considered his answer. “I’ve seen him around. He delivers flowers.”

“That’s very informative.”

“I try.”

She threw a rag at him. He caught it, smiling, and she hated that she was already starting to recognise that particular smile.

✦ ✦ ✦

By lunchtime he’d become part of the garage. Not officially. He wasn’t allowed to touch anything, and she’d told him three times he was standing in the wrong place. But he’d moved his crate next to the bench and seemed perfectly content to sit on it and watch her change the brake pads on somebody’s commuter bike.

“Why that wrench?”

“Torque wrench. The bolts go to a number. Too loose and something lets go. Too tight and you strip the thread or crack the caliper.”

“That makes sense.”

“Of course it does.”

She was different when she was concentrating. The sharpness stayed, but her hands went easy, reaching for things without looking, and she could hear a fault most people wouldn’t notice until it killed them. There was grease to her elbows and her hair was coming out of its tie and she looked entirely at home. He smiled.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“You’re looking at me again.”

“I thought I was allowed.”

“Not when you’re being creepy.”

He laughed. “Understood.”

“Do you actually have a job?” she said, without looking up.

“I’m a draftsman. For a practice on the forty-first floor of a tower called Meridian. I draw what the architects meant, so the builders don’t put the stairs where they wanted the window.”

“Buildings. How boring.”

“They can be. Mostly I argue with contractors and make sure nobody takes out a wall because they don’t like where it is.”

She snorted. “Customers are stupid.”

“Architects say that about clients.”

She laughed. It was becoming a problem.

At two Mrs. Tong came in from the noodle shop two doors down with a covered pot. She was small and old and had known Jinx since Jinx was fifteen and turning up at her back door with oil on her face. “Jinx! I brought your lunch.”

“Auntie, I told you not to bring food.”

“And I told you you don’t eat.”

Then she saw Raiden, who’d stood up the moment she came in. Her eyes went from him to Jinx and back, and brightened enormously.

“Oh. Ah.”

“Don’t,” said Jinx.

“Who’s this?”

“Nobody.”

“Raiden Lin. Good afternoon, Auntie,” said Raiden.

“Are you a friend?”

Jinx opened her mouth. He got there first. “Not yet.”

She turned round so fast she nearly dropped the wrench. “Excuse me?”

“Would you prefer acquaintance?”

Mrs. Tong laughed until she had to hold the bench. “Oh, he’s polite. Sit, sit. I’ll get another bowl. It’s beef brisket. Have you eaten?”

“Not yet. Thank you, Auntie,” he said.

“You don’t have to eat here,” said Jinx.

“I’d love to.”

“You don’t even know what’s in it.”

“Does it matter?”

Mrs. Tong beamed and went for a bowl. Jinx pointed at him with the wrench. “Don’t get comfortable. You’re not my boyfriend.”

“I know. Not yet.” He sat down on the crate.

She threw the rag again. He caught that too.

There was far more brisket than two people could eat. He ate it politely and thanked Mrs. Tong three times and listened to all her stories about the street. Jinx ate fast, interrupting to complain about a customer. Then Mrs. Tong noticed he’d moved every piece of choy sum to one side of his bowl, and reached over with her chopsticks and tapped the rim.

“Eat your greens.”

He looked at the greens. He looked at Mrs. Tong. “Yes, Auntie,” he said, and ate them.

Jinx stared at him. “How old are you?”

“Twenty-three.”

“And you still get told to eat your vegetables?”

“Apparently.”

“Good boy. He’s handsome,” said Mrs. Tong, and leaned over to Jinx and said, not quietly.

“Auntie.”

“And polite. And he eats. And he looks at you nicely.”

Jinx put her chopsticks down. “I’m going back to work.”

Mrs. Tong laughed so hard she had to cover her mouth. Raiden, who’d heard every word, drank his tea and looked extremely pleased with himself.

✦ ✦ ✦

The afternoon was busy. A carb that wouldn’t idle. A set of brakes. A bike with an exhaust leak whose owner swore it had got louder by itself. Raiden stayed. He carried a heavy toolbox when she asked and moved it again when she told him it was in the wrong place. He didn’t flinch when she swore at a seized bolt. When a man came in and said women shouldn’t be working on performance engines, Raiden didn’t say a word. He sat on his crate and watched her strip the man’s carburettor, find the blocked jet, and explain it in such detail that the man went red and apologised.

“You handled that well,” he said, when the man had gone.

“I know.”

“I admire you.”

She faltered. He’d said it as if it were obvious. No joke on the end of it. “Go and admire somebody else.”

“I’d rather not.”

At half past four a man brought in a perfectly good bike and asked for it to be painted gold. She looked at the bike, and at the man. “No.”

“What do you mean, no?”

“I mean I’m not painting it gold. It’ll look terrible.”

“It’s my bike.”

“It’s my shop.”

“I’ll pay double.”

“Still no.”

Behind her Raiden put his hand over his mouth. She looked at him. “Don’t.”

“I’m not saying anything.”

“Your face is.”

When the man had gone off muttering, Raiden said, “I like that you won’t do a thing just because someone offers you money for it.”

She looked down at the rag in her hands. “Money doesn’t make an ugly thing beautiful.”

“No, it doesn’t,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

At half past six he stood up and picked up his bag. “Would Thursday work?”

She went on wiping the bench. “For what?”

“Coffee.”

“You already brought three.”

“I could bring two. Or one.”

She looked at him. He waited. No pressure, no impatience. Just that quiet infuriating smile.

“What do you actually want?” she said.

His face changed a little. “To take you somewhere you don’t have to work.”

She stopped wiping. The garage seemed quiet.

“Thursday,” she said.

He blinked. “What?”

“Thursday. Six. Don’t come here. And don’t look so happy.”

“I’m trying.”

“You’re failing.”

He took a pen out of his pocket. Before she could ask what he was doing he’d taken her hand, gently, and turned it palm up. His fingers were warm. He wrote his number across the middle of her palm in small neat figures.

“What are you doing?”

“In case you change your mind.”

“You’re ridiculous.”

“I’ve been told.” He let go. Then she took the pen out of his hand, pushed his cuff up, and wrote her own number on the inside of his wrist, harder than she needed to.

“So we’re even,” she said.

He looked at his wrist. “Goodnight, Jinx.”

“Thursday. Don’t be early.”

“I’ll try,” he said, and went.

She stood there looking at the empty doorway, and then at her palm. His figures were neat. Almost annoyingly neat. She rubbed at them with her thumb. They didn’t come off.

“Idiot,” she said, and smiled.

✦ ✦ ✦

At 11:03 that night his phone buzzed on the drawing board.

Unknown: Are you asleep?

Raiden: Not yet. Working.

Unknown: On Sunday?

Raiden: Some of us don’t spend all day fixing motorbikes.

Unknown: Some of us have actual jobs.

Raiden: Fair.

Unknown: Thursday. Six. One coffee.

Raiden: One coffee.

Unknown: Goodnight.

He saved the number as Jinx, and under it, in the notes, wrote Thursday. Six. One coffee. The condensed milk one.

Across the city she lay on her bed scrolling back through four messages, and then saved his number. She thought about it. She typed IDIOT, in capitals. Then she turned the photograph on her bedside table face down, her first bike with her father standing beside it, because tonight she didn’t want to think about the past.

She wanted to think about Thursday, and a man who’d bought three coffees because he didn’t know which she’d like, and drawn her bike but not her face, and eaten his greens because an old woman told him to.

“Idiot,” she said into her pillow. For once, she didn’t mean it as an insult.

chapters.title: The Socialite Everyone Ignores
chapters.desc: A gallery on the fortieth floor, a man who plays the fool and counts the exits, and a confession on the fire stairs.
chapters.epigraph: “Nobody shoots the boy who can’t find his own coat.”
chapters.content:
Just after four on Thursday afternoon a courier came to the black door holding a long box at arm’s length, as if it might go off, and picked his way between three stripped bikes and a stack of tyres towards a woman with a ratchet in her hand.

“Jinx? Tai Hing Rope and Canvas?”

“Unfortunately.”

“Sign here. Sender’s R. Lin.”

She shut her eyes. Of course. She signed with a greasy thumb and let him put the box down on the only clean surface in the place, which was a bike seat, and when he’d gone she washed her hands twice and opened it.

Black tissue. Inside it a leather jacket, soft and heavy, high-collared, with discreet armour stitched into the shoulders and elbows. Under the jacket, a pair of black ankle boots in her size, and a card in small neat capitals.

You don’t have to wear these. I just wanted you to have something that fits. R.

She held the jacket up against herself in the lathe guard. It fitted across the shoulders. Nothing fitted across her shoulders. She bought men’s jackets and the sleeves hung over her hands. She found the label, and then the price, and her eyebrows went up into her hair.

Jinx: Are you insane?

Raiden: That’s not a no.

Jinx: Do you know what this costs?

Raiden: Yes.

Jinx: Then why

Raiden: The lining’s coming away at the shoulder of yours. I noticed on Sunday.

She stopped typing and looked at the hook behind the bench. Her own jacket was fifteen years old and had belonged to a man at her father’s shop who’d died. A cigarette burn on the left cuff. A zip that only went up if you held your breath. She hadn’t thought anybody had looked at it closely enough to see the lining.

Jinx: I have a jacket.

Raiden: I know.

Jinx: I don’t need another one.

Raiden: I know that too. I wanted to buy you something.

Jinx: I’m wearing the boots. The jacket stays here.

Raiden: All right.

Jinx: And don’t buy me anything else.

Raiden: I’ll stop.

She put the phone down and picked up the boots. They were beautiful. She hated that.

✦ ✦ ✦

At 5:56 he was on the pavement outside a tower on the harbour front. She came down the slip road on the bike and stopped beside him and pulled off her helmet. Black trousers, a dark shirt, a thin silver chain, the new boots, and her own old jacket over one arm.

He looked at the boots, and slowly upwards. He was in a dark grey suit with a silver waistcoat patterned like the inside of a watch.

“Don’t,” she said.

“I haven’t said anything.”

“Your face has.”

“I was going to say you look beautiful.”

She narrowed her eyes. “That’s worse.”

He laughed and held out his hand for her helmet. She gave it to him and looked up at the tower: forty floors of glass, a stone entrance, men in dark suits by the doors trying not to look like security.

“What exactly are we doing here?”

“A gallery opening. Architectural photographs, some installations, a couple of private collections.”

“Sounds expensive.”

“It is.”

“Sounds boring.”

“That too.”

“Then why are we going?”

“Because I was invited. And I wanted you to come.”

“You make everything sound like a line.”

“Is it working?”

“No.”

“Noted,” he said, and held the door.

The gallery took the top two floors. The lift opened straight into a wide white room full of low music and silk dresses and watches and shoes that cost more than the bike she’d spent three months rebuilding. She looked down at her boots on the marble.

“Are you sure this is the right place? Everybody here owns at least three flats.”

“Some of them own more.”

He offered his arm. She looked at it. “I can walk.”

“I know,” he said, and she walked on ahead, and he followed.

A tall man in charcoal came up before they’d gone five steps. “Raiden! I didn’t think you’d make it.”

“Wouldn’t miss it.”

The man looked at her. “And who’s this?”

“Jinx,” said Raiden, and nothing else. The man waited. She waited. Eventually he smiled and said “Lovely,” and drifted off.

“That’s it?” she said.

“He knows your name.”

“He doesn’t know anything about me.”

“That’s all right,” said Raiden, entirely untroubled.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first twenty minutes were more entertaining than she’d expected, and none of it was the art. It was him. She’d imagined he’d go stiff and polished in a place like this, and talk about architecture the way customers talked about bikes they’d paid too much for. Instead he turned out to have one particular talent. He played stupid. Beautifully.

A woman in cream stopped them beside a model of a waterfront block. “Raiden, darling. What do you think of the terraces? The cantilevers are so ambitious.”

He looked at the model with great seriousness. “Do you think people will fall off?”

The woman blinked. “Well, there’ll be safety measures.”

“Of course, would be a shame otherwise,” said Raiden, and he excused himself and moved on, and Jinx bit the inside of her cheek all the way to the next room.

“Do you actually not know what a cantilever is?”

“Of course I do.”

“Then why ask if people would fall off?”

“She was talking to me as if I’d designed it personally. I thought I’d let her enjoy herself.”

Jinx laughed out loud. He looked delighted.

It went on. In front of a huge iron sculpture a man explained its meaning to him at great length, and Raiden nodded and said it was interesting; he’d thought it might fall over. Somebody asked him whether he preferred minimalism or postmodernism, and he said with total sincerity, “Whichever has better parking.” She had to turn round and look at a wall.

She began to see why people underestimated him. He gave them every chance. He smiled at the wrong moments and asked foolish questions and never once seemed to want to prove he knew more than anyone. Pleasant. Harmless. Almost forgettable on purpose. And Jinx, who’d spent her whole life being underestimated, knew a performance when she saw one. She just didn’t know what it was for.

Then they stopped by a cluster of steel columns leaning into one another at strange angles, and she said, “What’s this meant to be?” and he answered her properly.

“Load. The columns look random, but the weight goes down through every joint to the base. See there? If that were fixed instead of pinned, the whole thing would behave differently.” He crouched to the lowest connection.

She crouched beside him. “So it isn’t just decoration.”

“Not entirely.”

“That joint’ll take a lot of stress.”

“It will.”

“You’d have to reinforce it.”

“Depending on the load, yes. An engineer would run the numbers and tell you how much.”

She nodded, and glanced at him, and saw he wasn’t looking at the sculpture any more. He was looking at the room. The lift lobby. The far wall. The ceiling. The columns that held the floor up. The windows. The fire stairs. It took him perhaps two seconds, and she’d have missed it if she hadn’t been watching his face.

“What are you looking at?”

“Nothing.”

“You’re counting something.”

“Am I? Old habit.” He smiled at the sculpture.

She let it go. For now.

✦ ✦ ✦

The trouble started just after seven by the eastern windows. A group of men came over, and one of them, heavy-faced, with a whisky, knew Raiden, and looked at Jinx the way certain customers did when they thought they could talk to her however they liked.

“Lin. Didn’t expect you here.”

“Mr. Yeung.”

Mr. Yeung looked her up and down, and his eyes stopped on her boots and then on the old jacket over her arm. “Your companion? Interesting choice. Is it a statement? The leather. Very industrial.”

“It’s called clothing,” said Jinx.

He laughed, and his friends laughed with him. “Forgive me. I thought this was rather an exclusive evening. Not everyone’s used to these circles.”

She smiled at him. “You’re right. Some people aren’t used to manners either.”

His smile went stiff. Raiden, who hadn’t said a word, put his glass down. “Jinx. Would you like to see the terrace?”

They walked away. Behind them Mr. Yeung called, “Introduce her properly next time, Lin!” and Raiden turned his head and said pleasantly, “Of course,” and followed her out.

The terrace ran round the building behind a glass rail with the city all lit up below. She leaned on the rail. “Your friends are charming.”

“He isn’t my friend. He works for one of my father’s partners.”

“Your father’s what?”

“Nothing important. Did he upset you?” He looked at her profile.

“No. I’ve heard worse.”

“I know. People like that think expensive clothes make them important,” he said, and something in his voice made her turn. He wasn’t pitying her. He was just looking.

“Do you?”

“No.”

“Good. Because you’re wearing boots I bought you, and I don’t want you getting ideas.”

She laughed despite herself. Then he looked at the glass doors. “Excuse me a moment. I have to say hello to someone.”

“Secret business?”

“Something like that.”

He found Mr. Yeung in the western lounge with two men and a fresh whisky, and asked for a word, and drew him two steps aside. His face stayed perfectly pleasant.

“You’ve a serviced flat near the old financial district.”

The man’s smile slipped. “That’s private.”

“Of course. I only mention it because it was declared vacant last quarter, and the meter says somebody’s living in it. I’m not threatening you. That would be very rude. I’d just be careful about discussing other people’s clothes while your own paperwork’s that untidy.” Raiden straightened his cuff.

He left the man standing there with a drink going warm in his hand and the realisation that somebody had been paying attention, and went back to the terrace without raising his voice once.

“Everything all right?” said Jinx.

“Everything’s fine.”

“Did you do something?”

“No.”

“You’re a terrible liar.”

“Perhaps,” he said. He looked exactly as he had all evening. Calm. Polite. Practically harmless. She didn’t believe it for a second.

✦ ✦ ✦

At two minutes past eight the gallery began to empty, and he took her down a back corridor to the fire stairs. The door shut behind them on the music. A concrete landing, a steel rail, a tall window full of the harbour. For the first time all evening they were alone.

She leaned on the rail. “Better.”

He’d loosened his collar. His hair had come out of whatever he’d done to it. She was looking at him, which was unfortunate, because he was looking at her too.

“What?”

“You’re beautiful.”

“Find a better line.”

“I’m not using a line.”

“Then stop saying things like that.”

“Why?”

“Because— You’re distracting.”

“Sorry,” he said, not sounding it. He’d come closer. Not much. Just enough that she could feel the warmth of him. His hand rested on the rail beside hers, and his eyes went once to her mouth, and she saw them go, and her breath caught.

“You’re doing it again. Looking at me like that.”

“Would you like me to stop?”

She thought about it, and shook her head.

He stepped closer, slowly, giving her every chance to move. She didn’t. His fingers brushed the back of her hand. “Jinx. Can I kiss you?”

She looked at his mouth. “You’re asking?”

“Yes.”

“Then—”

He stopped. She saw him decide something. He took a step back.

“There’s something I have to tell you first.”

Her face went hard. “That sounds promising. Another girlfriend?”

“No.”

“Married?”

“No.”

“Secretly a criminal?”

He almost smiled. “Not exactly. My surname’s Lin.”

“I know.”

“Lin Jian’s. He’s my father,” he said.

She didn’t understand straight away. Then she did. Everybody in the city knew that name. It was on hoardings all along the harbour and on half the cranes she rode past, and in the kind of newspaper story that never quite said what it meant. The Lins of the Walled City. Towers, warehouses, a family that made problems disappear before most people knew they’d existed. She looked at his watch. His shirt. The way nobody tonight had asked what he was doing there.

“You’re Lin Jian’s son.”

“Yes.”

“His only son.”

“Yes.”

She laughed once, not because anything was funny. “You’ve got to be joking.”

“I wish I were.”

“And you’ve been playing stupid all night.”

He leaned his back against the wall, and for the first time that evening he looked tired. “It’s safer. My father built something big, and there are people round it who want a piece. Family. Partners. Men who think standing near money makes them important. When I was small I learned it’s useful to be underestimated. If people think you’re foolish they stop watching you. They talk in front of you. They don’t count you. Nobody shoots the boy who can’t find his own coat.” He looked at the window.

“So you count them instead.”

“I know where the exits are in any room I’m in. I know which columns hold the floor up and where the cameras are and who keeps looking at the door. I know which conversations matter.”

She thought of his eyes going round the gallery, and the ridiculous questions, and the man with the whisky. “And Xiao Pan.”

He didn’t answer straight away. Then he nodded. “He delivers for my sister’s flower shop. Elowen. She married Zhao Zhendong. Xiao Pan thought he’d been caught somewhere he shouldn’t be. I didn’t want to bring any of that into your garage.” He watched the name land. Everyone round the Docks knew it, though nobody said it loudly.

“You brought yourself into my garage.”

“I know.”

“You knew all this before I even said yes to coffee. And you thought I’d be fine finding out on a fire escape?”

“No, I should have told you on Sunday. I was afraid you’d walk away,” he said immediately.

“That’s not your decision to make. You don’t get to decide what I can handle.”

“I know.”

“Then why?”

He didn’t have a clever answer. “Because I liked you. I liked that you didn’t know who I was, and didn’t care. I liked that you told me to get out of your garage without worrying whether I’d take it badly. And I wanted a little longer with that. I wasn’t pretending to be someone else with you. I was still me. I just wasn’t telling you everything.” He looked at her.

“That’s still lying.”

“Yes,” he said. He didn’t defend it. Somehow that made it worse.

She went to the door. He straightened. “Can I take you home?”

“No.”

“All right. Jinx. I won’t follow you. If you don’t want to see me again, I’ll respect that. But if you want to give me one more chance, I’ll be at the garage tomorrow at ten. Have a spanner ready. Any one you like. If you throw it at me, I’ll understand. I’ll go, and I won’t come back, and I won’t ask you to think again.” She had her hand on the handle.

She stared at him. “You’re insane.”

“Probably.”

She went through the door and he didn’t stop her, and when it closed he stayed on the landing a long time.

✦ ✦ ✦

At home she sat on the edge of the bed in her boots, not taking them off. Lin Jian. And Raiden had sat on a crate in her garage eating Mrs. Tong’s brisket and getting told off about his greens. She looked at her palm. The number had washed off days ago. She rubbed the place anyway.

Raiden: Did you get home safely?

Jinx: Yes.

Raiden: Good.

Nothing else. No explaining. No begging.

At 11:38 she was still awake. She got up and went down to the bench and opened the drawer and took out the thirteen-millimetre spanner. Her favourite. Worn at the edges, the chrome gone dull from twenty years of somebody’s hands, and then hers. She turned it over.

“Dramatic idiot,” she said, and put it on the little table by the door, and went back up to bed. Five minutes later she came down and moved it an inch to the left.

Just after twelve she opened his contact. IDIOT. She looked at it, and added a word. RICH IDIOT. It was stupid. She smiled anyway.

Just before ten the next morning she was standing in the garage looking at the spanner on the table by the door. She’d cleaned it, which was ridiculous. She’d wiped the handle, which was more ridiculous. Her phone buzzed.

Raiden: I’m outside.

She looked at the shutter, and at her hands. She honestly didn’t know whether she was going to throw it at him or use it to pull him inside. That was the most irritating thing about Raiden Lin. He’d made her unsure about the one thing she’d always been good at, which was what to do with a tool.

At ten o’clock exactly three soft knocks came on the door.

chapters.title: The First Kiss Smells Like Oil
chapters.desc: She throws the spanner a metre wide. Under her bike, he won’t kiss her until she tells him her real name.
chapters.epigraph: “I said I’d go if you threw a spanner. I didn’t say what happens if you miss.”
chapters.content:
At two minutes past ten on Friday morning, Raiden Lin found out that Jia Cao had excellent aim, and had decided not to use it.

He’d come in under the half-raised shutter with a cardboard tray. She was at the bench with her back to the door. She picked up the thirteen and turned and threw it, hard and flat and spinning, a metre to the left of his head. It hit the brick with a crack like a gunshot and dropped and skidded under a bike.

He didn’t flinch. He looked at the wall, and at the spanner, and at her.

“You missed,” he said.

“I never miss.”

“No. No, I don’t suppose you do.” He said it slowly.

Then he smiled, and it was a new one. It started in his eyes and took its time getting to his mouth, and when it got there it stayed. He crossed the floor and bent and fished the spanner out from under the bike and turned it over in his fingers.

“Your favourite.”

“How do you know?”

“You used it six times on Sunday. You put it back in the same place every time. You’ve looked after it.” He set it on the bench beside her, handle towards her.

“You’ve got a very strange survival instinct.”

“I’ve been told. I said I’d go if you threw a spanner. I didn’t say what happens if you miss.” He put the tray down.

“I wasn’t aiming for you.”

“Of course not.”

“Don’t look at me like that.”

“Like what?”

“Like you think you’re clever.”

“I wouldn’t dare. Good morning, Jinx,” he said.

As if nothing had happened. As if she hadn’t just thrown a spanner past his ear. She picked up a coffee so he wouldn’t see that her hands were shaking.

“Close the door,” she said, and he did, and just like that he was back.

There were four cups in the tray. Black. Milk. Condensed milk. And a fourth.

“What’s that one?”

“In case you want another.”

“Why would I want another?”

“You drank three on Sunday.”

“Because you brought three.”

“Exactly. Don’t start,” he said, and she stared at him, and picked up the condensed milk, and he smiled, and she pointed the cup at him.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t sit on the crate today. He walked round the bikes and asked her things. Real things.

“Why carbs on the old ones? Why not change them to injection?”

“Because I don’t want to. And a good carb isn’t automatically worse. Air goes through the venturi, it speeds up, the pressure drops, and that pulls fuel up through the jet into the air. No computer deciding anything. You can hear it. You can fix it on the side of a road with a screwdriver.” She had a carburettor body in pieces on the bench.

“So simpler.”

“Not simpler to get right. Jets, float height, needle position, the mixture. Cold mornings change it. Height changes it. Injection does it all off sensors. Finer, easier cold starts. But you need the kit and the map. Main jet. That one’s the pilot. Pilot’s idle and the bottom of the throttle. Main does the top. The needle does the middle.” She held up a small brass part.

“Like stages.”

“More or less. You’re actually interested.” She looked at him.

“I like knowing how things work.”

She studied him, and then put something tiny in his palm. “Hold that. Float needle. If it doesn’t seal, fuel keeps coming into the bowl and it floods.”

“Seems very small for something important.”

“That’s because you’ve never had one stick on a motorway.”

He laughed. She took it back and went on working, and for a while neither of them said anything. He watched her hands. She watched the carb. Somewhere between the jets and the teasing the stiffness of the night before began to come undone.

“Can I ask you something?”

“Depends.”

“Why bikes?”

She didn’t answer at once. “Because they make sense. People say one thing and mean another. They promise and change their minds. They make you guess. Engines don’t. If something’s wrong there’s a reason, and you find it, and you fix it. You can hear it. You can feel it through the frame. You can see it on a dyno sheet. Otherwise you’re just guessing.” She wiped her fingers.

“And when it’s right?”

“Then you know.”

He understood more of that than she’d meant him to. “That’s nice.”

“Don’t make it soppy.”

“I wouldn’t dare.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At twenty to twelve she wheeled her own bike onto the lift. “Come here. Help me. Not by the exhaust.”

“I know.”

“Do you?”

They got it onto the stand together, and she raised it to working height and checked the stops, and pulled out a mechanic’s creeper. Then another.

“Two?”

“One’s for you. You’re holding the torch.”

“An important job.”

“Don’t let it go to your head.”

She rolled underneath. He followed, more awkwardly, on his back with the torch. The underside of the bike filled his whole view.

“Left. Too far. Back. There. See the colour? It’s leaking at the gasket. The heat marks it. Near the head a leak can make the sensors lie to you and the whole thing runs rough. You can ask questions, but you don’t touch anything. Especially not that. And don’t move the torch.” She touched the exhaust joint.

“I won’t. Jinx?”

“Hm?”

“Is that your real name?”

The wrench stopped.

“Everybody calls you that. I wondered if it was the only one,” he said.

“Then it’s my name.”

“Is it?”

She didn’t answer.

“All right,” he said.

She looked across at him in the torchlight. “That’s it? You’re not going to ask again?”

“No. I’ve made a rule instead.”

“Oh God.”

“I won’t kiss you until I know your real name.”

The wrench slipped. Not far. Just enough to clink.

“You’re making rules now?”

“Only for myself.”

“Why?”

“Because I want to know who I’m kissing,” he said, perfectly seriously.

She stared at him upside down under her own bike. “You’re a very strange man, Raiden Lin.”

“Thank you.”

“It wasn’t a compliment.”

“I know.”

They worked another twenty minutes. She changed the gasket and checked the joint. He held the torch, mostly in the right place, and once, when she reached for a tool she couldn’t quite get, he put it in her hand before she’d asked.

“You’re learning,” she said.

“I’m observant.”

“Don’t get proud.”

When they rolled out she sat up and pushed her hair off her face and left a streak of grease right across her cheek. He had one along his jaw. She looked at him and laughed.

“What?”

“You look ridiculous.”

She reached for a rag, and then didn’t. She leaned forward and wiped the mark off his jaw with her thumb instead. He went completely still. Her hand stayed a moment longer than it needed to, and then she took it away.

“There.”

“You’ve got some too. May I?”

She hesitated, and nodded. He lifted his hand and drew his thumb along her cheekbone, slowly, as if it were something far more delicate than engine oil. Neither of them moved.

At half past twelve they were still sitting on the floor beside the bike with four mostly empty cups between them, her knee up, his back against the bench.

“You’re still waiting,” she said.

“For your name? Yes.”

“You’re really going to keep that stupid rule?”

“I made it.”

“You could break it.”

“I could. I don’t want you to feel rushed.”

Something went soft in her face. She looked down at her hands: grease under the nails, a small white scar across one knuckle. She rubbed her thumb over it.

“Cao Jia,” she said.

He didn’t move.

“My name. Jia Cao, if you write it the other way round, like they do on forms here. My father called me Jia when he remembered. The men in my father’s shop started calling me Jinx when I was nine. That stuck.” She didn’t look up.

“Cao Jia,” he said. And again, slower, as if he were learning it by heart.

“Don’t make it weird.”

“I’m not. I like saying it. May I kiss you now?” He leaned forward a little.

“You’re asking again?”

“Yes.”

A small reluctant smile. “Yes, idiot.”

He moved slowly. His hand came to her cheek, his thumb under her eye, and he leaned in and stopped just short. “Still yes?”

She grabbed the front of his shirt. “Do you want me to sign something?”

He laughed. “No.”

“Then stop talking,” she said, and kissed him.

It wasn’t graceful. Their noses bumped and she laughed against his mouth, and he smiled, and then she kissed him again and neither of them was laughing. His hand went to the back of her neck, careful. Her fingers twisted in his shirt. It tasted of coffee and, mostly, of oil. He drew back an inch to look at her.

“Why did you stop?”

“Checking you still wanted to.”

She pulled him back by the shirt. “Raiden. Kiss me.”

He did. She shifted closer and their knees knocked, and his hand went from her neck to her waist and she leaned into him, smiling between kisses, and when he tried to draw back again she caught his shoulder.

“Where are you going?”

“Nowhere.”

“Good.”

“You’re very demanding.”

“You’re very slow.”

“Would you like me to hurry up?”

“Please.”

He obliged. The concrete was getting hard under her, so she reached for the creeper behind her and pulled him by the collar onto the other one, and the wheels rolled, and their shoulders banged together, and he laughed outright.

“We’re going to hit something.”

“Then stop moving.”

“You’re the one pulling me.”

“Exactly,” she said, and kissed him again, and the two creepers drifted a few inches across the floor and a wrench went over somewhere with a clatter, and neither of them cared.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Jinx? I’ve brought—”

Mrs. Tong stood in the open doorway with a covered pot. Behind her were two men from the warehouse next door. All three of them had stopped dead.

Jinx was half lying across a mechanic’s creeper with her hand in Raiden’s collar. Raiden was on the other one. Both of them had grease on their faces, and both of them had obviously been kissing.

There was a long silence. Then Mrs. Tong’s face lit up like a lantern. “Oh!”

Jinx shut her eyes.

“Hello, Auntie,” said Raiden politely.

One of the dockers burst out laughing. The other one elbowed him and said, “Finally.”

Jinx sat up. “There’s no finally!”

Mrs. Tong came in and looked at the two creepers and the bike up on the lift and the grease round Raiden’s mouth. “Why are you both on the floor?”

“Working.”

“Working,” said Mrs. Tong.

“Yes, Auntie,” said Raiden.

The dockers had to hold each other up. Mrs. Tong put the pot on the bench. “Well. That’s nice. Yesterday he was not yet your boyfriend.”

Raiden looked at his knees. His shoulders were shaking.

“Don’t you dare,” said Jinx.

“And today?” said Mrs. Tong.

“Still not officially,” said Raiden.

“RAIDEN.”

Mrs. Tong considered him and nodded. “Then it’s almost.”

She turned to Jinx with great satisfaction.

“Now it’s yet,” said Tong.

“That’s not even a sentence!”

“It will be,” said Mrs. Tong, and Raiden laughed, and Jinx, despite every effort, laughed too.

✦ ✦ ✦

By half past one the garage was more or less back to normal. Mrs. Tong had gone. The dockers had gone, still laughing. Jinx had threatened to throw another spanner at anybody who mentioned it. Raiden had his sleeves rolled up and was helping her wipe down the bench, and there was still a trace of grease by his jaw. She took a rag and wiped it. Then his cheek. Then, deliberately, the corner of his mouth.

“May I?” he said.

“You’re getting very comfortable asking that.”

“Is it a problem?”

“Maybe.”

“All right. Who said you could go?” he said, and turned away. She caught his wrist.

He looked back at her smug face, and laughed, and bent and kissed her, and this time she didn’t bump his nose. Progress.

At three he looked at his phone. “I’ve got a meeting.”

“Then go.”

“In a minute.”

“You’ve said that for twenty minutes.”

He collected his things. At the door he turned. “Can I come tomorrow? Coffee.”

“How many?”

“Four?”

“Greedy.”

“Three?”

She thought about it. “Four.”

“Why four?”

“Because I might want four. Ten o’clock. Don’t be late.”

He came back across the floor and kissed her forehead. “Goodbye.”

“That’s a terrible goodbye.”

“Would you like another?”

She caught his shirt. “Obviously.” He kissed her until she’d forgotten whatever she’d been going to say, and she was smiling when he finally went.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the back of a taxi going into the city he opened his sketchbook and wrote at the top of a clean page, in capitals, DYNO. FORTUNE. It was something she’d said under the bike: that a dyno sheet would tell her whether a change had worked, and without one you were only guessing. He liked the certainty of it. The idea that a thing could be measured and tested and known.

He turned the page and began to draw. Two creepers. A bike up on the lift above them. A woman with grease on her cheek and one hand twisted in the front of his shirt. He drew her mouth first. Then her eyes. Then he stopped, and looked at it, and for the first time he didn’t rub her face out. It wasn’t right. But it was closer. Under it he wrote Cao Jia, and then: The first time she let me kiss her.

Just after ten that night her phone buzzed on the floor by the box of bolts she was sorting.

Raiden: Did you eat?

Jinx: Yes, mother.

Raiden: My jaw still smells of engine oil.

Jinx: That’s what happens under bikes.

Raiden: I thought it was the kiss.

Jinx: Don’t get arrogant.

Raiden: Too late.

Jinx: Four coffees. And breakfast. Something good.

Raiden: Of course.

Jinx: Goodnight, Raiden.

Raiden: Goodnight, Cao Jia.

She looked at her name on the screen. It looked different when he wrote it. Not because it had changed. Because someone had finally asked for it, and remembered.

chapters.title: The Van on the Way to Her
chapters.desc: Fourteen days of coffee and goodnights on her step. Then a van on the Docks road, a night at Harbourside General, and the back door.
chapters.epigraph: “I was on the pavement. I promise. I was on the pavement.”
chapters.content:
For fourteen days Raiden Lin brought Jia Cao coffee.

Fourteen days. Four cups every morning at ten, which she drank, all four, while he sat on his crate and drew. By the end of the first week he knew she wanted the condensed milk when she was tired, black when she was working, and the milk one when she was in a mood so bad he’d learned to put it down and step back. He knew which days she forgot lunch. He knew she hated being interrupted halfway through setting a carburettor, that she didn’t talk to engines but listened to them with her head on one side, and that she sometimes fell asleep sitting bolt upright in the broken chair by the bench. At one he went out and came back with Mrs. Tong’s beef and greens on the side. In the evenings he took her to places she’d never been, where the waiters knew him, and ordered for both of them without looking at the menu, and was always right. It was infuriating.

And every night on the step of the black door he kissed her goodnight, with his hands on her face and the cranes lit up over the roofs, and every night she nearly asked him in, and every night he stepped back first.

“Tomorrow.”

On the second Thursday she said it. “Why do you always leave?”

He was already on the bottom step. He turned round. “Because if I come up those stairs I’m not leaving until you throw me out.”

“So?”

“So I want you to be sure you won’t. I’m not in a hurry, Jia. I want all of it. I want it to take years.” He looked at her in the light from the door.

He stepped back. She caught him by the collar before he reached the pavement and dragged him back up the step and kissed him first, hard, against the door frame. The rule didn’t hold. His hands went into her hair and his whole weight came against her and he made a sound in his throat like a man losing an argument with himself. Then he took his mouth away. One inch.

“Tomorrow.”

“That didn’t count,” she said, and let go of his collar.

“It counted a bit.”

“It didn’t count at all.”

He went off up the street laughing. She shut the door and leaned on it with her eyes closed.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Friday the fourth of June she was forty minutes late.

She’d asked him to meet her on the Docks road at nine, by the little all-night shop at the corner of the shipyard road, because she had something to show him. She hadn’t said what. He hadn’t asked. He liked it when she surprised him. Then the new exhaust on her bike had fought her for an hour, and she’d been under it with the radio up and her phone face down on the bench.

He waited outside the shop under the strip light with his hands in his pockets, watching the wind come in off the water. At twenty past nine his phone went.

Jinx: Leaving now. Don’t complain.

He smiled. She wasn’t leaving now. She was still under the bike, and he knew it.

Raiden: Take your time. I’m here. Don’t rush.

At 9:56 he decided the wind off the Docks was colder than it had looked, and crossed to the quiet side of the road to wait under the streetlamp where he’d see her lights first. A van came down from the far end. Its lights swept across the tarmac. He stepped up onto the kerb, and looked down at his phone.

Jinx: Five minutes. Promise.

He was smiling at it when the van came through the junction far too fast. The brakes screamed. He looked up. There was no time to move.

The impact threw him sideways. His phone went skidding away across the road. He hit the ground and everything was noise, and then nothing was.

Somebody was shouting. Somebody was running. “Can you hear me? Don’t move. Don’t move, mate, help’s coming.”

The streetlamp above him was blurred. His chest hurt. His right wrist was lying at an angle wrists didn’t go. He tried to move, and a wave of pain stopped him, and his first thought, clear and practical, was that he needed his phone. Because she was coming. And she’d be furious if she couldn’t find him.

✦ ✦ ✦

Just after ten she came down the shipyard road and he wasn’t at the shop. There were a few people standing at the far junction. Then she saw something on the road, and her stomach dropped. A black phone case, the dull sensible kind she’d once told him an accountant would choose, lying cracked in the gutter under the lamp.

She stopped so hard the rear stepped out.

“Raiden?”

A man by the kerb turned round. “You looking for someone? The one who got hit? Ambulance took him. Harbourside General.”

“Was he awake?”

“I don’t know.”

“Was he—”

She couldn’t finish it. She rang him with her hands shaking. Once. Twice. Three times. In the gutter his phone lit up with her name. She picked it up and put it in her pocket and got back on the bike.

✦ ✦ ✦

Just after eleven she came through the emergency doors at Harbourside General with her helmet still in her hand.

“Raiden Lin. He was brought in. A van.”

“Are you family?” said the woman behind the glass.

“I’m—”

She stopped. What was she? His girlfriend? They’d never said the word. His friend? That was ridiculous. The woman who’d spent fourteen days drinking his coffee and dragging him back up her step by the collar?

“I’m with him,” she said.

“Please wait.”

“He’s alive?”

“He’s being treated.”

“That isn’t what I asked.”

“Please sit down, miss.”

She didn’t sit. She stood at the counter gripping the edge of it until her knuckles went white, until a doctor came through the swing doors. “Mr. Lin? He’s stable. Three cracked ribs, a broken right wrist and a concussion. The scans are clear, no bleeding inside, which is the important thing. We’ll be waking him through the night to check on him.”

The relief went through her so hard she had to hold the counter. “Can I stay with him?”

“Are you family?”

“No.”

The doctor looked at her face. “Let me ask the nurse.”

He was asleep when she went in. A dressing at his temple. His right arm in plaster to the elbow. A monitor counting his heart. He looked pale. Much too pale. She stood in the doorway and couldn’t make herself move. Then she pulled the chair up to the bed and sat and took his left hand. It was warm. That was the first thing that let her breathe.

“Idiot. You absolute idiot,” she said, and her voice cracked.

Forty minutes. If she’d left on time. If she hadn’t stayed under the bike. If she’d told him to come to the garage instead. She shut her eyes. No. She couldn’t think like that.

“You’re supposed to be waiting for me. Not in here,” she told him.

✦ ✦ ✦

Around half past twelve the nurse came to wake him, and his eyes opened, and wandered over the ceiling and found her. “Jia?”

She nearly cried. “I’m here.”

He looked at the room. The dressing. The plaster. The monitor. “Oh. I was on the pavement. I promise. I was on the pavement,” he said urgently, as if it were the most important thing in the world.

“I know.”

“I wasn’t kneeling in the road this time.”

She laughed once, and it came out wrong. “I know.”

“You were late,” he said.

Her face crumpled. “Don’t.”

“Hey. You’re crying.” He tried to lift his hand and the pain stopped him. She caught his left one.

“I’m not.”

“You’re terrible at lying. It isn’t your fault.” He waited until she’d put her forehead down on the back of his hand.

“Please don’t.”

He was quiet. Then he said, “Did you eat?”

She lifted her head. “You’re in hospital. You’ve got cracked ribs. Your wrist’s broken. And you’re asking if I’ve eaten?”

“Have you?”

She started crying properly then. His face went soft. “Oh, sweetheart. Come here. I’m all right.” She leaned in and he kissed her fingers.

“Don’t say that. You’re not all right.”

“Not entirely,” he admitted, and she laughed through it, and said “Idiot,” and he smiled and said that was better.

✦ ✦ ✦

The nurse woke him every two hours, and Jinx was awake for all of them. At three he shivered in his sleep and she took off her old black jacket, the one with the burn on the cuff, and laid it over his legs on top of the thin blanket. At a quarter to four he woke without anybody waking him and said, “Jia? Say my name.”

“Raiden.”

“Again.”

“Raiden.”

“Good,” he said, and shut his eyes, and she understood. He wanted to hear something that wasn’t this room. So she talked. About the exhaust. About the man who wanted his bike gold. About Mrs. Tong, who’d apparently decided he was already family. About the fan in the garage that had started making a noise. And every time he stirred, she said his name, until he slept.

At ten to five he woke again, properly this time, clear-eyed, and lay looking at her with her head on her folded arms on the end of the bed, grease still on her wrist.

“Jia.”

She sat up at once. “What? Pain? Water?”

“My family’s coming. Elowen rang the ward at four. They’ll be here by six. I need you to go before they get here. By the back.”

She didn’t understand. Then she did. “Why?”

“Because I don’t want them to see you here.”

It was said. It landed hard.

“Why?” she said again.

“My father will ask questions.”

“Then answer them.”

“It’s complicated.”

“Then explain it.”

He knew that expression on her. He’d seen it when men talked down to her about her own work: still, trying hard not to show it had gone in. “Please don’t make it harder,” he said.

“Harder for who? Are you ashamed of me?” She looked at the door and back.

“No. No. I don’t want you dragged into it.” It came out at once.

“Into what?”

“My family.”

She laughed, and it wasn’t a laugh. “Your family. You’re asking me to leave.”

He didn’t answer.

She stood. The chair scraped. There were a hundred things she wanted to say: that she’d sat there all night counting his breathing, that she’d seen his phone in the gutter, that she’d never felt so helpless in her life, that she wanted to climb onto that narrow bed and hold him. She said none of them.

“Fine. Get better.”

“I will.”

She went out without looking back, and left her jacket where it was, across his knees.

✦ ✦ ✦

At 5:37 she stood in the car park behind the hospital, where he’d asked her to go, with the sky going grey over the roofs and her hands shaking. She hated that. She hated the smell of the place and the light and the fact that she’d been sent out of a room she’d sat in all night. Most of all she hated that she half understood why. He had a family. A powerful one, in a world she’d never belonged to. And she was the girl from the garage who smelled of petrol, who’d nearly run him over, who’d kissed him under a bike.

She put her helmet on and rode home without her jacket.

✦ ✦ ✦

Just before six the corridor filled up. Lin Jian first, in the black suit, his face held still and his eyes not. Then Elowen. Zhao Zhendong. Evangeline. Eliana in a hoodie with her glasses on top of her head. Elara last, with her hands in her pockets.

“You’re here,” said Raiden.

“Of course we’re here, you idiot. You scared me.” Elowen hugged him round the shoulders, too hard, and he winced, and she let go at once.

His father stood at the end of the bed. “What happened?”

“A van.”

“Did the driver stop?”

“I think so.”

Lin Jian turned his head an inch, and somebody in the corridor went away to find out. He looked back at his son. “You should have rung.”

“I was a bit busy.”

“Don’t joke.” Lin Jian put his hand on Raiden’s good shoulder, and kept it there.

Eliana was the one who noticed the jacket. A nurse had folded it over the back of the chair. Black leather, cut for a woman, worn at the elbows, a cigarette burn on the left cuff, and the faint warm smell of an engine.

“Whose is that?”

“Mine,” said Raiden.

“Since when do you wear a motorbike jacket?”

“Since recently.”

Elara picked it up and looked at the cut of it, and at her brother, and her mouth curved. “Oh.”

“Don’t,” said Raiden.

“There’s someone,” said Eliana, delighted.

Elowen looked from one to the other. Evangeline said nothing at all, and looked at the jacket, and then at Raiden, and nodded once. Lin Jian looked at the jacket, and his face gave nothing away.

Zhao had been standing by the window. He looked at the jacket for four seconds. Then he crossed the room, took it out of Elara’s hands, folded it once, and put it in the bag over his shoulder.

“Hm,” he said, and went back to the window, and nobody asked him anything.

Raiden watched him do it. Zhao didn’t look back.

✦ ✦ ✦

At seven the room went quiet. Elowen had gone to find the doctor. Eliana and Elara were arguing in whispers about who’d stay. His father was on the phone in the corridor. Zhao had gone. Raiden lay looking at the empty chair.

She’d sat in it all night. She’d put her jacket over him when he was cold. And he’d sent her out of the back door like something he didn’t want seen. He’d told himself he was protecting her: from his father’s questions, from Elowen’s curiosity, from the people his family paid to find things out, from a world that had never been kind to people like her. He’d seen her face when she asked whether he was ashamed of her, and he’d let her go anyway.

She hadn’t asked to be protected. He’d never once asked her what she wanted. He’d just decided.

✦ ✦ ✦

At half past eight Jinx sat on the concrete floor of the garage beside her bike. The new exhaust was finished. It ran perfectly. She should have been pleased. Her phone said nothing. His was in her pocket, cracked across the screen, and she’d forgotten it was there. She took it out and put it on the bench and looked at it. Then she picked up the thirteen and threw it into the toolbox with a crash, and wiped her eyes on the back of her wrist, and went back to work.

At nine a nurse lent him her phone. He didn’t need to look the number up. He’d learned it off the inside of his own wrist.

Raiden: It’s me. Your phone was in my pocket. Mine’s in yours, I think.

Raiden: I’m sorry. I shouldn’t have sent you out like that.

Raiden: You stayed all night. I know.

Raiden: I was afraid of what my family would do once they knew. I should have trusted you enough to tell you that.

Raiden: I’m not ashamed of you. Not for one second.

Raiden: I wish you’d stayed.

She read it at the bench, twice. Her face softened. She didn’t answer straight away. She looked at the crate where he always sat, and the ring his coffee had left on the bench, and the drawing pegged on the string: her bike on an empty road, with a space beside it.

Jinx: You don’t get to decide that for me.

Raiden: I know.

Jinx: If you don’t want them to know about me, say so.

Raiden: I want them to know.

Jinx: Then next time don’t send me away.

Raiden: There won’t be a next time.

Jinx: Go to sleep, idiot.

Raiden: Only if you eat.

Jinx: You’re the one in hospital.

Raiden: I can still worry about you.

Elowen came back in and found him smiling at a borrowed phone. “Who are you texting?”

“Someone.”

“Someone with a name?”

He looked at the empty chair. “Cao Jia.”

Elowen’s face changed, and she looked at the chair too. “Oh. Does she know you’re an idiot?” she said.

“She does.”

“Then she’s already very patient,” said his sister, and squeezed his good shoulder.

At 11:47 the borrowed phone buzzed again.

Raiden: One question. When I get out, will you kiss me?

Jinx: Depends.

Raiden: On?

Jinx: Whether you’re still annoying.

Raiden: That’s permanent.

Jinx: Then probably.

He read it three times, and put the phone down on his chest, and shut his eyes. His ribs hurt and his wrist hurt and his head was heavy. But under all of it there was something small and steady. He’d nearly lost the chance to see her again. He wasn’t going to waste it.

And across the city, in a garage that smelled of petrol and warm metal, Jinx sat down on her creeper and finally let herself cry. Not because he was gone. Because he was still here, and she wanted him home.

chapters.title: A Bike That Goes Twenty Kilometres an Hour
chapters.desc: Three weeks of silence, then Zhao at her door with her jacket and two sentences. She builds a pale green bike that won’t go past twenty and rides it into his lobby.
chapters.epigraph: “If you’re going to draw in roads, you do it on this.”
chapters.content:
For three weeks Jia Cao didn’t answer a single one of Raiden Lin’s calls.

She read his messages, though. That was the unfortunate part. She read every one, on the lock screen, without opening them, which was completely different.

Raiden: Good morning. I’ve been told hospital coffee is legally classed as a punishment.

Raiden: Elowen says I’m not allowed to complain about the food because I’m lucky to be alive.

Raiden: I tried drawing left-handed. I think I’ve invented a new architectural style. It’s called Collapse.

Raiden: I miss your garage.

Raiden: I miss you more.

She turned the phone face down on the bench and let it buzz itself across the wood until it fell off the edge.

On the tenth day he rang. She watched it ring. On the eleventh he rang again, and she watched that too. On the fourteenth he sent a photograph of his plastered wrist held up beside a paper cup.

Raiden: The doctor says I have to be patient.

Jinx: Then listen to the doctor.

It was the first thing she’d said to him in two weeks. She looked at it after she’d sent it as if somebody else had typed it.

Raiden: I am. She isn’t as pretty as you.

She didn’t answer. On the eighteenth day he stopped ringing, which was worse. She told herself it wasn’t. She told herself she was busy. She didn’t need a rich idiot with a broken wrist and a family who could turn a hospital room into a board meeting. She especially didn’t need to miss him.

And every evening when she pulled the shutter down she caught herself looking at the crate by the bench where he used to sit, drinking tea out of his battered flask and asking questions that were sometimes intelligent, smiling at her as if the whole world had narrowed down to one woman with grease on her face. She hated that crate. She hated him a little. Mostly she hated herself for missing him.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the twenty-first day a car stopped in the street. Not a taxi. Something heavy that idled like a cat. When she looked up from under the red two-stroke there was a man in the doorway.

Tall. Rings. A beige suit with the collar open. A face that didn’t move unless it chose to. She’d never met him. She knew the face the way everybody round the Docks knew it, from across a street, and nobody said the name loudly. Zhao Zhendong.

He looked at her for four seconds. Then he came in and put a folded black leather jacket down on the bench, the one with the burn on the cuff, and stepped back from it.

“Yours,” he said.

She stood up slowly, wiping her hands. “Why have you got it?”

“Somebody had to take it off the chair.”

“Did he send you?”

“No.” He’d already turned to go.

“Zhao. Is he all right?” It came out before she’d decided.

He stopped at the door, and for the first time something like a smile went across his face. “He’s been unbearable,” said Zhao Zhendong, and got back into his car, and the car went away up the street of rope shops as if it had never been there.

She stood a long time with the jacket in her hands. Then she hung it on the back of the crate, and went back to work.

✦ ✦ ✦

The idea came from a stupid customer, the way her best ideas usually did. He brought her a photograph of an electric bike off the internet and said he wanted one like it, only faster, unique, something to make his friends sick.

“How fast?”

“Very fast. A hundred and fifty?”

“Then buy a motorbike.”

“I want something unique.”

“Then buy a painting,” she said, and he left offended. She watched him go. Then she looked at the frame that had been leaning against the back wall since February: a small light electric commuter she’d bought off a scrap man and never found a use for. She went and ran her hand along the top tube. And slowly, she smiled.

Three days later it was stripped. Five days later the motor was in. In a week she had a battery tucked under the frame and a controller hidden behind the seat tube and a panel of pale green bodywork drying on the bench. Mrs. Tong came in one afternoon while she was testing it up and down the street and stood watching with her arms folded.

“That’s not a motorbike.”

“It’s electric.”

“That’s not an explanation.”

“It’s a vehicle.”

“It looks like a tram. Pretty colour, though,” said Mrs. Tong, and that was its name.

It was. The pale green of new leaves after rain, sanded between every coat until the light ran down it like water. The motor was modest. The battery was small. And the controller had a limit written into it that nobody would ever get round. Twenty kilometres an hour. Not twenty-one, not twenty-two. Twenty. She could have built it to do a hundred. She built it to go not much faster than a man walking briskly, and put a wire basket on the front, and a small silver bell. It was absurd. It was impractical.
