In her professional opinion it was beautiful. And it had one destination.

On the twenty-seventh day she texted him.

Jinx: Are you still alive?

Raiden: I’ve been waiting three weeks for you to ask.

Jinx: That’s a dramatic way to say yes.

Raiden: It’s been a dramatic month. A van was rude to me.

Jinx: Are you at work?

Raiden: Yes.

Jinx: Don’t move.

Raiden: That’s not a difficult instruction. The doctor has been clear.

✦ ✦ ✦

Meridian Tower wasn’t the kind of building where people arrived on a pale green garden ornament. Glass and steel and dark stone, a lobby floor you could see your face in, a reception desk like a sculpture, and security men chosen for looking dangerous without moving. At sixteen minutes past two on Friday the second of July, Jinx rode the tram through the revolving door’s wide side panel at a leisurely twenty kilometres an hour, in her old jacket and boots, and stopped in the middle of the marble.

A guard stood up. “Miss, vehicles aren’t permitted in the lobby.”

“Then it’s not a vehicle. Tell Raiden Lin that Jinx is here,” said Jinx.

On the forty-first floor the practice’s receptionist put her head round the door of the drawing room, where Raiden was bent left-handed over somebody else’s section. “Mr. Lin? There’s a woman downstairs on a bicycle. She says her name’s Jinx.”

He put the pen down slowly. “She’s here?”

He stood up too fast and his ribs caught and he winced, and the receptionist said, “The doctor said—” and he said, “Please hold the lift,” and was already walking.

The doors opened on the ground floor and there she was beside a small pale green bike in the middle of the lobby. He stopped. He looked at her, and at the bike, and back at her, as if he couldn’t decide which to look at first. He was thinner. His right arm was still in plaster and he was moving carefully. He was trying hard not to look too happy, and failing completely.

“Hi,” she said.

“Hi.”

She tapped the handlebar. “I brought you something.”

“What is it?”

“Your transport.”

He came closer. “It has a basket.”

“Useful.”

“And a bell.” He pressed it with his left thumb. It went tring. He stared at it and began to laugh and stopped at once, holding his side.

She pointed at him. “Don’t.”

“Why is it so small?”

“Because you’re not allowed to fall off it.”

“How fast does it go?”

“Twenty.”

“Twenty?”

“If you’re going to draw in roads, you do it on this,” said Jinx.

His face went soft all at once. “You built this for me.”

“Somebody had to stop you walking into traffic.”

He laughed again this time. Then he looked at her properly. “You came.”

Her smile faded a little. “Yes.”

“I didn’t think you would.”

“I know.”

He tried it in the end, in front of three security men and a receptionist, slowly, once round the lobby: three metres, a stop, a backward look of total delight. “Jia. I think it’s broken.”

“It isn’t.”

“It’s barely moving.”

“That’s the point.”

He rode it all the way round the fountain at twenty kilometres an hour, which he could have beaten on foot if he’d been in a hurry, and he didn’t hurry, and he looked about twelve.

✦ ✦ ✦

The security team let the tram go up in the service lift after Raiden informed them it was a company asset. Jinx laughed all the way up.

His flat was on the forty-third, which apparently came with being the chairman’s son whether or not you’d asked for it. She stood at the window and looked down at the city and then turned round. “We need to talk.”

He sat down carefully on the edge of a sofa. “Yes.”

“Why didn’t you tell me?”

He knew what she meant. He looked at his hands. “I was afraid you’d become a target.”

“Because you like me?”

“Because I love having you in my life. People know my name, Jia. They know my father’s. They know Elowen’s, and who she married. Some of them watch us because they want something from the family and some because they want to hurt it. When I was small I was hidden. Not for a week. For years. On a farm a long way north, with a woman who wasn’t my mother, and no photographs, and no school friends, and nobody allowed to know I was anybody’s son. I came home when I was ten. What I learned there was that the way you keep something is you make sure nobody knows you’ve got it. So the minute I knew how much I wanted you, I started thinking about all the ways someone could use you against me. And I hid you. In a car park at five in the morning.” He didn’t take it back or turn it into a joke. He was quiet a moment. He looked up.

She didn’t speak. “So you decided to make me disappear first.”

“Yes. It was wrong.”

“You don’t get to decide what I’m strong enough for. You don’t get to keep me in a separate box because you think it’s safer. And you don’t get to hold my hand all night and then send me out the back like something you’re ashamed of.”

“I’m sorry.”

“I don’t need you fearless. I don’t need you to pretend your family’s simple. I don’t even need you to tell me everything at once. But stop treating me like a problem you can solve without asking me.”

“You’re right.”

“I’m still angry.”

“How angry?”

She thought about it. “Enough to hit you with the bell.”

“Fair,” he said.

She sat down beside him, leaving a space. “Terms. Your family has their side and I have mine. Your people don’t come to my garage. They don’t follow me, they don’t ask about me, they don’t send someone to check I’m safe. And you don’t send me away again.”

“Never.”

“Don’t promise what you can’t control.”

“I can control that. If there’s a risk I’ll tell you, and we’ll decide together.”

She studied him, and nodded. “Good.”

He looked down at his plaster. “There’s one more thing. I made a rule. While my wrist’s in plaster, I don’t kiss you.”

She turned her head slowly. “Who made that rule?”

“Me. Because I can’t hold you properly.”

She laughed in his face. “You are genuinely the stupidest man I’ve ever met. Do you want to kiss me?”

The teasing went out of him. “Yes.”

“Then ask.”

“May I kiss you?”

“What about your rule?”

He sighed. “Apparently I’m going to break it.”

“Good,” said Jinx.

He leaned in with his left hand light at her waist, and didn’t draw her any closer until she moved into him, and then he kissed her, carefully, with three weeks of silence and hospital lights between them. She put her hand on his cheek and he made a small sound, and she smiled into his mouth.

“Careful,” she said.

“You came here.”

“To give you a bike. Now I’m leaving.”

His whole face fell. She laughed. “Idiot,” she said, and pulled him back by the shirt.

✦ ✦ ✦

He asked her to stay. Just that night, he said. She didn’t have to forgive him or decide anything. He only didn’t want to wake up and find her gone again.

“Yes. But you’re not allowed to be dramatic about it. And if you hurt yourself, I’m leaving,” she said.

He cooked for her one-handed in a kitchen where every knife pointed the same way: eggs and rice and greens and a small soup, slower than usual, cheating with his right hand when he thought she wasn’t looking, until she told him off. Then she found the rolled drawings by the low table in his sitting room and wanted to see them, so he spread one on the floor, a block of flats, and she lay on her front over it.

“Why does that wall look like a corridor?”

“Because it’s meant to.”

“You’re hiding something in it.”

“That’s the idea. A strong room. The building has to work whether anybody knows it’s there or not.”

“Even your buildings have secrets. Do you ever get tired of hiding?” she said, and then.

His smile went. “Yes.”

“Then stop. Not all at once. Start with me.”

He was quiet. Then he nodded, and she reached up and kissed him, and this time it didn’t stop. Her hand went into his hair. His good arm came round her waist and he lay down beside her on the floor among his drawings, careful of his ribs, and she pushed herself up and looked down at him.

“Does it hurt?”

“A little.”

“Then lie still, and let me,” she said.

She undid his shirt one button at a time and put her palms flat on his chest, and felt his breath catch under them. She took off her own shirt, and he looked at her as if she were the only drawing in the room worth keeping, and lifted his left hand and touched her, slowly, her collarbone, her breast, the curve of her waist, all one-handed and so careful she wanted to shake him. She unbuckled him herself. He said her name, the real one, and she kissed him quiet. Then she climbed astride him on the paper with the city burning in the window behind her and took him into her, slowly, watching his face, and he shut his eyes and opened them again as if he couldn’t bear to miss it. She moved over him, unhurried at first, her hands braced on the floor either side of his head, his one good hand gripping her hip, the plaster lying useless and white against the drawings. He tried to lift up into her and his ribs stopped him, and she laughed against his mouth and said “Lie still,” and set the pace herself, deeper, until he couldn’t talk at all. When she came it was with her forehead pressed to his and his name in her throat, and he followed her a moment later, holding on to her as if she were the only fixed point in the world.

Afterwards they lay on a crumpled section of somebody’s block of flats, and she started laughing.

“What?”

“You’re going to have to redraw that.”

“Worth it,” said Raiden.

Later he walked her to his bedroom, slowly, and she asked whether he was all right, and he said yes, and asked her again whether she wanted to stay. She answered him by taking his face in both hands and kissing him, and the door shut behind them, and the second time was slower still, in his bed, his plaster on a pillow and her drawing a small green bike on it in ballpoint with her tongue between her teeth before she let him touch her.

✦ ✦ ✦

She woke first. He was asleep on his side facing her, his good arm loose round her waist, and his face had nothing in it at all. No exits being counted. No careful smile. No pretending to understand less than he did. Just Raiden. She brushed his hair off his forehead and his eyes opened, confused for a second, and then they found her and he smiled.

“You’re still here.”

“Did you expect me to vanish?”

“I hoped you wouldn’t.”

He was quiet a while. “Can I tell you something? I think I like the bike.”

“You’re welcome.”

“And I think I like the person who built it. She’s difficult. She ignores messages. She throws tools.”

“Only when I miss.”

“I love her,” he said.

She went still. He didn’t take it back. He waited. She looked at him a long time, and then she leaned over and kissed him, and against his mouth she said, “I know.”

“That’s all?”

“For now.”

He laughed and his ribs caught, and she pointed at him. “Don’t.”

Just after nine her phone buzzed on the bedside table.

Mrs. Tong: Where are you? I have your breakfast.

She held it up to him. “She knows.”

“I might have mentioned I was hoping you’d come.”

She threw a pillow at him. It hit his good shoulder, and he laughed out loud, and despite his ribs and his wrist and everything else, Raiden Lin had never in his life been so happy to be hit with something.

“Idiot,” she said.

“Your idiot?”

She thought about it. “Unfortunately.”

chapters.title: Her Father’s Chop Shop
chapters.desc: His plaster comes off and he rides pillion for the first time. From a roof she shows him her father’s chop shop under the flyover. He goes home and maps every way out of it.
chapters.epigraph: “First word I ever read was torque.”
chapters.content:
The first thing Raiden Lin did with his right hand, the afternoon the plaster came off, was try to pick Jia Cao up. The second was find out she was a great deal harder to lift than he’d planned.

“Put me down.”

“Wait. I’ve nearly got you.”

“You’ve got my jacket.”

He looked. He had. His left hand had a fistful of the back of her jacket and his newly freed right one had missed her waist entirely, and she was standing in front of him with her arms folded, looking profoundly unimpressed.

“That went better in my head,” he said.

“Your head was concussed two months ago. I wouldn’t trust it.”

He laughed and tried again, properly, both arms, and lifted her clean off the garage floor, and she grabbed his shoulders with a sound she would later deny making. “Raiden!”

“There.”

The wrist was thin and pale and strange, like something kept in a drawer, and the doctor had said rebuild it slowly. The ribs had knitted. The only thing left of the van was a thin scar through his left eyebrow where the kerb had opened it. He’d been waiting six weeks for this.

“Put me down. You’re showing off.”

“Terribly. Can I keep holding you?”

“You’ll break it again.”

“You’re not that heavy.”

Her eyebrows went up. “Excuse me?”

“I mean you’re very easy to carry.”

“That’s worse. Idiot.” She caught his collar and pulled his face down. He kissed her, and she kissed him back with a hand in his hair, and when he finally set her down he did it with great reluctance, and she straightened his shirt.

“Congratulations. You can lift things. I’ve got a list. First, you’re taking me somewhere.” She picked up her helmet and held out the spare.

“Where?”

“You’ll see.”

“Should I be worried?”

“Probably.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He’d never been afraid of motorbikes. He respected them. He understood the engineering, the balance, why a rider leans into a corner, why a machine feels steady at one speed and nervous at another. Understanding one and sitting on the back of one with Jia Cao driving were different things.

“You’re sure?” he said, looking at the pillion seat, which was much smaller than he’d hoped.

“You’re not made of glass.”

“I was recently made of plaster.”

“Don’t tell me you’re scared.”

“I’m assessing the available space.”

“Draftsman.”

“Mechanic.”

She tapped the seat. “Get on. Hold on. Not like that. Properly. Don’t lean on me at lights. Don’t try to help me steer. If I say move, move.”

“Yes, ma’am.”

The first corner made his arms tighten. The second made him laugh. By the long straight past the industrial estate he was laughing so hard she could feel it all the way through her back. “What?” she shouted.

“Nothing! This is wonderful!”

The city went past in wide strokes of sun and concrete and warehouses and trees shoving up through the pavement. It wasn’t the controlled laugh she knew from his drawing office, or the polite one he used at dinner tables when people said stupid things. It was unguarded, almost a boy’s. He put his cheek against her shoulder for a second. “Again!”

“You don’t get another go just because you liked it. I’ve got somewhere to be.”

“Can we go the long way?”

“No.”

“Please?”

At the next junction she took the long way. He laughed the whole of it.

✦ ✦ ✦

They stopped at a drinks stall by the old railway line and sat on a low concrete wall with two cold teas.

“You’re very happy,” she said.

“I am. I’ve never done that before.”

“Never?”

“Not on a motorbike. A tractor, once. On the farm.”

“A tractor.”

“It was a very good tractor.”

“Did you laugh on that?”

“No. It went at about twenty. I’ve got a bike like that now.” He looked at her sideways.

She laughed and nudged his knee. “What was it like? The farm.”

“Quiet. Too many chickens. A vegetable patch they kept escaping into. A barn whose roof leaked whenever it rained. A dog that slept outside it, brown and ugly, that I named Architect.” He thought about it.

“Why?”

“He was always digging holes.”

“That isn’t architecture.”

“He was creating negative space.”

She nearly choked on her tea, and he looked pleased with himself, and went on. Auntie Lan, who wasn’t his aunt but his mother’s cousin, and who’d raised him, and who made a soup so terrible that he ate it every night for years because she was old and frightening. The tractor that only started if you did a particular thing with your foot. The first gate he’d ever mended. Drawing buildings on the backs of feed invoices, because there wasn’t any proper paper.

But whenever she asked about the end of it, his answers got shorter.

“How did you get back?” she said eventually.

He looked into his cup. “I walked.”

“From the north?”

“Yes. One day I’ll tell you that part.” He smiled, not very well.

She looked at him. “All right.”

“You’re not going to ask?”

“I could. But you don’t have to tell me everything before you’re ready. Besides, I want to hear more about the dog.” She nudged his knee again.

He laughed. “Architect was a menace,” he said, and told her.

✦ ✦ ✦

Just before sunset she turned off the main road under the flyover and took a narrow lane that ran behind a row of warehouses, and he noticed everything change. Older buildings. A surface patched three times over old concrete. Drains along the edges, some grated and some open and black. A tyre shop. A welding shed. A food stall with three plastic tables. She stopped by a rusted stair on the side of a low building.

“Get off. Come on.”

The stair had lost most of its paint. They went up two flights onto a flat roof that looked across the lane, and there, under the huge grey belly of the flyover, was a workshop. Bikes outside, some whole, some down to frames. Stacked tyres. Steel shelving. A roller shutter half up. A man in a vest smoking by the door, another under a frame, a third by a van with its back doors open. It was noisy, but not the way an honest shop was noisy. No rhythm. No order. Just metal being moved and engines tried and voices going up and down under the road.

His eyes went round it. The shutter. The side door. The passage behind. The open drain. The stair on the next warehouse. Then he looked at her.

“Is this it?”

“My father’s place.”

“That’s a chop shop,” he said.

“Yes.” No pride in it and no shame. A fact.

She leaned her elbows on the parapet and watched it a long time before she said anything.

“When I was little I thought it was an ordinary garage. I thought everyone had a place like this. My father came home smelling of oil and cigarettes. Sometimes he brought parts home. Sometimes money. I liked the parts. I used to sit on the floor and take things apart. Radios. Fans. Clocks. My mother hated it. She wanted a proper girl. Nice dresses. Nice shoes. Things that didn’t leave grease on you. I was terrible at all of it.” Her mouth moved.

“I can imagine.”

“Don’t agree too fast. She left when I was small. I don’t remember the day. I remember the suitcase. Blue, the hard kind. She packed it while he was downstairs. I asked where she was going and she said she needed some time. People always say that when they don’t want to say they’re leaving.” She looked down at the shutter. A short laugh.

“Did she come back?”

“No. After that it was him and me. Mostly.” It left no room for another question.

He heard the word. He let it lie.

“When I was eight I found a manual under the bench down there. An old workshop manual for a twin from the seventies. Cover torn off, half the pages stained, somebody’s notes in the margins in pencil. I couldn’t understand most of it. I loved the drawings.”

“Exploded views.”

“Yes.”

“I thought you might.”

She said, “First word I ever read was torque. I didn’t have many books. Manuals were easy to get. I learned part numbers and torque figures and wiring before I could tell you what was wrong with a person.”

“You still do that.”

“Probably. That’s why they called me Jinx down there. The first car I stripped on my own, at nine, the police found every part of it inside a week, and after that nothing I’d touched ever sold. Before that they had other names for me. Jinx was better.” She tapped the parapet.

His face changed, and she was already looking away.

“Something happened when I was seventeen,” she said.

He didn’t move.

Down in the lane a bike started. The man by the door flicked his cigarette into the drain. She watched the place as if the noise came from some other year.

“I don’t want to tell you what.”

“All right.”

“You’re not going to ask?”

“I’m curious. But you said you don’t want to tell me,” he said.

She looked at him. He wasn’t pretending not to care, and he wasn’t telling her it didn’t matter. He was just letting the line stand where she’d drawn it.

“It changed things,” she said.

“I believe you.”

“You don’t even know what it was.”

“I know it changed things.”

Her jaw set. “After that I stopped going down there. I can work on bikes from there. I can talk to people who come from there. I can even talk about it. But I don’t go down.”

“Why bring me?”

“Because you keep trying to understand where I’m from. And I wanted you to see it. Not all of it. Enough.”

“Thank you.”

“Don’t make it important.”

“It is,” he said, and didn’t add anything.

The sun went behind the flyover. The workshop lights came on.

“Is your father still in there?” he said.

“Yes.”

“Does he know you’re here?”

“No.”

“Does he know about me?”

“No.”

“All right.”

“You’re very well behaved today.”

“I’m trying to impress you.”

“You’re doing a terrible job.”

“Can I try again?”

She took him by the shirt and kissed him. Nothing gentle or careful about it: hard and sudden, her fist in his collar as if she needed something solid to hold on to, and after a surprised sound he kissed her back with one hand at her waist and the other on the parapet. He forgot the height and the lane and everything down there, and there was only her mouth and her fingers at the back of his neck and the feeling that she was trying to tell him something without using any words.

Then his foot slid. The edge of his shoe went over the lip of the parapet and his weight went with it.

“Raiden!”

She had him by the shirt and hauled him back, and he stumbled into her, and his hand hit the wall. For one long second neither of them moved. Then he looked down. Two storeys.

“What is wrong with you? Your foot was over the edge!”

“I know.”

“Then why were you standing there?”

A small helpless smile. “Because you kissed me.”

She hit him in the chest, not hard. “Don’t.”

He laughed, and then saw her face, which was furious and frightened both, and stopped laughing. “Hey. I’m sorry.”

Her fingers were still knotted in his shirt. “Don’t scare me like that.”

“I won’t.”

She put her forehead against his chest, and he put his arms round her, carefully and completely, and kissed her hair. After a while she said into his shirt, “You’ve got terrible balance. Draftsmen are meant to understand gravity.”

“We do. We just underestimate it now and then.”

She laughed once, and he held her until her breathing settled.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t ask to see the shop again on the way down. He didn’t ask what had happened at seventeen. At the bottom of the stair she handed him the helmet.

“You’re quiet.”

“I’m thinking.”

“About?”

“Your father’s shop.”

She frowned. “Me bringing you doesn’t mean you have to do anything.”

“I know. Can we go the long way?” he said.

She sighed, and started the bike, and he got on, and this time he didn’t laugh so much. He held her, and watched the city go past.

✦ ✦ ✦

Just before eleven he was home, showered, at his desk, with a blank document open on the laptop. He typed a heading. WORKSHOP UNDER THE FLYOVER. He looked at it. He didn’t know who owned it, or whose name it was registered under. He deleted it and wrote: SHOWN TO ME BY JIA. AUGUST 2021. Then he opened a map.

By 11:08 he’d marked the main road. By 11:17 the lane behind the warehouses. By 11:24 the stair to the roof. By 11:39 the open drain. By 11:51 the passage between the welding shed and the building next to it, which didn’t appear on any public map. He made notes. Main access: flyover lane, heavy traffic, poor sightline from the east. Second access: service lane behind the warehouse row. Roof: external stair, two flights, rail damaged, no light at the top. Drain: open along the south boundary; covered by the tyre shop.

He leaned back. He knew exactly what he was doing. That was the trouble. He’d spent his whole life learning to read a building before he walked into it: where it would hold, where it wouldn’t, where a door was hidden, where a person could be trapped. It was his work. It was also the life he’d been raised for. And tonight he was doing it because she’d stood on a roof and said that something had happened to her at seventeen that had made her stop going down a set of stairs.

He opened another layer. The nearest junctions. The bus stop. The open road past the flyover. The route to her garage. The route to the nearest hospital.

Just after twelve his phone lit up.

Jinx: Home?

Raiden: Yes. You?

Jinx: Yes.

Raiden: Thank you for today.

Jinx: You already said that.

Raiden: I meant it twice.

She sent a photograph of a small green screw in her palm.

Jinx: Found this in your helmet. Your bike’s falling apart.

Raiden: It was built by a irresponsible mechanic.

Jinx: I want a refund.

Raiden: I’ll pay in coffee.

Jinx: Four.

Raiden: Always four.

Jinx: Goodnight, Raiden.

He put the phone down and went back to the map. By one o’clock the document was six pages. Every road. Every door he could see. Every alley that joined the lane. Every drain. A small red circle on the roof where she’d stood beside him. He looked at it a long time. He thought about her hands on the parapet and her face when his foot went. It hadn’t been fear of the workshop. It had been fear of losing him.

At the bottom of the document he typed: DO NOT GO IN WITHOUT HER KNOWING. He looked at it. Underneath he added: DO NOT GO NEAR HER FATHER.

He saved it. He knew that mapping every way out of a place he’d never been invited into wasn’t the same as looking after someone. He knew she’d given him a piece of her past, not permission to investigate it. He shut the laptop.

Just before two he picked up his phone again.

Raiden: Thank you for showing me something you don’t show many people.

Jinx: Don’t make it weird. And don’t think too much.

He looked at the closed laptop.

Raiden: I’ll try.

Jinx: I liked having you there.

He read it twice, and went to bed. But the map stayed on the computer. Six pages. Every street, every exit, every drain, every way out. He hadn’t told her about it. He hadn’t decided whether he would.

chapters.title: He Asks Her to Marry Him on a Napkin Drawing
chapters.desc: At Mrs. Tong’s he slides a napkin across the table with their whole life drawn on it at 1:50. She says yes, on five conditions, signed in chilli oil.
chapters.epigraph: “Yes. A registry. Not your father’s house.”
chapters.content:
Raiden Lin had been planning to ask Jia Cao to marry him for eleven days, and he had three drafts.

The first was a letter, abandoned because he couldn’t get past the first sentence. The second was a conversation over dinner somewhere, abandoned because he couldn’t decide whether a dinner was too ordinary or whether making it extraordinary would only make her want to leave. The third was a drawing. Naturally. He’d spent his whole life drawing things he wanted to understand. He could draw a building before it existed. He could draw her bike and her hands and the curve of her shoulder over an engine and the crease between her eyebrows when a bolt wouldn’t come, and the garage, and the crate she let him sit on, and the little green tram he’d become embarrassingly fond of. Drawing a future with her had taken eleven days. He still wasn’t sure he’d got it right.

✦ ✦ ✦

Mrs. Tong’s was nearly empty on Friday the tenth of September. Rain had kept everyone home. A small television muttered in the corner, the windows were fogged from the kitchen, and the room smelled of broth and ginger and chilli oil. Jinx slid into their booth by the window. He sat opposite.

“You’re strange today,” she said.

He let his shoulders down. “Better?”

“No. Are you hiding something?” She leaned across.

He considered lying, and didn’t. “Yes.”

“At least you’re honest. Is it expensive?”

“No.”

“Illegal?”

“No.”

“Is anybody dead?”

“Not that I know of.”

“All right. Tell me when you’re ready,” she said.

That was one of the things he loved about her. She’d interrogate him for ten minutes about a missing screwdriver, and when something really mattered she knew exactly when to stop asking.

Mrs. Tong brought two bowls and a dish of chilli oil and looked at him. “Why are you sitting like that?”

“See?” said Jinx.

“Did you do something wrong?”

“Not yet,” said Jinx, and Mrs. Tong said “Young people,” and went back to her kitchen.

He waited until Jinx had eaten half her bowl. Then he took a folded paper napkin out of his inside pocket and put it beside her chopsticks.

“Is that a bill?”

“No.”

“An apology?”

“Not exactly.”

She opened it. Not a sketch: a plan, ruled and measured and lettered in his small neat hand, and across the top it said: CAO JIA & LIN RAIDEN. PROPOSED HOME.

She went still.

Not the forty-third floor of Meridian, but the garage. Her garage, behind the black door under the TAI HING ROPE & CANVAS sign: the uneven floor, the bench, the spares shelves, the lathe, the place by the door where the helmets lived, the old fan, the narrow kitchen at the back, the two rooms upstairs. The crate was there. There were dimensions. A little legend in the corner. A note by the bench: JIA’S SIDE. Another by the kitchen: SHARED. Beside the crate: RAIDEN’S PLACE TO BE ANNOYING.

She laughed, small and startled, and he breathed again.

“It’s to scale,” he said.

“On a napkin?”

“One to fifty.”

There was a room at the back marked BEDROOM, and beside it in smaller writing, Only if you want one.

Her finger stopped there.

He said, “I know it’s yours. I know you won’t leave it, and I don’t want you to. So I thought we’d start with what’s already there. The walls stay. The bench stays. The door stays. One day we might sort out the drains and the back wall and the wiring that frightens me. There’s room for somewhere to live without touching the shop. And the crate stays.”

“Why?”

“Because it’s yours. And because I’ve spent a lot of time sitting on it.”

She laughed again, and her eyes had started to shine.

He said, “I used to think home was somewhere you went to be safe. Walls and locks and a roof that didn’t leak. I think now it’s who you’re allowed to be when you’re in it. I don’t want you to have to be somebody else to live with me. I don’t want you to give up your work or your shop or anything that makes you Jia. I want to come home to you. I want to make coffee badly enough that you complain. I want to hear you swearing at an engine from the next room. I want to argue about where the tools go and lose every time.”

“You would.”

“I know. And I want to be there when you don’t want to talk, and know when to leave you alone and when to sit beside you anyway. Jia Cao. Will you marry me?” He looked straight at her. The television went on in the corner. Something rattled in the kitchen.

She looked at the napkin and then at him. He wasn’t playing. He wasn’t counting exits or pretending to be stupid. He was a man waiting for an answer.

“You’re proposing on a napkin.”

“Yes.”

“A used napkin.”

“It’s clean. I checked.”

She laughed and a tear ran down, and he reached across and stopped just short of her hand. “Is that a no?”

“No. Yes, you idiot. Yes. A registry. Not your father’s house,” she said, and his face fell, and she laughed harder.

He shut his eyes. When he opened them they were wet. “Yes?”

“Don’t make me take it back. Conditions.” She took his hand across the table.

“Anything.”

“Hear them first. One. A registry office. No hall, no hundreds of people, nothing I’d have to wear. Two. Nothing in the Walled City. Nothing your family arranges.”

His smile went, because he knew exactly what she meant, and then came back. “Nothing in the Walled City.”

“Three. My shop stays mine. My work stays mine. Your family doesn’t decide where we live or how or what I do. Four. If something happens, you tell me. You don’t disappear and you don’t send somebody else to explain. Five. I’m not the only one bending. You don’t get to keep your whole life exactly the way it is while I fit myself into a corner of it. You make room for me too.” She looked at the napkin.

He looked at her. “I will.”

“Then write it down.”

“On the napkin?”

“Where else?”

He took out his pen and began, and he was halfway through the second condition when Mrs. Tong appeared at the end of the table with her hands on her hips and read WILL YOU MARRY ME? upside down.

“Oh!”

Jinx covered her face. “Auntie, please.”

“You’ve finally asked?”

“Yes,” said Raiden.

Mrs. Tong turned to Jinx. “And?”

Jinx pointed at the napkin. “I said yes.”

Mrs. Tong slapped the table so hard the chilli oil jumped. “Finally!”

Then she pulled out a chair and sat down and read every word of the plan and every condition, and laughed until she had to wipe her eyes at RAIDEN’S PLACE TO BE ANNOYING.

“Very accurate. Good. A woman should know what she’s agreeing to. And you should listen. Where do I sign?” She was serious by the end, and held out her hand for the pen.

Witness: Tong Mei-fung, she wrote at the bottom. Then she looked at the chilli oil and smiled. “Now make it proper.”

The terms were signed in chilli oil. Mrs. Tong insisted. Jinx dipped the end of a clean chopstick and made a small red mark beside her name. Raiden’s was crooked.

“Your signature’s terrible.”

“It’s a legal document in chilli oil.”

Mrs. Tong added her own mark and folded her hands. “Now kiss.”

“Auntie. You’re still here.”

“I’ve seen you two kissing under a motorbike. Don’t pretend to be shy now.”

Jinx looked at him. He was still smiling, and the smile made her chest feel too full. So she got up and came round the table and sat down on his knee, and took his face in both hands and kissed him, slow and warm, until his arms came round her waist and she could feel him smiling into it.

“Hello,” she whispered.

“Hello.”

She kissed him again. Mrs. Tong cleared her throat. Jinx ignored her.

“Good, now eat your noodles before they go cold,” said Mrs. Tong, eventually.

✦ ✦ ✦

They walked home in the warm wet dark with the napkin inside his jacket.

“You’re keeping it?”

“It’s our first legal document.”

“That’s not how legal documents work.”

“Mrs. Tong witnessed it.”

“Mrs. Tong also told us to kiss.”

“She seems very qualified,” said Raiden, and Jinx slipped her hand into his.

At the corner he stopped. “Are you happy?”

She thought about it properly. “Yes. Are you?”

“Very.”

A few steps on she said, “You’re going to be my husband,” as if trying the word out to see whether it would bear weight.

“Apparently.”

“Poor you.”

“I think I’ll manage.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He’d made himself rules, of course. Thirteen of them, in his notebook, under the heading THINGS I SHOULD NOT DO WHILE ENGAGED TO CAO JIA. He considered thirteen a sensible number. She considered it an invitation.

Rule 1: No kissing before breakfast. At 7:12 the next morning she came into his kitchen on the forty-third floor in one of his shirts, put her arms round his waist from behind while he was making tea, and kissed the back of his neck. He went still and turned round.

“It’s seven. We haven’t eaten.”

“I know.” She kissed him.

“That’s rule one.”

“What rule?”

He shut his eyes, and kissed her back.

Rule 2: No kissing while I’m working. On Monday she came up to the forty-first floor with two coffees and kissed his cheek while he was checking a section. “I’m working,” he said. She kissed him again. “Rule two.” “How many rules are there?” “Thirteen.” “Interesting,” said Jinx, and kissed him a third time while the receptionist pretended to be on the phone.

Rule 3: No kissing when you’re meant to be angry with me. On Tuesday he made the mistake of rearranging her kitchen shelves over the garage. Heavy pans low, cups together, utensils in a rack.

“Why?”

“The old arrangement was inefficient.”

“It was my kitchen.”

“Our kitchen,” he said, and heard himself, and she came across the floor and took him by the collar.

“Say that again.”

“Our kitchen?”

She kissed him. He laughed against her mouth. “That was supposed to be an argument.”

“It was. I’m furious,” she said, and kissed him again.

By Wednesday he’d started keeping a tally in the margin. By Thursday the margin was full, and she found the notebook on the bench and read the heading and looked up at him.

“You’re counting?”

“You’re very undisciplined.”

“You proposed to me.”

“I’m documenting the frequency.”

“How many?”

He hesitated. “Twenty-seven.”

She leaned on the bench and looked at him. “That’s all? You’re slipping.”

“Would you like to improve the number?”

“Gladly,” she said, and he added another mark afterwards.

✦ ✦ ✦

Mid-Autumn fell on the Tuesday after that, the twenty-first. His family was having dinner at the Walled City at seven. Elowen had sent the arrangements. His father had asked him to come early. At five his phone rang, and it was Ah Sim, who’d cooked for the Lins since before he was born.

“Young Master. Your father asks me to confirm. Dinner is at seven.”

He looked at the message from Jinx above it on the screen. Making something. Don’t be late.

“Tell him I’m not coming, Ah Sim. I have plans.”

A pause. “Should I tell Madam Elowen?”

“Yes, please.”

Another pause, longer. She didn’t ask whose plans. She’d known him since he was ten and walked in through the back gate on his own, with a rucksack and mud to his knees. “Please eat properly, Young Master, and don’t work too late,” she said, and rang off.

Jinx had made too much food. Enough for six. “How many are coming? Two. Then why—” he said.

“Eat,” she said, and he ate. There were two small mooncakes, and he cut them in half, and she watched him.

“Your family’s eating together tonight. You’re not there. Do you feel bad?”

“A little.”

“You don’t have to choose between me and them.”

“I know. I chose to be here tonight. That doesn’t mean I don’t love them. And I don’t expect you to give up anything of yours. I just want to build something with you that doesn’t need anybody’s permission.” He put his chopsticks down.

She pushed half a mooncake across to him. “Good.”

“Besides, your food’s better,” he said.

“That’s a very dangerous thing to say.”

“I’ll risk it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On Saturday she made the rings.

He came at ten with four coffees and found her at the lathe with two steel washers out of an old parts box, measuring the bores. “What are those?”

“Nothing. Don’t ask.”

He didn’t. He sat on his crate and watched her clamp the first one and take it down in small passes, stopping, measuring, putting it back, never hurrying. He noticed she’d picked two that weren’t the same size. He didn’t say anything. When she’d finished she polished the edges by hand and held them under the lamp: plain, brushed, one a little wider than the other.

“They’re not expensive. They’re not gold. They’re washers,” she said.

“I know.”

“I thought we should have something.”

She put the wider one in his palm. He turned it over with his thumb. “You made our rings.”

“Don’t sound so surprised.”

“They’re perfect.”

“They’re different sizes.”

“That’s why. One’s yours and one’s mine. They don’t have to match,” he said.

She didn’t say anything. She took his hand and slid the wider one on, and it fitted. He put the other on hers, and it fitted too, and he lifted her hand and kissed the ring and then the knuckles.

“Don’t get soppy,” she said.

“Too late.”

Rule 9: No kissing while Jia is operating machinery. He broke it himself that afternoon. She’d shut the lathe down and was wiping the bench with the rings on the tool tray beside her, and he’d been quiet for several minutes, and when she looked round he reached out and caught the front of her overalls, not roughly, and drew her in, and kissed her. She made a small startled sound and then smiled against his mouth and took his shirt in both fists and pulled him closer, and the kiss went deep and slow there against the bench, his hand spread at the small of her back, until neither of them was thinking about rules at all.

“Rule nine,” she said, when she could.

“I know.”

“You broke it.”

“I wanted to kiss my fiancée.”

“That isn’t a valid reason.”

“It is to me,” he said.

That night he opened the notebook and turned the page of tallies over, and on a clean page wrote THINGS I WANT TO REMEMBER. The napkin. One to fifty. Chilli oil. Mrs. Tong’s face. Jia on his knee. Two washers on a lathe. Then, underneath, on its own line: She said yes.

Around half past eleven a photograph came of her hand on the bench with the narrow ring on it.

Jinx: It needs polishing.

Raiden: It looks perfect.

Jinx: You’re biased.

Raiden: Completely.

Jinx: Goodnight, fiancé.

He looked at the word. Then he took the napkin out of the drawer, soft at the folds now, with a faint red stain by their names, and looked at the little plan with the bench and the crate and the kitchen and the room they might share one day, and the note in the corner. RAIDEN’S PLACE TO BE ANNOYING. He’d always thought a home was something you designed. Something measured and built strong enough to keep the world out. Now he thought it might be a garage with an uneven floor, a woman who swore at engines, a crate always in the wrong place, four coffees, two washers, and a napkin with chilli oil on it.

He put the napkin beside the rings, and turned off the lamp. For once he didn’t draw a single exit.

chapters.title: The Trophy Husband Has Dinner Ready
chapters.desc: The old-town registry, two washers for rings, Mrs. Tong crying louder than anyone. Then her husband moves into her two rooms with a wok.
chapters.epigraph: “Somebody has to cook. You’d put soup in a gearbox if I let you.”
chapters.content:
He’d been up since five. She could tell, because there were four abandoned cups of tea on her windowsill and he was standing in the middle of her two rooms over the garage in his silver waistcoat with the buttons done up wrong. All of them. One off, all the way down.

“I can’t do it. I’ve done it four times. My hands won’t work. I’m a draftsman, my hands always work,” said Raiden Lin, on the morning of Thursday the thirtieth of September.

“Come here.”

He came. She undid every button and did them up again from the bottom, while he stood breathing through his nose like a horse, and then took his collar in her fist and straightened it so hard his head came forward.

“You’re very calm,” he said.

“Somebody has to be.”

She looked at him. No jacket; she’d vetoed it because it made him look as if he were going to his own funeral. No tie. No watch, at her insistence. A white shirt and a silver waistcoat and his hair, for once, almost tidy.

“You’re staring,” she said.

“Yes.”

“Stop.”

“I don’t think I can.”

She was in a cream blouse and black trousers and the boots he’d bought her in May, with her hair tied back and a few strands loose. No dress. No veil. Just her. He’d told her once that morning she was beautiful and she’d accused him of trying to make her nervous, so he didn’t say it again. He thought it loudly instead.

“Idiot,” she said.

“Your idiot.”

“Not yet.”

He looked at his bare wrist. “Eleven minutes.”

She threw a hair tie at him. He caught it.

✦ ✦ ✦

Mrs. Tong came at a quarter to nine with a small bunch of pale yellow chrysanthemums tied with red ribbon and pushed them into Jinx’s hands.

“Auntie. Why?”

“Because you’re getting married. You need flowers. Don’t make that face at me. The face that makes me cry.” Her eyes were already wet.

Raiden took the flowers off Jinx before anybody could start crying on the stairs. Mrs. Tong straightened his waistcoat and patted his cheek. “You look after her. And don’t let her work till midnight.”

“I’ll try.”

“Don’t try. Do it.”

“Why is everyone giving him instructions?” said Jinx.

“Because someone has to,” said Mrs. Tong.

The registry was on the ground floor of an old municipal building in the old town: cream walls gone soft with age, wooden doors, a staircase that creaked, and a waiting room that smelled of paper and polish. Three other couples were ahead of them. An old pair holding hands. A girl fixing her fiancé’s collar. A man reading his forms for the third time. They sat side by side with their fingers laced between them.

“Rings?” said Jinx.

He opened the little box. Two steel washers, polished till the edges were smooth, one a little wider than the other.

“You’re not worried someone will notice?” he said.

“They’re rings.”

“They’re washers.”

“They’re our washers,” she said, and he laughed and kissed her knuckles, and the old couple opposite smiled, and she pretended not to see.

The registrar had silver glasses and a calm practised voice. She checked their papers and their names and explained what would happen. At one point she looked up. “Mr. Lin. Your attention, please.”

“Sorry,” said Raiden, who’d been looking at his bride.

She read the declaration. They gave their consent, both of them clearly. There was no music and no aisle, only the quiet room and the registrar and Mrs. Tong in the front row, and two people who’d decided to build a life. When the registrar said they were married, neither of them moved for a second. Then Jinx took hold of the front of his waistcoat in both hands.

“Over here.”

“Yes, wife,” he said, and she pulled him down and kissed him. It wasn’t careful, and it wasn’t polite. She kissed him hard enough that he laughed into it and his arms went round her, and from the front row came a sob so loud the registrar looked over her glasses. Mrs. Tong was crying as though she’d raised them both from birth and seen them through a war.

“Auntie!”

“Of course I’m crying! Don’t laugh at me, I’m happy!”

“Thank you for being here,” said Raiden, which made it much worse.

They took the certificate in both hands. He looked at her. Wife. The word went somewhere deep in his chest and settled there.

“I love you,” he said.

Her face went soft. “I know,” she said, and kissed him again, and Mrs. Tong shouted, “Again!”

✦ ✦ ✦

Lunch was at Mrs. Tong’s. There was no argument about that. “You met here, you ate here, you get married, you eat here,” she said, and put the chilli-oil napkin in a cheap wooden frame behind the counter, which Jinx objected to and Raiden supported, which led Jinx to threaten divorce before the soup came, which Raiden said was a little early. Dumplings, noodles, roast duck, greens, a steamed fish, a soup they were ordered to finish.

He was serving her fish when his phone went. Father. His hand stopped. She saw it, and didn’t say anything. He went out into the street.

“Where are you?”

He looked back through the window. Jinx was listening to Mrs. Tong complain about the price of choy sum, smiling, the narrow ring catching the light as she lifted her cup.

“At work.”

“Elowen says you’ve cancelled Sunday again.”

“I’ve got something to finish.”

“You’ve been very hard to reach. Come home this weekend. We need to talk about your future.” His father’s voice cooled by a degree.

He looked down at the washer on his finger. “All right.”

When he came back in she pushed a dumpling across to him and said, without looking up, “Eat. You don’t have to tell them today.” Then, low, so only he could hear:.

He found her hand under the table. “I know.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At the foot of the stair to her two rooms that night, she turned round and crouched.

“Get on.”

“What?”

“You’re my husband. Do you want carrying or not?”

“You’re not serious.”

She hooked one arm behind his knees and the other round his back and lifted him, and he made a noise he’d deny for years. “Jia!”

“Don’t wriggle.”

“My wife is carrying me up the stairs.”

“Shut up. You’re heavier than you look.”

He kissed her cheek and she nearly missed a step. “Stop kissing me while I’m carrying you. Don’t tell anyone. Especially Mrs. Tong. She’d make me do it again.” Three steps later he did it again. She got him to the top anyway and put him down in front of her own door and pointed at him.

The two rooms were exactly as they’d always been: the narrow kitchen, the mattress against the wall, the window that never quite shut, the fan, the overalls on the hook by the door. Except for a certificate on the little table, and a man in the middle of her floor in a silver waistcoat with a washer on his finger.

“You’re inspecting,” she said.

“I live here now.”

“Do you?”

“That’s what the certificate says.”

“Then you should probably take the waistcoat off.”

“Yes, wife. Leave it. Hello, Mrs. Lin.” He did, and his shirt, and she caught his hand before he could fold it. He sat on the edge of the mattress and she stood between his knees, and he looked up at her.

“Don’t call me that.”

“What should I call you?”

“Jia.”

“All right. Are you happy?” He kissed her palm.

“Very.”

She undid her blouse herself and let it fall, and he put his hands on her waist as if she were made of something that might crack, and she laughed and pushed him back onto the mattress and came down over him. He kissed her throat and her breasts and the scar on her knuckle, slowly, the way he did everything that mattered, until she was the one who was impatient. “Raiden. Now.” He turned them over then, careful even in that, and came into her looking at her face, and she wrapped her legs round him and held on. They moved together slow and then not slow, the city noise coming in through the window that wouldn’t shut, the old fan turning, his breath ragged against her ear, her heels at the backs of his thighs, and she came first, with her teeth in his shoulder and his name in her mouth, and he followed with his face in her hair saying hers.

Afterwards he lay with his cheek on her stomach, and said, into her skin, “I love you.”

“I know,” she said, and stroked his hair.

“Are you ever going to say anything else?”

“Maybe. When you deserve it.”

“How long will that take?”

“Let’s find out,” said Jinx.

✦ ✦ ✦

He moved in three days later with one duffel bag and a wok.

“That’s your luggage?”

“And a bag.”

“You’re moving into my house with a wok.”

“Our house. It’s seasoned,” he said, and put it on the counter as carefully as if it were a model of a cathedral. A few shirts. His work clothes. Books. Sketchbooks. A box of pencils. A framed photograph of an ugly brown dog in front of a wooden gate, with a farmhouse behind it.

“Architect?”

“Architect.”

“He looks like he ate a shoe.”

“He probably did. Where do my things go?” He put it on the shelf.

“Top shelf. There’s room. Raiden. Put your clothes away,” she said. There were already clothes on it. Hers. He looked at them. He did, and afterwards the cupboard looked different. Two people’s clothes, side by side.

That evening she saw him change her name in his phone from Jinx to Tyres.

“Tyres?”

“You keep me running.”

“That’s terrible. Change it.” She took the phone and changed it back. He took it back and changed it again.

“Marriage is about compromise,” he said, and she hit him with a pillow.

✦ ✦ ✦

By the end of October he’d learned three things. She never put a tool back in the same place twice. The kitchen was shared until somebody touched her good pan. And she had strong opinions about dumplings.

He found that out on a Sunday. He’d made the filling himself, cabbage and mushroom and prawn with ginger and spring onion, and the dough from scratch, and rolled every wrapper into a circle, and she came up the stairs at seven to flour on his shirt and a tray of dumplings on the counter.

“You made these?”

“Yes.”

She looked impressed, and then suspicious. “Why? What’s wrong with you?”

“Nothing. You like dumplings.”

She ate one. Then another. “The wrapper’s too thick. The filling needs more ginger. Your pleats are uneven. But they’re good.” She ate a third.

“Thank you.”

“You’re very domestic.”

“Somebody has to cook. You’d put soup in a gearbox if I let you,” said Raiden.

“You’re a trophy husband. Pretty. Quiet. Makes dinner.”

“Pretty?”

“Don’t get excited. Go and wash up.” She pushed his shoulder.

In November he asked whether she’d come to a small dinner with his family. “Not yet,” she said, over her coffee.

“All right. Not yet. All right,” he said. Two weeks later Elowen invited them both to lunch. He never sulked and he never argued and he never made her feel she owed him anything. But she noticed he never stopped hoping either. One night she found him looking at a family photograph on his phone.

“Do you miss them?”

“Sometimes.”

“Do you want to go?”

“Not without you. I’m not asking. I’m just telling you.” He put the phone down.

She took his hand. “Maybe one day.”

“One day’s enough,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

At the end of November it rained for a week, and the window that never shut let it in at the bottom corner in a thin dark line down the wall. She’d always put a towel under it. One night she woke at two and found him crouched there with a roll of tape, pressing it carefully along the frame by the light from the street.

“What are you doing?”

“Fixing this.”

“It always leaks.”

He smoothed another strip into the corner and sat back on his heels and looked at it, frowning, and said, to the window, not to her: “Not good enough for my wife.”

She went still. He didn’t know she’d heard. She pulled the quilt round herself. “Come here.”

He came and sat beside her. She put her head on his shoulder. “I don’t need you to turn this into Meridian. I don’t need expensive windows. I married you, not your ability to fix buildings. And I like this place. Even the window.” She touched the washer on his finger.

“The window?”

“The window too,” she said, and kissed him, and pulled the quilt over them both. The tape held.

On the first Sunday in December he was at the counter making dumplings again, thinner wrappers this time, more ginger, and she came up behind him and watched, and then dipped her finger in the dish of oil by the stove and drew it down his cheek.

He stopped. He turned his head slowly. “You’ve put oil on me.”

“Your face was clean.”

He looked at her. Then he put his finger in the flour and touched the end of her nose.

“Now it’s balanced,” he said.

She laughed and took him by the shirt and kissed him, and the dough was forgotten. His hands found her waist and he lifted her onto the counter in a cloud of flour, and she pulled his shirt over his head and left white handprints all down his back, and he laughed against her neck and kissed his way down her throat while she undid him. She told him the dough could wait. She hooked her ankles behind him and drew him in, there on the counter with the tray of dumplings pushed to one side and flour everywhere and the rain on the window, and he braced one hand on the wall beside her head and moved in her until she was gripping the edge of the counter and saying his name to the ceiling, and he followed her over with a sound that was half a laugh, his forehead against hers.

“You’re a terrible cook,” she said, when she could.

“You’re a terrible distraction.”

She looked at the oil on his cheek, and kissed it, and then kissed him properly, and the kitchen was no use to anybody for the rest of the night.

chapters.title: The Roof That Will Never Fall
chapters.desc: Winter to spring. A lawyers’ letter says her building has been sold, and it has, to her. A dyno, a steel room behind the tools, a roof that won’t leak, and a napkin a month.
chapters.epigraph: “It’s in your name. Only yours. I’m sorry. I know I promised I’d only use it when it was important.”
chapters.content:
The letter came on the second Monday in December, from lawyers for the Tai Hing Rope & Canvas Company.

The company had stopped making rope in 1994. Now it was three old cousins in three countries who owned the building and argued about it by email. She’d paid them rent for three years, in cash, on the first of every month, to a man on a scooter. Dear Tenant. We write to inform you that the property at the above address has been sold. She read it standing at the black door with grease on her hands, and went cold all over. The lathe weighed a tonne and a half. It had taken four men and a hired crane to get it in.

Then she turned the page. There was a second letter under the first, from a different firm, on cream paper. Notice of Transfer. The new registered owner of the building, and of the narrow one next door that had been empty since the ship chandler died, was CAO JIA. Only her. No company. No Lin anything. No other name.

Upstairs something was sizzling in the wok. She went up with both letters in her hand.

“Did you buy something?”

He came out of the kitchen with a spatula, saw her face and the cream paper, and put the spatula down.

“Did you buy my building?”

“Yes.”

“And next door?”

“Yes.”

“With whose money?”

“Mine. Mama’s. What she left me. It’s in your name. Only yours. I’m sorry. I know I promised I’d only use it when it was important.” He didn’t look away.

“You did this without telling me.”

“The cousins had taken an offer from a developer. They’d have knocked it down for flats. I could have let it go. I knew what it meant to you.”

“You don’t know what it means to me.”

“No. Not all of it,” he said.

“I told you before we married. You don’t decide things for me. You can’t buy me a building and call it looking after me.”

“I’m not.”

“Then what are you calling it?”

“A place I wanted you to have that nobody could take away. Everything’s in there. The sale, the title, the surveys, the old drawings. No loans. No other names. You can sell it, keep it, rent it, do nothing at all. I won’t make one decision about it without you. If you tell me to sell it, I’ll sell it tomorrow.” He put a folder on the table.

There was a note clipped inside the folder in his small capitals. You should have somewhere no one can take from you.

“I need to think,” she said, and went down the stairs with the folder, and he turned the gas off under the smoking wok, and waited.

✦ ✦ ✦

She sat in her van in the street for twenty minutes with the engine off and the radio on. Her building. For three years it had been somewhere she could be thrown out of with a month’s notice. Now it was hers, and she was angry, and frightened. Not of the building. Of having something given to her so completely. Of how quickly thanks turned into owing. Of how much she wanted it.

He hadn’t argued. He hadn’t told her she was being unreasonable or reminded her what it had cost. He’d said she could sell it.

Jinx: I’m still angry.

Raiden: I know.

Jinx: Don’t touch the building. Don’t hire anyone. Don’t make drawings.

Raiden: I’ll try.

Jinx: I’m keeping it. It’s mine. I decide what happens to it.

Raiden: Completely.

Jinx: You can help. If I ask.

Raiden: I’d like that.

When she went back up the food was in boxes and the kitchen was clean and he was sitting at the table. She put the folder down in front of him. “I’m keeping it. I want the survey. I choose the engineer. And nobody knocks a wall down because you’ve had an idea.”

“Understood.”

“Don’t buy me anything like that again without asking. Even if you think I’ll say yes.”

“I’ll ask.”

She framed his face with her hands and kissed him, and then rested her forehead on his. “You’re a very expensive idiot.”

“Apparently. Dinner was meant to be twenty minutes ago.”

“Good. I’m hungry.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The first drawings didn’t start until January, after she’d chosen the engineer herself: Ms. Bok, a small sharp woman who looked at the two of them across the table and said, “Who’s the client? Good. Then everything comes to you.” Jinx put her hand up.

The old building was worse than Jinx had thought. The roof was rotten in places. Two beams were too small for what they’d been carrying for seventy years. The back wall was wet. Raiden asked about load paths and steel and how the new frame would meet the old walls. Jinx asked about power and extraction and drains, and whether a bike could be wheeled from one building to the other without being lifted over a step. Ms. Bok answered all of it and then looked at Raiden’s preliminary sheets.

“Mr. Lin’s drawings are ambitious. A full steel frame, reinforced walls, a new roof, and a protected room inside the workshop.”

Jinx turned. “A protected room?”

“The back can take one without losing any floor.”

“Why would I need one?”

“You don’t have to have one. I wanted you to have somewhere nobody can reach you.” He said the second part more.

“We’ll talk about the room later. I want power for the machines, proper extraction, drains that work, a floor that takes a lift, and a door wide enough for the van,” said Jinx to Ms. Bok.

By the end of the meeting the building had stopped being something he’d bought her and started being something they were making together.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the first morning of January there was a napkin beside her coffee.

A ship. A large one, with a small cabin at the stern and a workshop below decks, and on the bow, small, two figures and a row of chairs.

“Again?”

“A wedding. A proper one. Where my family could come. On a ship, possibly,” he said.

“Where would I work?”

“Lower deck.”

“And you?”

“Being seasick.”

She laughed and folded it. “Not yet.”

“All right,” he said, and put it in his sketchbook.

In February it was a treehouse with a bridge and a workshop round the trunk and the chairs on the lower platform. “Where’s the bathroom? Behind the stair. Terrible place for a bathroom. Not yet.”

In March it was a crane, a real dockside one, converted, with a platform hanging from the jib for the vows and the workshop at its foot. She looked at it a long time.

“You want to get married inside a crane. I thought you’d like the mechanics. You’re insane. Not yet,” said In February. He kept every one. So did she, after he’d gone to sleep, in the back of his sketchbook where he wouldn’t notice she’d been looking. Neither of them mentioned it.

✦ ✦ ✦

New Year at the Walled City was on the first of February, and he went alone.

Before he left he took the washer off his finger and threaded it onto a bit of string. She watched him do it.

“You don’t have to,” she said.

“I know. Just tonight.” He tied the string at the back of his neck, badly, and she reached up and tied it again for him.

“Don’t let them make you ashamed of it.”

“I’m not ashamed.”

“Then wear it.”

He touched the ring through his shirt. “I am.”

At his father’s table, between Elowen and Lin Jian, with too many dishes and too many relatives and too much polished wood, he felt it the whole evening against his breastbone. Elowen saw the small shape under his shirt and looked at him, and her face went gentle. “Is it comfortable? Yes,” she murmured. She went back to her soup.

“You’ve been absent,” said his father.

“I’ve been working.”

“Elowen says you spend a great deal of time away from the office.”

“On a building.”

“Whose?”

“A private one.”

“You’re being deliberately vague.”

“I’m answering the questions I want to answer,” said Raiden, and the table went quiet. He thought about taking the string out and laying the washer by his father’s bowl. He thought about Jia’s fingers on the clasp, and the napkin, and the conditions written on it in his own hand. Nothing your family arranges. He said nothing. His father looked away first. The ring stayed against his chest all night.

✦ ✦ ✦

The steel supervisor was gone by the end of February.

Mr. Sung had been recommended by the builder, and he was good. He knew his numbers and he didn’t talk down to her, and Jinx liked him. Then, at a site meeting by the back door, with Raiden going through the security drawings, he said lightly, “With the owner’s name on the deeds and this street, there are risks. A young woman alone in a place like this—”

“My wife doesn’t live alone,” said Raiden.

“I only meant—”

“You put her name and her street in the same sentence as a threat.”

“I’m talking about security.”

“You’re talking about her as something somebody could use.”

Raiden closed the folder and turned to the builder.

“Mr. Sung won’t be continuing on this job,” said Raiden.

Jinx found out two hours later, from Ms. Bok, on the phone. She found him in the empty building next door by a new steel column.

“Did you sack Mr. Sung?”

“He said—”

“I know what he said. Did you ask me?”

He looked at her. “No.”

“Then you did it again. This is my building. My job. My name’s on the title. If you think someone’s wrong for it, tell me. Show me. Let me decide.” She pointed at the column.

He didn’t defend it. He didn’t say the man had made a threat, or remind her who’d paid for the steel. “You’re right. I’m sorry.”

“Don’t make me ask to be let into my own life. You can tell me when you’re frightened. You can be protective. You can’t turn it into control.”

“I understand.”

“Do you?”

“Yes. I’m sorry, wife.” He took her hand.

“Don’t use that word to get out of trouble.”

“I wouldn’t dare,” he said, and she let him off, nearly.

✦ ✦ ✦

It took three months of dust and noise and concrete and steel and delays, and redrawing, and inspections, and arguments over millimetres, and Jinx learning that a building could be every bit as stubborn as an engine. The old floor came up. The steel went in. The roof came off and a new one went on. The two buildings were opened into each other through the old party wall so the workshop doubled and the black door stayed where it was. He was there almost every day, and he didn’t decide anything without her. They argued for forty minutes about one floor drain until she put her finger on the plan and said, “Water runs downhill. Put the drain where the water goes,” and he looked at it and said, “You’re right,” and she said, “Good husband,” and he said, “Good wife.”

In March a lorry brought something she hadn’t ordered. She came through the door expecting a compressor and found a motorcycle dynamometer: a proper one, heavy roller, load cell, control unit, extraction, its own computer, sitting on a floor Ms. Bok had checked for it, on its own circuit. Raiden stood beside it with his hands in his pockets, looking almost shy.

She walked round it twice. Then she looked at the shop around it: level floor, good light, sockets where she needed them, room to move, room to get things wrong without shifting everything else first. She looked at him, and couldn’t find any words, and in the end said “Thank you.”

He went still. She’d thanked him before, for coffee and dinner and holding a torch. Not like this, not with that much behind it. He touched her cheek and she leaned into his hand.

“Don’t think this means you can buy me another one,” she said.

“I wouldn’t dare.”

On the last Saturday in March she noticed that one section of the tool wall stood a little deeper than the rest. He moved a cabinet aside, pulled a recessed handle, and a panel swung in on a narrow steel-lined room: its own air, emergency light, a telephone, water, a cupboard of supplies, room for two people to sit. A door that locked from either side. A hatch in the ceiling of the back passage onto the roof and a protected way across to the stair of the building next door.

She didn’t go in straight away. “Why?”

“Because I know what it’s like to need somewhere nobody can reach you. I don’t ever want you to need it. But if you do, it’s here.” He didn’t look away.

She went in then and put her hand flat on the steel. “Can I open it from in here? Can I get out by the roof?”

“Yes. And yes.”

“Show me. You built a room behind my tools. You’re ridiculous. Don’t ever lock me in there.” He showed her all of it. Then she came out and took him by the shirt and kissed him hard enough that he went back a step.

“I won’t.”

“Promise.”

“I promise.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The roof was finished at the start of April. Ms. Bok went through her final report and Jinx asked three questions and signed it. When the engineers had gone she stood in the middle of the floor with the afternoon light coming through the new roof lights across the steel, and the smell of new concrete and machine oil.

“Come here. Look,” she said, and took his hand.

The shop. The dyno. The two doors. The walls. The roof.

“You built me a roof that won’t fall,” she said.

“That’s what roofs are supposed to do.”

“Not this one. This one means something. Thank you, husband.” She kissed him.

They were both filthy by evening, so she ran the bath upstairs, the new one, the first bath she’d had in that building, and he stood in the bathroom door with two towels and looked at it.

“What?”

“I’m wondering whether there’s room.”

“It’s a bath. Come here.” She took the hem of his shirt and pulled it over his head, and he looked at her and said, “Are you sure?” and she said, “We’ve been married six months,” and kissed him, and got in, and he got in after her, and half a wave of water went over the side onto the new floor. They both froze. Another wave followed it.

“Sorry,” he said.

She was helpless with laughter. “You’re doing it on purpose.”

“I’m trying to sit down.”

He got his legs arranged at last and she settled back against his chest, and the water calmed, and for a while there was only warmth and steam on the window and the rain beginning on the new roof. “It’s strange. Having a house,” she said.

“It’s still two rooms.”

“Two rooms with a bath. And a dyno.”

“Don’t put the dyno in the bathroom.”

She turned round in the water to face him, and more of it went over the side, and neither of them noticed. “I want this. The whole thing. The shop. The roof. Your stupid secret room. This bath,” she said.

“The bath’s negotiable.”

“It isn’t,” she said, and kissed him. She came astride him in the water and he held her by the hips and she took him into her slowly, both of them laughing at the water slopping out over the floor, and then not laughing at all. She moved on him with her arms round his neck and her forehead on his, the rain loud on the roof he’d built, his hands sliding on her wet back, until she came apart against him with a long sound she didn’t try to keep quiet, and he followed her, holding her so tightly she felt his heart.

Later, wrapped in towels, he stood in the doorway looking at the floor. “That’s a lot of water.”

“Leave it.”

“I’ll mop it.”

“You’re a trophy husband. Pretty. Good at dinner. Terrible at baths. Good at roofs,” she said.

“Anything else?”

She kissed him. “Good at being my husband,” she said against his mouth.

“That’s my favourite one.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On the first Saturday in April she got to the shop before him, and there was a napkin on the bench. Not a ship, or a treehouse, or a crane. The first plan. The garage. The crate. The kitchen. But redrawn: the two buildings joined, the dyno in its place, the steel room behind the tools, a small arrow up through the roof. CAO JIA’S HOME, it said in the corner. Revised April 2022. And at the bottom, small, a row of chairs under the new roof lights.

He was in the doorway with four coffees.

“Another one?”

“A wedding. Here. When you’re ready,” he said.

She looked at the chairs, and at him, and touched the washer on his finger. “Not yet.”

“All right.”

She pulled him in by the shirt and kissed him. “But I like this one best,” she said.

For years she’d thought the past was a place she could only look at from across a street. Now she had a key, and a choice, and a door she could stand in without needing to leave.

“Come on. Let’s see if your expensive present works. And bring the coffee,” she said.

He picked up all four cups. Above them the roof held, and for once she didn’t look up to check.

chapters.title: The Meanest Engineer in the City
chapters.desc: A charity gala full of people who know his father, and a racing driver with kitchen-scissor hair who catches him looking at a crack. A gearbox, a dark gold bike, and a sidecar called Architect.
chapters.epigraph: “She could build a bike faster than you could crash it. I’d bet money. I’d bet your money.”
chapters.content:
The rice burned because Raiden Lin made the mistake of sitting down.

He’d turned the gas down. He’d set the timer. He’d moved the pan off the hottest part of the ring. Then, on the evening of Friday the eighth of April, his wife called him over from the green sofa in the two rooms over the shop, where she sat in one of his old shirts with a bottle of black nail varnish balanced on her knee, and asked whether her nails were dry.

He looked. “Not yet.”

“Then blow on them.”

“All of them?”

“Do you want to do them one at a time?”

He crouched in front of her and took her hand, holding her fingers apart so they wouldn’t touch anything, and blew across the wet black with his brows drawn together and his whole face concentrating, as if it were a structural survey. She watched him and smiled.

“You’re very good at this.”

“Thank you. Other hand.”

There was a smear of black on her thumb, and a thread of grease by her wrist she’d missed at the sink. He thought she was beautiful. He thought it every day, and it still surprised him. He kissed her palm.

“You’ll ruin the varnish.”

“Sorry.”

She caught his shirt with her free hand and pulled him in, and it was meant to be a quick kiss, and then his arm went round her waist and she pulled him down onto the cushions and it wasn’t quick at all.

“Jia. The rice.”

“You’re obsessed with that rice.”

“It’s dinner.”

“We’ll make more,” she said, and kissed him until the kitchen began to smell of something dark and definitely burning. He lifted his head. She shut her eyes.

“Don’t.”

“I think—”

“Don’t.”

A thin grey thread was rising out of the pan. “My rice,” said Raiden, and she laughed until she had to hold the arm of the sofa.

✦ ✦ ✦

By the time they left, the rice had become noodles. He stood at the mirror doing up the cuffs of a black shirt, and she came up behind him in a black dress, plain, close at the waist, slit to the knee so she could walk without fighting it, her hair loose for once, her nails gone glossy and hard. He turned round and forgot what he was doing with his cuff.

“What?”

“You look beautiful.”

“That’s all?”

“Would you like a technical assessment? Excellent proportions. Very elegant. Dangerous to my concentration.”

She laughed, and he put his hands at her waist and kissed her bare shoulder, and she said, “You’ll make us late,” and he said, “One minute,” and she turned round and gave him one.

She took his left hand on the way out and ran her thumb over the washer on it. “You’re wearing it.”

“Yes.”

“Good.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The children’s hospital gala was in a hotel ballroom over the river, the kind of room where everyone seemed to know everyone. Company directors. Doctors. Donors. People who shook hands for photographs and talked about generosity while working out what every introduction was worth. He’d grown up at evenings like this. He knew which men would ask after Lin Jian before asking after him, and which women would admire Jinx’s dress while trying to work out where she belonged. He knew where the service doors were before he’d finished his first glass of water. He knew his father was on the guest list.

At the door she leaned in. “Do you want to leave?”

“Not yet.”

“You’re doing your thing. Exits. Columns. People.”

“Am I that obvious?”

“To me.”

He took her hand. “Stay close?”

“You’re asking?”

“Yes.”

“I’m here,” she said.

His first mistake was letting a Mr. Shek introduce him to three people one after another. His second was pretending not to understand a question about his family’s latest development. His third was letting someone fill his glass. By the far side of the room he’d been asked about his father’s health, his ambitions, and whether he’d be joining the board, and he’d answered all of it with polite fog, and somewhere along the way he’d taken the washer off his finger and put it in his inside pocket, because three different people had looked at it.

Then he found a crack. A thin diagonal line on one of the ballroom’s decorative columns, nearly hidden by the paint. Probably shrinkage. But the position was odd. He followed it up to the joint, and then to the ceiling, and was so far into it that he didn’t notice the woman beside him until she spoke.

“Are you planning to arrest that column?”

She was about his age. Short hair hacked off unevenly at the jaw as if someone had gone at it with kitchen scissors and lost interest halfway. A black suit with the sleeves shoved up. An old burn on the back of her right hand. A watch loose on her wrist. A glass of water. A sharp face.

“You’ve been staring at it for four minutes. Either you’re an architect or you’ve found an interesting way to avoid people,” she said.

“A draftsman. It’s close.”

“Is it going to fall on me?”

“Probably not. I’d want the original drawings before I promised.”

“You’re one of those. Can’t enjoy a building without checking it won’t kill you.”

“Buildings are more enjoyable when they don’t.”

She laughed. “Fair. I’m only here because somebody promised free food and a chance to make rich people feel bad about not giving enough. I drive racing cars. I’m practical. Serafina Song.” She held out her hand.

“Raiden Lin.”

Her eyes narrowed a fraction. “Lin. You’re married?” She didn’t explain whatever she was thinking. She glanced down at his hand instead, and at the pale band of skin where a ring had been.

He looked at his finger. He could feel the washer in his pocket like a stone. “Something like that.”

“Secretly?”

“Not exactly.”

“That’s what people say when it’s exactly that.”

He laughed, and took the washer out, and put it back on. It settled against the skin. He looked at it a moment. “She’s here.”

Across the room Jinx was at the silent auction table, looking at a framed photograph of a child holding a toy motorbike and talking to one of the hospital volunteers.

Serafina followed his eyes. “That’s her? She looks as if she could win an argument with a wall.”

“She probably could. She builds bikes. She could build a bike faster than you could crash it. I’d bet money. I’d bet your money,” he said, and his face had gone soft.

✦ ✦ ✦

Jinx found them a quarter of an hour later and handed him a glass of water.

“Jia, this is Serafina Song. She races.”

Jinx looked at the hair. “That’s a dangerous haircut.”

Serafina blinked, and laughed. “I did it myself. Kitchen scissors.”

“That explains it.”

“You’re very direct.”

“She’s an engineer,” said Raiden.

“He says you build bikes faster than I could crash them. Good. I need someone to tell me why my gearbox hates me,” said Serafina.

“Gearboxes don’t hate people.”

“Mine does.”

“Then you’re doing something wrong to it.”

Serafina stared, and laughed again, and Raiden looked delighted. “You’ll get on.”

“Don’t decide that,” said Jinx.

Serafina’s eyes went to his hand. “Nice ring.”

“She made it. On her lathe,” said Raiden.

“Don’t advertise.”

“It’s much better than the ones people buy,” said Serafina.

“At least it fits. Stop showing it off,” said Jinx, and caught his wrist when he turned it to the light.

Serafina looked from one to the other. “Right. So it’s real. I thought he was one of those men who wear a ring so they look unavailable.”

“Are there men like that?” said Jinx.

“Apparently,” said Raiden.

Jinx turned back to Serafina. “He’s unavailable.”

“I gathered,” said Serafina, grinning.

After that the evening got easier. Serafina talked about the difference between a car that felt fast and one that was, and about Nonna, her grandmother’s red rally hatchback with three hundred thousand kilometres on her, whose original gearbox had been jumping out of third for two months. Her own mechanic wanted to put a new box in. She’d rather die. Jinx asked whether it jumped under load or off the throttle, and whether it went back in clean, and at the end of it Serafina said, “You really know it. Can I bring it to you?”

“Bring the whole assembly. I don’t diagnose from a complaint.”

“Does she let you design things at home?” Serafina asked Raiden.

“He designs. I reject,” said Jinx.

“Sometimes,” said Raiden.

“Most of the time.”

“Sounds healthy,” said Serafina.

“It is,” said Raiden, and looked at his wife, and she looked back.
