His father never came over. Raiden saw him once across the room by the windows, talking to a minister, and saw his father’s eyes find him, and find the woman beside him, and stay there a moment. Then somebody spoke to Lin Jian and he turned away.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the taxi home she sat with her hand on his thigh and watched the clock on the dashboard. 11:58. He was looking out of the window. She touched the washer on his finger.

“Raiden.”

He turned.

“Happy birthday.”

He looked at the clock. 11:59. Then at her. “You remembered.”

“Of course I remembered.”

“I never told you what I wanted.”

“What do you want?”

He looked at their hands. “You.”

“That’s a terrible answer.”

“It’s the true one. Happy birthday, husband,” he said, and she kissed him, and at the next red light kissed him again. His phone buzzed twice. Elowen, wishing him a happy birthday and a good night. And then a number he didn’t know.

Unknown: Serafina Song. Your girl’s terrifying. I like her. Gearbox next week.

He showed Jinx. “Good. She’s got a gearbox,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

Serafina came on the Wednesday with the gearbox in the back of a van and pointed at him across the shop. “You’re the draftsman. And you’re the meanest engineer in the city.” She pointed at Jinx.

“Who told you that?”

“Your boyfriend.”

“I didn’t,” said Raiden.

“Your face did.”

It took Jinx two weeks. The dogs on third had worn from square to rounded, so that under power they pushed themselves apart, and the fork had been hammered trying to hold them; thirty years of a family driving it hard and a granddaughter driving it harder. She found good used gears instead of new ones, because Serafina wanted the car to stay itself, and set the fork true and checked every tolerance and ran it through every gear. When Serafina came to collect it she brought a second box: a close-ratio sequential from the team’s old car, sitting in storage, used but properly kept. “A trade. Your work for this, and whatever difference you think is fair.”

“Why?”

“Because I want someone who understands what she’s working on. And because I’ve seen what you do. This place is something.” Serafina looked round at the shop, the dyno, the steel, the floor.

“It’s mine,” said Jinx.

“That’s better still.”

Then Serafina asked whether Jinx could build her something. Not a race bike. A road bike that didn’t look like anything else, fast and exact. It took three months. Jinx sketched round Serafina’s reach and weight and how she sat, tuned the engine for the middle of the rev range, set the suspension for her, and painted the bodywork a deep dark gold that looked almost brown under the shop lights and like old bronze in the sun. Raiden brought coffee and held lights and carried parts, and learned fast not to touch anything without asking.

She handed it over at a petrol station on the edge of the city at the end of July. Serafina walked round it slowly and swung a leg over and found the levers exactly where her hands went, and the pegs exactly where her feet went, and started it, and blipped it twice, and looked up.

“You remembered the lever reach.”

“Yes.”

“This is perfect.”

“Ride it before you decide.”

Serafina got off and hugged her, hard and sudden, and Jinx went stiff for half a second and then laughed and hugged her back. “She’s terrifying. And very good. You’re both unbearable,” Serafina told Raiden over her shoulder.

✦ ✦ ✦

He’d mentioned the sidecar once. One evening after closing, watching her set up the suspension on an old bike, he’d said, almost to himself, “I’ve always wondered what it would be like to ride beside you. Not behind.”

“You want a sidecar?”

“Maybe. I like being able to see your face.”

She’d laughed and gone back to work, and he hadn’t asked again. She remembered. Once the gold bike had gone, she found a frame. She put the chair on the left, the kerb side, the way the road went here. She designed the mounting and worked out the loads and stiffened the attachment points, and set the bike to lean two degrees away from the chair and the chair wheel a centimetre toe-in, so the whole outfit wouldn’t drift for the gutter. Every part of it was built to carry a person safely: proper brackets, bracing, a wheel that tracked true. She built the seat round him. More leg room than she’d have given anyone else. A backrest. A grab rail. A locker under the seat. A screen low enough that it wouldn’t get in the way of him looking at things. She painted it dark green, and on the side fixed a small brass plate that said ARCHITECT.

She finished it on the morning of Saturday the tenth of September and texted him.

Jinx: Petrol station. Bring your helmet.

Raiden: Is something wrong?

Jinx: No.

Raiden: Are you sure?

Jinx: Raiden.

Raiden: Coming.

He stopped at the edge of the forecourt when he saw it. He walked round it slowly, his eyes going over the brackets and the suspension and the seat, and then he saw the brass plate and stopped.

“You built this?”

“Unless you know another idiot called Architect.”

He touched the letters with his thumb. “There’s a backrest. And a rail. And somewhere to put things.”

“I thought of everything you’d complain about.”

He laughed, and then he didn’t, and he pulled her into his arms on the forecourt under the strip lights and held her tightly with his face in her hair. “Thank you. Thank you,” he said. And again.

“Happy birthday. Late,” she said into his shoulder.

“My birthday was five months ago.”

“I know.”

She strapped him in and checked the rail and swung onto the bike and looked round. “Ready?”

“Always.”

She let the clutch out and the sidecar came with them, smooth as anything, and he laughed out loud. Not politely, not quietly. The same helpless laugh as the first time on the back of her bike, when he’d begged her for the long way. She heard it over the engine, and took the long way home.

That night he sat on the floor of the shop beside the sidecar with far too many photographs on his phone. She was cleaning tools.

“Jia? Would you make another one?”

“Why?”

“For the tram.”

She laughed until she dropped the cloth. “A sidecar. On a bike that does twenty.”

“Possibly.”

She came and sat down beside him and he leaned his shoulder on hers.

“Do you remember the first time? You were kneeling in the middle of a race,” she said.

“I was.”

“And now you’re sitting in a sidecar.”

“An improvement.”

He kissed her hair. “I love you.”

Her face went soft. She took his hand. “I know. I love you too.”

He went completely still.

“What? Your face is doing something,” she said.

“Sorry.”

“Don’t be,” said Jinx, and kissed him.

He’d spent his life looking at buildings for where they’d fail. The cracks. The distances. The ways out. That night he looked round the shop under its new roof and saw something else: a woman who built things that worked, a life that wasn’t hidden, and a seat beside her, made for him.

chapters.title: Proud of Her for an Entire Week
chapters.desc: Her black bike wins Best in Show up north, and her husband tells a petrol station, a toll booth and a coach party. He tells everyone except his own family.
chapters.epigraph: “I’d like everyone to know. I’d like a plane to write it in the sky. I’ve looked into it. It’s very expensive and the wind spoils the letters.”
chapters.content:
Raiden entered the motorbike without telling Jinx.

In his opinion this was perfectly reasonable. He hadn’t entered her without permission. He’d entered the bike. There was a difference.

The bike was called Carp. She’d named it years ago, after a customer had stood in the shop and insisted that a motorbike had to be red, because red was the colour of speed, and she’d told him that if he wanted a fish he should buy one. The customer left. The bike stayed black: a deep, nearly liquid black with graphite under it, the tank shaped to follow the frame instead of shouting over it, an exhaust she’d bent herself, and not one bracket or weld or setting on it that didn’t have a reason. Not the most expensive thing in the shop, or the most powerful, but the only one she’d ever built without a client to argue with.

He loved it. He loved the woman who’d built it. And he had decided the Northern Custom Show should see both.

Category: Custom Motorcycle. Entrant: Cao Jia. Machine: Carp. He arranged the transport, paid the fee, read the regulations twice, booked a room near the hall, and wrote the description for the card:

Built and engineered by Cao Jia. A study in restraint, mechanical balance, and the beauty of a machine that knows exactly what it is.

She would have objected to the last part. Which was why he didn’t show her. He made only one mistake: he left the confirmation open on his laptop. On the evening of Wednesday the fifth of October she went looking for a supplier’s invoice for a set of brake lines and found the show’s logo instead.

When he came out of the kitchen with two bowls, she turned the screen round.

“I entered Carp in the Northern Custom Show,” he said.

“Without telling me.”

“Yes.”

She read the last line aloud. “A machine that knows exactly what it is.”

“I thought it was accurate.”

“Why?”

He put the bowls down. “Because it’s beautiful. Because you built it. And because I think people should see what you can do. I know you don’t build things for applause. I know you don’t need a trophy to tell you your work’s good. I just think you deserve to have people look at it properly.” She folded her arms, and he didn’t look away.

It was easier when people admired the finished bike. It was much harder when he looked at it and saw her.

“When?”

“Saturday week.”

“You’ve paid.”

“Yes. And the van’s booked, and there’s a room.”

“I’m paying my own costs. And I’m not wearing a dress.”

“I’d never expect you to.”

She picked up a bowl. “Fine.”

He tried not to look pleased and failed completely, and she pointed her chopsticks at him. “You can thank me for not throwing the laptop at you. There’s still time.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The hall was three hours north, an exhibition shed on a ring road, and it smelt of polish and tyre rubber and coffee. There were bikes everywhere: immaculate restorations, elaborate customs, machines whose owners had plainly spent more on chrome than most people spent on a car. Carp went into her bay under good lights, and Jinx straightened the front wheel and checked the stand and rubbed one fingerprint off the tank with her sleeve, and stepped back.

For the next hour he behaved himself. Mostly. He didn’t touch the bike. He didn’t answer for her. He didn’t explain the engine when people asked. He stood a little way off, fetched coffee, and watched her talk: the frame, the intake, the exhaust routing, the suspension, why the weight sat where it did and why she’d kept the bodywork quiet. A man asked if the black was meant to make it look expensive.

“No.”

“Then what?”

“Black.”

Raiden coughed into his hand. He loved the way she talked when a question was worth answering. Her hands moved when she described a part. Her eyes went sharp when she corrected someone. She didn’t perform knowing things. She just knew them. He was so proud he thought his chest might actually hurt.

The rival came just before judging. His name was Victor Cheng, and his bike sat two rows away, huge and chromed, with bodywork like a wedding cake and a price that Jinx suspected would buy a small flat. He walked round Carp with two friends.

“Interesting. Very understated. Almost unfinished. A personal project? That explains it. Good luck. These things tend to reward more substantial work.”

Jinx’s face didn’t change. Raiden’s did, a little. He stepped up, polite as a waiter.

“Could I ask what you mean by substantial?”

“Engineering. Fabrication. Complexity.”

“Of course. It’s only that the hall’s rules say a quarter of a tank at most, filler cap sealed, battery off. Yours is full to the neck. I could smell it from the aisle. And the battery’s still connected, I think, because you want to start it for the judges. It may be fine. I’m not saying it isn’t. I’m suggesting we have lunch with the fire officer. We could all learn something.” Raiden glanced along the row at the chrome. He smiled.

Victor stared at him. One of his friends looked at the tank. Victor said something under his breath and walked off, and ten minutes later a steward with a clipboard and a roll of tape was standing beside the chrome bike, and Victor was draining fuel into a can in the car park.

Jinx was watching her husband as if she hadn’t decided whether to be impressed or annoyed.

“You’re mean,” she said.

“Only when necessary.”

“Don’t start a fight.”

“I didn’t.”

“You threatened him with lunch.”

“An educational lunch,” he said, and went back to standing beside her.

✦ ✦ ✦

The judging took nearly two hours. The rear suspension. The frame. The electrics. One judge asked why she hadn’t used more decoration, and she looked at Carp. “Because the shape already works. I didn’t want to add things just to prove I’d made it.” The judge nodded slowly and wrote something down. Raiden didn’t say a word. Once she glanced across and he smiled at her, and she rolled her eyes, and her mouth went soft anyway.

When they read the awards out, he held her hand and she could feel his thumb going back and forth over her knuckles.

“You’re nervous,” she whispered.

“I have less control over the outcome than you do.”

Best in Show came last. The presenter opened the envelope and smiled. “Cao Jia, for Carp.”

She didn’t move. People began to clap. Raiden turned to her, and all the careful composure had gone off his face and he looked about fifteen. “Jia.”

“That’s me.”

“Yes.”

Then he took her by the waist and swung her clean off her feet, and a laugh came out of her she didn’t recognise, and he put her down and kissed her right there, in front of the stage and the judges and the whole hall, as if the prize had been handed to both of them.

“You won,” he said.

“We won.”

“No. You.”

The plaque said BEST IN SHOW — CARP — CAO JIA. She looked at it, and then she smiled, wide and with nothing guarding it, and he thought he had never seen anything as beautiful in his life.

✦ ✦ ✦

He told the petrol station first.

“Excuse me. My wife won Best in Show today. Would you like to see the bike? She built it. From the frame up,” he said to the man at the till. Jinx, behind him, closed her eyes.

“Raiden, pay,” she said.

He told the woman in the toll booth, who said, “Congratulations?” as if it were a question. He told a coach party at a rest stop in the dark, while Jinx was buying water, and when she came back there were seven people round his phone looking at Carp, and one of them wanted to know if she’d build him one, and another’s nephew liked motorbikes, and as they boarded a man gave Raiden a thumbs up and shouted, “Good wife!”

“Very good,” Raiden called back.

She took him by the sleeve and towed him to the van. “You told an entire coach.”

“Not the entire coach.”

“How many?”

“Seven. Possibly eight.”

“You can’t tell every stranger in the country.”

“Why not? I’d like everyone to know. I’d like a plane to write it in the sky. I’ve looked into it. It’s very expensive and the wind spoils the letters.” He looked honestly puzzled.

She sighed, and took his hand, and drove.

He sent a photograph to Mrs. Tong, who replied with seventeen exclamation marks and a voice message nearly two minutes long. He told the man at the coffee counter. He told a small boy who’d been staring at the trophy. But he didn’t tell Lin Jian, and he didn’t tell Elowen, and he didn’t send the picture to the family chat, and that was the part Jinx noticed, because she knew how much he wanted to.

Their marriage hadn’t been announced. He’d agreed to her terms on a napkin a year before: no family ceremony, no introductions, nothing in the Walled City. She’d never asked him to be ashamed. She’d only asked him not to drag their marriage into a world she hadn’t chosen. And he’d kept his word.

It was past eleven and she didn’t drive tired, so they stopped at a roadside hotel with a buzzing sign. She came out of the shower and found him sitting on the side of the bed with his phone, and a message on the screen.

Elowen, Jia won Best in Show today. Carp took the top prize. I wish you could have seen her face—

He looked at it. Then he deleted it.

He hadn’t seen her in the doorway. She came and sat beside him. “What were you writing?”

He showed her the empty box.

“You wanted to tell her.”

“Yes. And my father. I wanted them to know what you did. I don’t regret it. I regret that I can’t share every part of my life with everyone I love. But I don’t regret choosing you. And I don’t ever want you to feel I’m waiting for you to become acceptable to my family.” He took her hand.

“You’re not,” she said, and put her forehead against his.

“No.”

She took the phone out of his hand and put it face down on the bedside table, and then she climbed into his lap with her knees either side of his hips, and he made a small surprised sound and caught her.

“I’m proud of you. For not making me fight you over it,” she said.

“That’s a very low standard.”

“Don’t ruin it.”

She kissed him slowly. He was still in yesterday’s shirt, and she undid the buttons one by one with her eyes on his face, and pushed it off his shoulders, and put her mouth to his collarbone, and then his throat, where his pulse jumped. He pulled the towel loose from her and it fell away, and his hands came up her bare back and stayed there, spread wide, holding her as though she were the prize. She was the one who reached down between them. She was the one who lifted herself and sank onto him, slowly, a breath at a time, until he was all the way inside her and his head had gone back and her name had come out of him like something breaking. She rode him in the yellow light from the car park, unhurried, her hands on his shoulders, watching every change in his face, and he let her see all of it. When he came apart it was with his face pressed into her neck and his arms locked round her, and she followed him a moment after, his fingers finding her exactly where she needed them, his voice in her ear telling her she was extraordinary, over and over, until she laughed into his hair and told him to be quiet.

Afterwards he lay with his cheek on her stomach and she ran her fingers through his hair.

“You can tell me when you miss them. You don’t have to pretend it doesn’t hurt,” she said.

“I know,” he said, and this time he didn’t look at the phone again.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Sunday evening, at home, his phone buzzed once.

Zhao: Best in Show. Well done to her. Your sister hasn’t heard it from me.

Raiden stared at it. “How does he know?”

Jinx read it over his shoulder. “He knew about us the night you were in hospital. He’s never once told anyone. Don’t ask him how. He won’t say.” She handed the phone back.

He didn’t ask. He typed Thank you and put the phone down, and Jinx noticed that it was the first time all weekend his face had looked completely easy.

✦ ✦ ✦

The trophy sat on the workbench for two days while she decided where it should go. He suggested the shelf over the dyno. Too high. The office. It wasn’t an office. The living room. She threatened the bathroom.

On Tuesday night she stood in front of it with her hands in her pockets, and he came in with two mugs of tea.

“Maybe up there,” she said.

He looked at the shelf. “Good.”

“You’re still proud.”

“Yes.”

“How long are you going to keep it up?”

He considered. “A week. At least. I was proud of you before you won. When you were building it. When you spent three nights arguing with the rear suspension.” He stepped closer.

“Two.”

“Three.”

“Two and a half.”

“I was proud when you explained the frame to the judges, and when you told that man black was black. And I was proud when you won, because everybody else finally got to see what I see every day.”

She put her hand on his face. “You’re very good at making a person feel loved.”

“I’m trying.”

“Come upstairs.”

He’d run the bath while she closed the shop, with two towels on the rail and her soap by the tap. They got in carefully this time. Neither of them wanted another flood. He leaned back against the end and she leaned back against him, and for a while there was only the water and the rain on the roof.

“You know what I liked best? You didn’t talk over me. You didn’t explain my own bike to the judges,” she said.

“I was tempted.”

“Raiden.”

“I didn’t.”

“And you didn’t tell your family. I know what that cost. You kept your promise when you wanted something else. You were proud of me without needing anyone else to know. You’re allowed to be proud. You’re allowed to tell strangers. You’re allowed to tell Mrs. Tong.” She found his hand under the water. She turned her head and kissed him.

“She already knows.”

“You’re allowed to tell Zhao.”

“He knew before I did.”

She laughed, and settled back against his chest. Down in the shop the trophy sat over the dyno, catching a little light from the stairs.

“I think I’ll be proud of you for another week. Perhaps two. And after that I’ll start again,” he said into her hair.

chapters.title: Memes at 2 A.M.
chapters.desc: He sends her memes from the next pillow at two in the morning. Then he tells her about a freezer and eleven hours, and she works out what his steel room is.
chapters.epigraph: “You built me a freezer with the light on.”
chapters.content:
At 2:07 in the morning, in the week after Christmas, Raiden Lin sent his wife a picture of a cat falling off a table.

me trying to sleep after saying goodnight six hours ago.

Jinx looked at her phone. Then she turned her head. He was lying beside her on his back, holding his own phone about six inches from his face.

“You sent me a meme.”

“Yes.”

“From there. Your arm is touching me.”

“I know.”

“You could have spoken.”

He thought about that, and sent another: a skeleton sitting up in bed. me waiting for sleep to arrive.

She reached across him, took his phone, and put it face down on the bedside table. “Enough.”

“All right.”

Rain on the window. The old building ticking as it cooled. A bike going by in the wet street. She shut her eyes, and beside her he shifted once, twice, and turned on his side, and she felt his fingers find the hem of her shirt and hold on to it.

“Jia? Are you awake?”

“No.”

“Goodnight.”

“You’ve said that.”

“I wanted to say it again.”

She caught his hand and kissed it. “Goodnight, idiot.”

For a while she thought he might really sleep. Then she felt his breathing change, not into sleep, but into the careful, even rhythm of someone trying hard to persuade another person he was resting. She knew the difference. She’d known it for more than a year. Raiden could sleep through a neighbour drilling concrete. He could fall asleep on the sofa with half a drawing under his cheek, or upright in the van after a long day. But some nights, in the middle of the night, his body seemed to forget that the room it was lying in was safe.

She turned over. His eyes were open, looking at nothing.

“What’s wrong?”

“Nothing. Really.”

She didn’t argue. She moved closer and put her palm flat on his chest. His heart was steady. A little too steady.

“Do you want me to stay awake with you?”

He nodded. It was such a small movement that she nearly missed it.

✦ ✦ ✦

At 2:43 he said, “You know about the farm.”

She did. The chickens and the vegetable patch and the barn roof that leaked. Auntie Lan’s terrible soup. A dog called Architect who dug holes. Drawings on the backs of feed invoices. He’d told her all that on a Sunday in August with his plaster just off. He’d never told her much about why he’d been there, or about the end of it, and she’d never asked.

“When I was nine, somebody came. I don’t know who. I never found out. Auntie Lan heard cars on the track, more than one, and she took me by the arm to the back shed. There was an old chest freezer in there. It hadn’t worked for years. They kept feed in it. She’d emptied it that week, I don’t know why. Maybe she knew something. She told me to get in. I thought it was a game, at first. She put a blanket round me and told me to be very quiet, and she shut the lid, and then I heard her drag a sack of feed on top of it so it wouldn’t look as if it had been moved,” he said to the ceiling. His fingers moved on the blanket.

Jinx’s hand had gone still on his chest.

“The seal was gone. That’s why it didn’t work. That’s why I could breathe. I couldn’t see anything at all. It smelt of feed and old metal. I could hear them in the yard. Men. Somebody laughing. A dog barking, and the chickens going mad. I heard them in the house. Doors. Things being moved. And then somebody came into the shed. Somebody kicked the side of it. Once. Not hard. Just the way you’d kick something that was in the way.” He said it as if it were a technical point.

“Raiden.”

“I thought they knew. I tried not to breathe. I thought if I made one sound Auntie Lan would be in trouble. I was very good at being quiet.” His voice cracked on the last word and he looked away.

“How long?”

“Eleven hours.”

The rain went on against the glass.

He said, “I counted. Mostly. When I lost my place I started again. My legs went numb at about four thousand. I was very cold. When she opened the lid it was dark outside as well, so it didn’t make much difference. She was crying. She kept saying my name. She lifted me out and held me for a long time, and I couldn’t stand up, so she carried me into the kitchen and made soup.”

“Was it terrible?”

A small broken laugh came out of him. “Absolutely. She left a lamp on that night. A little yellow one, on the table. I could see the whole room. She said nobody was coming back.”

“Did you believe her?”

He was quiet. “Eventually. A few days later some soldiers came up the valley to see what was left, and when they’d gone there was a tin of peaches on the kitchen windowsill. No note. Nobody would say where it came from. Blue and yellow label, cold from the window. I got it open with a kitchen knife and ate them one at a time and saved the syrup till last. I thought about that tin for years.” He almost smiled.

She opened her arms and, after a moment, he came into them, his forehead against her shoulder. He was taller than her and heavier, warm and familiar, and she could feel how hard he was holding himself together.

It came to her in pieces. The steel room behind the tool wall. The air he’d had checked twice. The emergency light on its own circuit. The telephone. The door that locked from either side. The hatch to the roof and the way across to the next building. She’d thought it was Raiden being thorough. An architect’s draftsman who knew the difference between a room and a refuge. He’d never once called it a safe room. He’d called it the room.

“Raiden, your room. Downstairs,” she said.

He lifted his head a little.

“The air keeps moving. You can sit down. Nobody can lock you in. It opens from inside. There’s another way out. And the light stays on, whatever happens to the rest. You built me a freezer with the light on.” She touched his face. She heard her own voice go.

He stared at her.

“You made it bigger. You made it so nobody would ever be shut in it in the dark,” she said.

Something in him gave way without a sound. His face turned into her neck, and his whole body went tight as if he could hold it in by force, and she felt the first tear on her skin, and then another. He didn’t sob. He didn’t make any noise at all. He just cried, silently, with his shoulders moving in small hard jerks, and she held him with one hand at the back of his head and the other between his shoulder blades. She didn’t tell him it was all right. She didn’t tell him he was safe, as if fifteen years could be undone by a sentence.

“You’re here. You’re here with me. I’ve got you,” she said.

His fingers knotted in the back of her shirt.

“I’ve got you.”

He cried, and she let him.

✦ ✦ ✦

Just after three she reached for the glass of water and he drank a little and gave it back.

“Sorry.”

“What for?”

“Keeping you awake.”

She pinched his cheek, gently. “Are you apologising to me for being nine?”

“No.”

“Good. Because that’s ridiculous.”

She lay back and pulled him down with his head on her chest and began to stroke his hair. After a while she started to count.

“One. Two. Three.”

At thirty he opened his eyes. “What are you doing?”

“You counted in there. So I’m counting now. You’re waiting for something. I’m giving you something else to wait for.”

“That isn’t how counting works.”

“It is tonight.”

She didn’t hurry and she didn’t lose her place. When he shifted she moved her arm, and when he opened his eyes she kissed his forehead and went on from where she was. At a hundred and six he whispered, “You don’t have to.” At three hundred and twelve his fingers loosened. At seven hundred and forty his breathing slowed. By two thousand her voice had gone to a whisper. At three thousand nine hundred and ninety-nine she stopped, and his eyes opened a fraction.

“Still here?”

“Yes.”

“Good.”

“Four thousand. Four thousand and one,” she said.

He was past the place where his legs had gone numb. He was asleep.

“Four thousand and six,” she said and stopped, and lay awake with her hand in his hair. She thought about a little boy in the dark under a sack of feed, counting. A woman crying as she pulled him out. A yellow lamp. A tin on a windowsill that nobody would explain.

He wasn’t there any more, she whispered into his hair. He was home.

✦ ✦ ✦

He woke just before eleven to an empty pillow, a window open a crack, and the smell of coffee and something frying.

Jinx: Breakfast. Don’t come down without a shirt.

Jinx: And no more skeletons.

He went down. She was at the stove and didn’t turn round. “Sleep?”

“Yes.”

He put his arms round her from behind and his chin on her shoulder. “Thank you. For last night.”

“You don’t have to thank me for holding you.”

“I know. Sit. You’re in the way.” He held on a little longer, until she pointed the spatula at the table.

They didn’t talk about the freezer for the next few days. Not because she’d forgotten, or because he wished he hadn’t told her. They let it settle. He slept better. Not perfectly. There were still nights he woke and checked the window, or lay too still. But now, sometimes, he reached for her hand. And sometimes she counted, and sometimes she didn’t need to.

On Friday afternoon she went into the shop for a torque wrench and found his legs sticking out from under a customer’s bike, an inspection lamp in his hand.

“You’ve got oil on your shirt.”

“The damage is done.”

“What are you doing?”

“Checking the rear mounting bracket. I heard a noise.”

She lay down on the creeper beside him and pushed in until their shoulders touched. The bracket was fine. “Then why are you still under here?”

“I like it under here. It’s where we started.”

“We met on a road.”

“Then it’s where you kissed me.”

It was. She looked at him in the narrow space under the frame, with grease on his cheek. He was smiling, and it wasn’t the careful smile he used to avoid questions, or the polite one he wore for strangers. It was small and warm and his own. She wiped the grease off with her thumb.

“I love you. I love you, Jia,” he said. And then, because she’d smiled and said I know, he said it again. No joke after it. No rule. He just looked at her.

She kissed him, slowly, and then again, lingering, until he smiled against her mouth.

“I love you too,” she said.

“I know.”

“Don’t steal my line.”

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening she went down alone and unlocked the room. The door swung in without a sound. Steel walls. The fan’s quiet breath. The emergency light. The telephone. Everything exactly as he’d built it.

She went back upstairs for the little lamp from the bedroom, with its warm yellow shade, and put it on the shelf beside the emergency light. Then she took a tin from the kitchen cupboard and found him at the sink, drying two cups.

“Peaches?” he said.

“Come with me.”

He followed her down. When she opened the door he saw the lamp, already lit, and the tin beside it, and he didn’t say anything at all.

She said, “It’s not much. I thought it could use something that isn’t an emergency. And people should have something to eat. We’ll put a proper chair in. A blanket. It’s not a freezer. It’s not somewhere you have to keep quiet until someone decides it’s safe to open the lid. It’s a room. You can walk into it, and you can walk out of it, whenever you like.” She took his hand.

His eyes had gone wet. He pulled her against him and they stood under the yellow light.

“It’s the right colour,” he said into her hair.

“I thought so.”

“Can we leave it on?”

“Of course.”

“Even when nobody’s in here?”

“That’s when it matters.”

She’d brought a tin opener in her back pocket, because she wasn’t an amateur, and one fork. They sat on the steel floor with their backs to the wall and the door wide open on the dark shop, and ate the peaches out of the tin, passing the fork back and forth, the syrup running down his wrist. He licked it off. She told him he was disgusting. He said it was the best tin of peaches he’d ever had, including the first one, and she said that was a sentimental thing to say about fruit.

After a while she noticed that he wasn’t looking at the door. Every other time she’d seen him in a room, any room, a restaurant or a ballroom or a hospital ward, some part of him had been keeping count of the ways out. Now he was looking at the lamp, and at her, and at the last peach going round in the syrup, and nothing else.

“Have it,” she said.

“We’ll share it.”

She cut it in half with the edge of the fork, badly, and gave him the bigger piece.

✦ ✦ ✦

At 2:07 the next morning her phone lit up. He was lying beside her, looking at her.

Raiden: [a peach in sunglasses] when you survive the freezer and finally get a room with snacks.

Jinx: You’re sleeping on the sofa.

Raiden: Is the lamp staying on?

She looked across the pillow. His smile was small and a little shy. She put the phone down and took his hand.

“Yes, now go to sleep,” she whispered, and kissed him.

He closed his eyes, and this time he did.

chapters.title: Ten, Walking Home Alone
chapters.desc: How a boy of ten copied a road map onto his arm and crossed a border in a fish truck. At two in the morning she rides him to the red door in his father’s back wall.
chapters.epigraph: “Nobody was coming. So I went to them.”
chapters.content:
He told her on a Saturday afternoon in the middle of January, not because he’d planned to, but because she was sitting cross-legged on the shop floor fighting a seized bolt on a customer’s bike, and she asked.

“How did you get home?”

He looked up from the drawing on his knee.

“From the farm. You told me once you walked. You said one day you’d tell me that part. You don’t have to. I’m only asking,” she said, and gave the bolt another heave.

He put the drawing down.

“I walked,” he said.

Her spanner stopped.

“I was ten. After the freezer it was never quite right there. Letters came. Auntie Lan wouldn’t let me see them. A man came to the gate one afternoon and asked her questions in a nice voice, and then he came again. She telephoned the city. I heard her in the kitchen at night saying yes, and I know, and how long, and crying when she put the phone down. Then one night in spring the man came back, late, and she took me out through the vegetable patch to the back wall. She gave me her old coat and the money out of the egg tin and half a loaf, and told me to go down the river road to the market in the old ferry town and wait by the fish stalls, and she’d come for me in the morning. And if she didn’t come, I was to find a police station.”

“Did she come?”

“I waited till the stalls packed up. Nobody was coming. So I went to them.” He looked at his hands.

“The police?”

“Home. I didn’t want the police. I’d spent eleven hours in a freezer because of men who came in cars. I wasn’t going to get into one.” He smiled, not very well.

He took out his phone and found a photograph. An old sheet of paper, yellow and soft at the folds. Roads in pencil, little arrows, a river, the names of towns in a child’s careful capitals, and symbols in the margins he must have invented.

“Auntie Lan kept a road atlas in a drawer. I wasn’t allowed to touch it. I used to copy it when she was out with the chickens. The farm, with the water tower. The river road. The old ferry town. The border. And here. The paper got wet when it rained, so I drew the important roads here, in biro. Every morning I checked. If it had faded I drew it again.” He pointed. He turned his left arm over and tapped the inside of the forearm.

She imagined it. A small boy in a coat far too big for him at the side of a road, studying the inside of his own arm.

“How did you cross?”

“In a fish truck.”

She shut her eyes.

“I know. There was a man loading crates at the market. I asked if he was going over the border. He told me to get lost.”

“Good.”

“I thought so too. So I climbed in between the crates when he went inside for his money. The cold wasn’t as bad as the freezer. The smell was worse. When the truck stopped I heard voices outside speaking differently, and knew we’d crossed. It wasn’t one truck. Six days. I got out when I could. I slept in places I didn’t know. A woman at a bus stand gave me a boiled egg. A man told me I shouldn’t be travelling on my own, and I told him my name was Ah Fai and my uncle was in the toilet, and ran.” He looked towards the roll-up door.

“Did anyone hurt you?”

He was quiet. “Nobody did anything I couldn’t get away from.”

There were a hundred things she wanted to ask. Where he’d slept. How hungry he’d been. Whether he’d cried, and who had seen. At ten she’d been under a bench in her father’s shop with a carburettor in her lap and men stepping round her, and she’d thought that was the worst place a child could be. She’d been wrong about that. She’d had a bench. She’d had a door that was always open, even if nobody good came through it. He’d had a road, and his arm, and a biro. She looked at his face and understood that the answers weren’t all hers to ask for. She put down the spanner, and reached across the bike, and took his hand.

“You were a little boy.”

“I didn’t think of it like that. I just wanted to get home.”

“To your father.”

“To my father.”

✦ ✦ ✦

“Tell me about the door,” she said.

“There’s a gate at the back of the house, in the lane. A red door in the wall. Ah Sim uses it, and the boys with the rice. I’d never been through it. I’d only ever seen the house in a photograph he brought to the farm at New Year. I got there just after dark. The map on my arm was nearly gone. I stood outside so long I found a crack in the wood beside the lock and kept my finger in it.” He smiled a little.

“Why?”

“I was afraid he wouldn’t be there. Or that he wouldn’t know me. He’d only ever seen me once a year. Then I knocked three times.”

She waited.

“I heard feet. The bolt. And it was him. I’ve never known why. He never uses that gate. He just stood there and looked at me, and I think he thought he was seeing things. Then he said my name. Not loudly. Just my name. And he sat down.” His voice went.

“Sat down?”

“On the step. As if his legs had stopped. He looked at my face and my clothes and my arm, and touched my hair, and then he pulled me in and held on. He didn’t ask where I’d been or how I’d got there. He kept saying, You’re home. Over and over. His coat smelt of cigarettes and rain. And then, still on the step, he told me why I’d been away all my life. That I’d been sickly from the day I was born, and the city air was bad for me.” He was looking at something a long way off.

“Was it true?”

“No. I believed it for thirteen years. The real reason isn’t only mine to tell. Part of it belongs to my sister.” He met her eyes.

She didn’t push. She knew enough about the Lin family to know their house had more locked rooms than his steel one.

“That night I made them all laugh at dinner. Elowen thought for years that I’d been lucky,” he said.

She got up off the floor, and came round the bike, and put her arms round his neck and her cheek on his hair.

“Take me there.”

“Where?”

“The door. Not the house. Not your family. Not anyone. I just want to see where you came home.”

“Jia. You said nothing in the Walled City.”

“That was about the wedding. This is me,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

At two in the morning the city belonged to people with nowhere urgent to be. She rolled the bike out with the green sidecar under the streetlamp, ARCHITECT on its brass plate, and handed him a helmet.

“I can drive,” he said.

“I know. Get in. I want to see your face.”

The Walled City was quieter than she’d expected, and never empty: lights behind old windows, a man smoking under an awning, a television somewhere, cables slung across the narrow streets, walls patched over walls. He directed her without an address. Left here. Straight. Not that one, the next. His voice had changed. He wasn’t reading the buildings for their structure. He was remembering. At the mouth of a lane between high blank walls he said, “Here,” and she cut the engine.

The red door was set into the wall at the top of three worn steps. The paint was fresh. The bolt was brass. Beside the lock, in the wood, there was still a small crack.

At the far end of the lane a man in a dark jacket stood under a light with his hands in his pockets. He looked at Raiden for a long second. Then he turned and looked the other way, as he’d been paid to do all his life.

Raiden stood at the bottom of the steps. He looked down at his left hand, and at the washer on it, and started to work it off.

She caught his wrist. “Keep it on.”

“If somebody comes out—”

“Then they’ll see it. You’re my husband. You don’t have to hide that from a door.” She rubbed her thumb over the ring.

Something moved across his face. He nodded.

She went up the three steps and lifted her hand and knocked on the wood, three times. His face changed as if he could hear it all again: the feet, the bolt, his father’s voice.

“Sorry,” she said.

“No.”

“What did you think, when it opened?”

“That I’d made it. Not that anything was mended. Not that I understood anything. I thought I could stop walking.”

She came down and leaned her shoulder against his. “Then you can stop now. We’re not going anywhere.”

He bent his head and kissed her. It wasn’t like the kisses in the shop with grease on their hands, or the ones at home while the kettle boiled. It was slow and careful, as if he were letting himself remember the door without having to stand in front of it alone. She held his face between her hands, and when he lifted his head she put her forehead against his.

“You’re home,” she whispered.

“Yes.”

They didn’t go at once. Across the lane there was a low wall under a shuttered window, and he sat on it and she stood between his knees, and he looked over her shoulder at the red door.

“Do you think he’d know me now?”

“He knew you at ten, filthy and starving in somebody else’s coat. Of course he’d know you. You’re still you.” She brushed her thumb over his cheekbone.

He was quiet. “I want you to meet him. Not tonight. Not until you want to. I don’t want you to feel that because we’re married you have to walk into my family. But I want it.” He looked at her.

There was no demand in his face. Only a wish. She looked at the door, and thought about the man behind it, whom she’d only ever seen across a ballroom with his eyes on her. The father who’d sat down on a step. She wasn’t ready. Not yet. But for the first time she could imagine a day when she might be.

“One day,” she said.

He went still. “Really?”

“One day. Don’t tell them. Don’t arrange anything. And don’t buy a building.”

He laughed. “That seems unnecessarily specific.”

“Raiden.”

“I won’t buy a building.”

“Come on, husband. Home,” she said, and the ring caught the streetlight as she pulled him up.

She took the long way, down out of the old streets and along the harbour, where the water was black and the cranes stood over it with their red lights blinking. She kept the bike at forty and the sidecar ran true beside her. Every time she looked across, he was already looking at her. At the lights by the ferry pier he leaned over the edge of the chair and said something the engine took.

“What?”

“Thank you for knocking,” he said, louder.

The lights changed. She didn’t answer. She put her hand out instead, flat on the top of his helmet for a second, the way you’d steady something you’d built, and then she let the clutch out and took them home.

✦ ✦ ✦

The thirteenth napkin since January last year came with breakfast. He drew it opposite her while she drank her coffee: a wall, three steps, a red door with a crack beside the lock, standing open. A small boy outside. A man in the doorway, sitting down.

“Would you have a family wedding with me? One day. Near that door. With all of them,” he said.

She looked at it. No demand, no date: a picture of something he wanted, with her in it, and a door that had once meant the end of a long walk. She folded the napkin carefully and put it beside her cup.

“Not yet.”

“All right.”

“You knew that was the answer.”

“I like drawing you things.”

“You’ll run out of napkins.”

“I’ll buy more.”

She reached across the table and took his hand. “Maybe one day.”

He lifted her hand and kissed her ring. “I’d like that.”

That night he told her the old map itself was up in the flat on the forty-third floor of Meridian, in a box of farm things he’d never unpacked, and she said, “Bring it home.” Lying in the dark she asked what he’d thought when he first saw the red door, after the six days.

“That it was the most beautiful thing I’d ever seen.”

“Because it was home?”

“Because it was open.”

She lay listening to him breathe and thought about all the doors he’d drawn since. The one downstairs that opened from inside whatever the power did. The hatch to the roof. Every exit he counted in every room he walked into. A boy who’d stood outside a gate so long he’d found the crack in it, and had spent every year since making sure that no door he drew would ever keep anyone out, or shut anyone in. She put her hand flat on his chest, over his heart, and left it there until he was asleep.

In the morning she found the napkin tucked into his sketchbook. Beside the door, in his neat capitals, he’d written: THE FIRST PLACE I EVER WANTED TO GO BACK TO. She took his pencil and wrote underneath, in her own scrawl, Not the last, and put the sketchbook back, and went down to make breakfast.

chapters.title: A Commission From the Syndicate
chapters.desc: She finds drawings on the kitchen table for a hidden steel room on the Peak road with C.S. in the corner. Their worst fight ends on the workbench, and on Monday he bolts a safe to the floor.
chapters.epigraph: “Nobody looks at me. That’s the whole point.” “I looked.”
chapters.content:
Jinx found the drawings because Raiden had forgotten to put them away, which he never did.

He left tea mugs in places that defied architecture. He sent her cats at two in the morning. He could turn a shopping list into a scaled diagram with a north arrow. But client drawings lived in a locked drawer at the practice on the forty-first floor of Meridian, and what came home were sketches. So on the last Saturday in June, when she ran upstairs because his phone was ringing on the kitchen table beside a bowl of peaches, and found a roll of plans under it with the elastic off, she looked.

A house on the Peak road. A long drive, a garden terrace that faced the harbour, two staircases, a service entrance, a small lift from the garage to the upper floors. Elegant, the way his work always was, the rooms opening out of each other like a sentence that made sense.

Then the room.

It was under the main staircase, behind what the plan called a storage wall. Steel-lined. Its own air. Its own power. A telephone line that didn’t go through the house. A hidden door, and a second way out under the garden. She turned the sheet. A washroom. Water. Shelves for food and medical supplies. Sections through the stair showing the slab thickened and two columns stiffened to take the weight. It had been built for six.

In the top corner, in his small capitals, were two initials.

C.S.

She didn’t have to want to be wrong for long. Everybody who’d grown up under the flyover knew those letters. Half of what had come into her father’s shop at night, with the plates already off, had come in for men who answered to them.

She heard him on the stairs with a box of compressor fittings. He came in, saw her, saw the table, and his face changed. Not much. Enough.

“Chen Si,” she said.

He put the box down. “Yes.”

“You’re building him a safe room.”

“Designing it. Yes.”

“How long?”

“Three weeks. His man Qian came to the practice at the beginning of June. I said no. Then Chen Si asked to see me himself. He was in the room under Elowen’s shop the night it was finished. He remembered it. The house is new, they bought it in the spring, and nobody’s meant to know they have it. The room’s for Aurelia.” He didn’t look away.

“Is that why you’ve been going to the Peak?”

“Yes.”

“How many times?”

“Four. Once he was there. Last Tuesday. He wanted to talk about the door.”

“And you weren’t going to tell me.”

“I was going to.”

“When?”

He had no answer, and they both heard him not have one.

She put the sheet down carefully. “You built a room for us. Downstairs. With the lamp in it. And now you’re building one for him.” Her voice wasn’t steady and she hated that.

“The principles are the same. Air, power, a line out, more than one exit. Those aren’t unusual—”

“Don’t explain engineering to me.”

He stopped.

“Does he know about ours?”

“No.”

“Does he know where we live?”

“He knows I have a workshop project. Not where. I’m doing the room and nothing else. His engineer, his builder, his project manager. I don’t touch his security or what goes on the shelves.” He was still.

“I didn’t think it would affect you,” he said, a moment later, and heard it as soon as it was out.

“Say that again. Slowly,” said Jinx.

“That isn’t what I meant. I meant I didn’t think the work would put you in danger.”

“That’s better?”

“No.”

“It’s what you used to say. Before the van. You’d decide what I needed to know because you were protecting me. Do you know what I see when I look at that drawing? A man who knows how to build a room nobody can find. Who knows how to keep people alive when someone comes looking. And I see my husband carrying all of that up the Peak road four times without telling me.” She walked to the window and looked down at the yard, at the roll-up door of her own shop, and came back.

“I accepted it because I thought I could do it safely.”

“You’re the key, Raiden. You know where the steel is and where it isn’t. Where the air comes in. How the door’s hidden. How to get in and out. What happens when somebody wants that? Or wants the room to keep someone in instead of out?” She put her finger on the hidden door.

“I’d never design it to trap anybody.”

“I know you wouldn’t. They might want you to. That’s what frightens me.” Her jaw had gone tight and her eyes were bright, and she let him see both.

She had never said it before. Not when he bought her building, not when he sacked the steel man, not when she’d found out he’d mapped every drain round her father’s shop. She’d been angry and she’d been hurt, but she had never once said frightened, and he went white.

He took a step. She put up a hand.

“I know how clever you are. I know you can walk into a dangerous room and look so harmless that everybody forgets to be careful of you.”

“Nobody looks at me. That’s the whole point.”

“I looked. You think because you can see the exits, you can always get out. You can’t design your way out of everything.” Her hand dropped.

“I don’t think I’m invulnerable.”

“No. You think you’re responsible for everyone. And you think that means nobody gets to question the risks you take.”

“That’s not fair.”

“Neither is finding out from a drawing on my kitchen table.”

He was quiet for a long breath. “I should have told you. Before I said yes. I was wrong.”

She knew he meant it. It didn’t undo three weeks or four trips or the two letters in the corner.

“Are you going to finish it?”

“I haven’t decided.”

“You’ve started.”

“Yes.”

“Then you’ve decided.”

“Jia, I don’t want to fight with you.”

“Then you shouldn’t have kept this from me.”

“I know.”

“Stop saying you know.”

There were things she couldn’t get into the right order: that she hated the Peak road, hated that Chen Si now knew how to reach him, hated that their room, with the lamp and the tin of peaches, had become a reference for somebody else’s. That she was terrified of loving a man who could walk into a place like that and call it work. So she did what she did when words wouldn’t come. She took a fistful of his shirt.

He looked down at her hand, and then at her, and she pulled.

He kissed her before she could, hard, with no care in it at all, one hand at the back of her neck. She kissed him back as if she were furious with him for being there, and he kissed her as if he knew he had no right to make her stop being furious. When she broke off she was breathing badly.

“You’re still an idiot.”

“Yes.”

“An extremely expensive idiot.”

Something helpless crossed his face. She kissed him again, and he lifted her, and she locked her legs round his waist, and he carried her down the stairs into the shop with the plans still lying on the table above them and the fight still lying between them, and neither of them pretended otherwise.

The bench was cold under her palms when he set her on it. He pushed the tools back with one arm. She pulled his shirt over his head and threw it somewhere near the compressor, and he dragged her vest up and off and put his mouth to her collarbone, her breast, the place under it where her heart was going too fast. There was nothing playful in it. No rules. No teasing. He stopped once, with his forehead on hers.

“Are you sure?”

“Yes. I want you. Now.” She already had his belt open.

He got her out of her work trousers with a kind of desperate clumsiness that would have made her laugh on any other day, and she pulled him in by the hips, and he pushed into her in one long slow stroke that took the breath out of both of them. She held on to his shoulders. The bench knocked against the wall. A socket set slid and went over the edge in a crash of steel, and neither of them looked. He moved in her hard and deep, his hand flat on the small of her back to keep her from the edge, his eyes on her face as if he needed to watch every bit of it, and she wrapped herself round him and met him and dug her nails into his back, angry and wanting and still in love with him, all of it at once. When she came it went through her like current. She bit his shoulder to keep from shouting and he said her name into her hair, Jia, Jia, and followed her with a sound she’d never heard him make.

It forgave nothing and solved nothing upstairs. It was just the one thing they could still reach for without having to explain.

Afterwards they lay on the old canvas dust sheet on the floor because neither of them could face the stairs. He was on his back with his arm under his head. She was looking at the steel joists in the roof he’d built her.

“Your back?” he said.

“Fine.”

“Your shoulder?”

“You’re the one with teeth marks.”

He found her hand. She let him have it.

“Are you still angry?” he said.

“Yes. Are you?”

That surprised her, and she turned her head.

“I’m angry I made you find out like that. I’m angry I thought keeping it quiet was the same as keeping you safe. And I’m angry because I don’t know how to do this without getting it wrong.”

“Then get it wrong where I can see it. Don’t decide things behind my back and call it protection,” said Jinx.

“I won’t.”

“Don’t promise something you can’t keep.”

He thought about it properly, which she loved him for, even now. “I’ll tell you before I agree to anything like this again. Even if I haven’t decided what I’m going to do.”

“That’s a start.”

There was something she didn’t say, lying there. There was a letter in the kitchen drawer under the tea towels, from the Births and Deaths Registry, that had come on Thursday. After twenty months of statutory declarations, of Mrs. Tong swearing in front of a commissioner that she’d fed Cao Tiehan’s daughter noodles from the age of three, of her father’s old account books with milk, Jia in the margins of the parts orders, the Registrar had consented. Twenty-five years late, Cao Jia had been born. She hadn’t told him yet. She’d been keeping it to choose her moment, and she lay on the floor of her shop knowing exactly what that made her.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Monday morning he bought a safe.

It was small and heavy, meant for documents, and he had it bolted to the concrete in the shop office behind the parts cabinet. She found him testing the lock.

“Would you like the combination?”

“Why?”

“So you can open anything I put in it. Copies of my contracts. Project papers. Anything about the house or my work that I’d otherwise keep somewhere you can’t see.”

“That doesn’t solve the problem.”

“I know. It isn’t meant to. It’s somewhere you can see what I’m keeping. So I can’t quietly move things out of sight and pretend they don’t exist.” He closed the door.

“That’s a very expensive apology.”

“Probably.”

She held out her hand, and he told her the numbers, and she put them in herself. Inside were two folders. HOUSEHOLD. WORK, PRIVATE. The Peak drawings were in the second one.

“You’re organising your secrets.”

“I’m trying to stop having them.”

She went upstairs, and came back down with the registry envelope, and put it in the safe on top of his folders. He looked at it, and at her.

“Mine. Read it,” she said.

He read it standing by the cabinet. She watched him get to the end, and watched his face go through about four things. “Thursday?”

“Thursday.”

“And you didn’t—”

“No. Same as you. Don’t.” She shut the safe.

“I wasn’t going to say anything.”

“Your face was.”

He folded his arms round her from behind and put his chin on her head and didn’t say anything for some time. “So we can go back and sign the book.”

“In September. When the clerk’s back from leave. Still angry, by the way.” She tipped her head against his chest.

“Understood.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The Peak commission went on. He’d started it, and he wasn’t going to walk out halfway and leave somebody else to guess at his steel. But the way he did it changed.

Raiden: Going up.

And later:

Raiden: Back.

The first time she didn’t answer. The second time she sent Eat something. The third time she sent Back where? and he sent Coast road. Ten minutes and she sent Don’t text and drive and he sent Stopped, and she rolled her eyes, and when he came in she looked at his face. He let her. After a while it was ordinary. Going up. Take the drawings. Back. Dinner. Sometimes he sent the harbour from the terrace. Sometimes she sent him a sheared bolt. Once she sent a customer asleep in the waiting chair with his mouth open, and he replied with a sleeping dog, and she banned animals after midnight, and he sent a goat.

They weren’t uncomplicated. But the quiet between them had stopped being comfortable, and Jinx liked that better.

✦ ✦ ✦

In August he mentioned the wedding over the stove.

“Aurelia’s decided Elowen never had a proper one. She said so at Sunday lunch with a glass of wine in her hand and nobody was brave enough to argue. The shop’s closing for three days. The twenty-third of September. Thirty people,” he said, stirring soup.

“Didn’t Elowen already marry Zhao?”

“At a registry on a Tuesday. No flowers she didn’t carry herself. Aurelia’s very upset about it on her behalf.”

“Your family’s exhausting.”

“Sometimes. Elowen told me to bring whoever it is I keep disappearing to.” He didn’t look round.

Jinx’s hands stopped on the box of connectors she was sorting.

“She doesn’t know. She knows there’s someone. She thinks it’s a girlfriend I’m embarrassed about,” he said.

“Zhao knows.”

“Zhao knows everything. He hasn’t told her because I haven’t.”

“Who’s going?”

“Family. Some old friends. Chen Si and Aurelia, she’s running it. My father.” He put the spoon down.

She thought about the red door at two in the morning, with his ring catching the streetlight, and her own voice saying one day. She hadn’t expected one day to come with flowers.

That night, on the bed, he asked her properly. She was brushing her hair out and he was folding shirts.

“Do you want to come?”

“Do you want me there?”

“Yes. She’s my sister. I think she’d like you. And I want to stand next to my wife. Not as a secret. Not as someone I brought and didn’t explain. As you. We’ll go together and leave when you want. You don’t have to speak to anyone you don’t want to.” He sat down beside her. He took the brush out of her hand and worked it gently through the ends.

“And Chen Si?”

“I’ll keep the work out of it. If he talks to you, you decide whether you answer.”

“All right. I’ll come,” she said.

He looked so pleased that she pointed at him.

“Don’t. And I’m not wearing anything ridiculous. And don’t buy me a dress. And don’t tell your sister my size.”

“I wasn’t going to.”

She got up and opened the wardrobe and held a black dress against herself and put it back, and he watched her do it with his whole face lit up, and she said “Don’t” again without turning round.

“What colour is Elowen’s dress?”

“I don’t know.”

“Find out. And what kind of flowers.”

“White ones, I think.”

“That’s no use.”

“I’ll ask.”

She stood there a moment longer with her hand on the wardrobe door. “I want to meet your sister. Now tell me what Aurelia’s like. I’m not walking into a wedding without knowing who I’m standing next to,” she said. Then she sat back down on the bed.

So he told her. Elowen, who would cry first. Zhao, who wouldn’t, and would want to. Chen Si, who would cheer like a schoolboy at exactly one moment and be frightening for the rest. Aurelia, who ran fashion weeks and would run this. Which of them arrived early, which talked too much, which would pretend not to notice anything at all. She listened with her knees drawn up, already thinking about boots, and whether her good jacket would do, and he looked at her doing it.

“What?” she said.

“I like this.”

“Me thinking about clothes?”

“You thinking about coming with me.”

“Don’t get used to it.”

“Too late,” he said, and kissed her hand.

chapters.title: Meeting the Family Properly
chapters.desc: Elowen’s wedding in the flower shop. “This is Jinx. My wife.” Thirty people go silent, Lin Jian walks out into the street, and she goes after him.
chapters.epigraph: “I’ve always wondered what happened to you.”
chapters.content:
Three weeks before the wedding, on Friday the first of September, they went back to the registry in the old town.

The same cream walls, the same creaking stair, the same registrar with silver glasses, who remembered them. “The washers,” she said, and smiled, and opened the big book and wrote it in at last, with the twenty months of declarations clipped behind it: Lin Raiden. Cao Jia. That day’s date. In the eyes of the people who kept books, they’d been married for about four minutes. Raiden signed and then stood looking at the page as if it were a drawing he hadn’t expected to like. Out on the steps he said, “Two years and four minutes,” and Jinx said, “Don’t,” and he said it again on the bus.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the day of Elowen’s wedding she spent the morning under a taxi and the afternoon getting taxi out from under her nails.

The cake had come to her on the Thursday. Elara had made it in secret, four tiers, and wouldn’t say what was in it, and had looked at the sidecar and then at Jinx and asked, politely, whether the bottom tier could travel by motorbike. Jinx had gone downstairs and built a steel box for it with a foam-lined cradle and a lid that clamped, so that the tier would stay level if she went over a kerb, a speed bump, or a man. It sat strapped into ARCHITECT’s seat. Raiden, who’d been demoted to the pillion, photographed it eight times before they’d left the yard.

“It’s a cake,” said Jinx.

“It’s my sister’s cake, in a box you made, in a sidecar named after a dog. Somebody should be documenting it.”

They parked across the street from the flower shop just before four. It was a narrow old place, its windows full of white roses and green, and inside, through the glass, she could see more people than she’d been promised, all of them moving at once: tables under linen, buckets pushed to the back, greenery hung from the ceiling, a woman in pearls with two phones directing everybody. Aurelia, she supposed.

“That’s more than thirty,” she said.

“Some of them are helping.”

“That’s what people say when they invite forty.”

“Do you want to leave?” He wasn’t teasing. He was watching her face.

She looked through the window. Elowen with her hair pinned up and a phone in one hand. Zhao near the back, still, talking to an old man. A girl with wavy brown hair in a claw clip and round glasses up a stepladder, threading lights through the ceiling greenery. And at the front, in a black suit, a grey-haired man she’d seen across a ballroom once and outside a red door in her head a hundred times.

“My father,” said Raiden.

“I know.”

She lifted the steel box out of the sidecar, and then she reached into her jacket pocket for the little square of cloth with her ring in it, the way she always did after riding so it wouldn’t catch on her gloves, and put it on. She looked at his collar. There was a bit of string under it. There had been, on and off, for two years.

“Take that off,” she said.

He looked at her for a second as if he needed to be sure what she meant. Then he put his hand to the back of his neck and snapped the string, and the washer dropped into his palm, and he put it on his finger. It was a little loose. She’d made it that way, because she hadn’t known how his hands would change, and because she’d cared more about it not cutting him than about it looking elegant.

“Ready?” he said.

“The cake’s ready. You’re the unstable component.”

He laughed, and took her free hand, and they went in.

✦ ✦ ✦

He walked her into the middle of thirty people and stopped.

“Everyone. This is Jinx. My wife. She built Xiao Pan’s bike. Don’t touch her tools,” he said.

The shop went completely silent. Someone put a glass down slowly.

“That’s my mechanic,” said Xiao Pan.

The girl on the ladder said, “Since when?”

“Two years next Saturday.”

“Two years?”

“We were going to tell you.”

“When?”

Raiden considered. “Today, as it turns out.”

Elowen crossed the shop and hit him on the arm, quite hard, and then put both arms round him. “You idiot.”

Then she turned to Jinx, and Jinx braced herself, and found she was trying not to laugh.

“I’m furious,” Elowen told her.

“I know. He said you would be.”

“Thank you for marrying him.”

That one went somewhere Jinx hadn’t guarded. She looked at the steel box in her hands for a second. “He makes very good fish,” she said.

Behind them, on the step, Lin Jian had come in with a box of fruit. He’d stopped when he heard my wife. He looked at his son, and the ring, and the girl wearing the other one, and he put the fruit down on the step and walked back out into the street.

Nobody moved. Jinx put the cake down on the nearest table and went after him.

He was standing on the pavement with his hands at his sides, looking at nothing. She stood next to him with her hands in her jacket pockets. She didn’t say anything. She’d stood next to her own father like this enough times to know there wasn’t anything to say. Traffic went by. A bus. Somebody’s radio.

After a while he looked at her properly, the way you’d look at an engine you thought you recognised. Then, quite he pointed at her, and his whole face changed.

“Cao Tiehan’s girl. Under the bench. Fifteen years old, with a carburettor in pieces on a newspaper,” he said.

“Twelve.”

“Twelve. He cooks, you said? My son?” He laughed, short and startled.

“Better than you.”

Then he laughed properly. “Dinner. Next week. Bring him,” he said.

She remembered it now. A man in a dark coat in her father’s doorway, come to collect something that had been wrapped in a blanket in the back. He’d stood over her bench and asked whether she was sure she could put that back together, and she’d told him that if he knew how to do it better he could do it himself.

“You were very rude to me,” said Lin Jian, as if he’d followed her thinking.

“You deserved it.”

“I did. I’ve always wondered what happened to you.” He looked at her ring again.

“This,” said Jinx, and held up her hand.

He nodded slowly, and picked up his box of fruit from the step, and went inside, and she went in after him and stood by the door, next to a pale, quiet woman with a black ribbon in her hair who Jinx knew must be Evangeline. Neither of them said a word. They stood side by side and watched the street, and it was the most comfortable five minutes she’d had all day.

✦ ✦ ✦

The shop started breathing again. People looked at her hand and then at his. She’d expected that. She hadn’t expected Raiden to look so pleased with himself about it that she had to send him to fetch water.

She unclamped the steel box and lifted the tier out, and it was perfect: not a crack in the icing, not one sugar petal shifted. The rest of the cake was on a table by the wall, four tiers of lemon under camellias so fine you could see the light through them. Elara, pink to the ears, came and looked at the bottom tier and then hugged Jinx so that Jinx went stiff for half a second before she hugged her back. A tall man in gold-rimmed glasses had already taken up a position beside the cake, alone, as if somebody had asked him to guard it. Nobody introduced him. Every time Elara walked past, he looked at her, and then at nothing.

“Who’s that?”

“No idea,” said Raiden, which she didn’t believe.

There were people she knew only by reputation. Chen Si, by the window, in a dark suit, with the room leaving a little space round him without anyone deciding to. Aurelia, in blue, with the phones. And a young man in a dark suit who stood by the window all evening and every so often looked up at the roof of the building across the street, and then at Evangeline by the door, and said nothing to anyone.

“Who’s the one watching the roof?”

“Song Wei Long. He’s a detective.”

“Why is there a detective at a wedding?”

“He’s a friend of Elowen’s.”

“Does he know he’s at a wedding?”

“I think so,” said Raiden, and she caught his sleeve before he could go and check.

“Do you want me to introduce you?” He meant Chen Si.

She looked across the room. Chen Si turned his head as if he’d felt it and gave her a small nod, the nod of a man who knew exactly whose drawings were on the Peak road. She gave him one back.

“Not yet,” she said, and Raiden didn’t ask again, and she was more grateful for that than she let him see.

✦ ✦ ✦

The rain stopped at half past nine, and the shop filled with grey light and the smell of wet roses. Elowen came down the narrow aisle in plain ivory with yellow roses and white lisianthus, and her father walked beside her in his black suit with his reading glasses forgotten in his breast pocket, crying before they’d taken three steps and not wiping it. Halfway down he stopped and asked Zhao, across the whole room, how the lemon tree was. Zhao’s face changed. “Nine lemons.” Lin Jian nodded as if that settled everything, put his daughter’s hand in Zhao’s, and went and sat in the front row and held Evangeline’s hand instead.

Jinx stood at the back with Raiden, their shoulders touching. When Elowen got to the part about ordinary mornings, and a hand finding hers under the table, he slid his fingers between Jinx’s. She looked up. He was watching his sister with a face that had a little sadness in it and a lot of relief, and she squeezed his hand and didn’t say anything, and he didn’t need her to.

At nineteen minutes to ten the lights came on all at once, hundreds of them, threaded through the greenery overhead by the girl on the ladder, and Zhao kissed his wife under them, long and slow, with both hands on her face. Chen Si cheered like a schoolboy. Aurelia cried into a handkerchief. Lin Jian looked down at his hands and smiled.

“Thank you for marrying me,” Raiden said into Jinx’s hair.

“Not during your sister’s wedding.”

“Right. Sorry.”

She looked at him a second longer, and then went up on her toes and kissed the corner of his mouth. “Later.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Zhao ate two pieces of cake and was accused of eating Elowen’s. Raiden danced with her between the tables, badly, and she let him. Lin Jian came and sat opposite them for ten minutes while they ate, and asked what Raiden cooked, and laughed when Raiden said whatever she wants and Jinx said within reason.

“Bring your wok on Saturday. Ah Sim always said you’d make a good cook if you stopped setting fire to things,” said Lin Jian.

Jinx turned. “You set fire to things?”

“Once,” said Raiden.

“More than once,” said his father.

Later Elowen found her alone at the back by a shelf of pots, and stood next to her for a while choosing her words.

“I’m still angry, a little.”

“That’s fair.”

“He’s always been like this. If he wants something, he acts as if he doesn’t mind. If he’s frightened, he looks bored. If he’s hurt, he makes a joke. With you he doesn’t seem to be doing any of that.” She looked across the shop at her brother, who was arguing with Xiao Pan about the gearing on a bike that wasn’t there.

“He still acts stupid.”

“I know.”

“Constantly. On purpose.”

“Especially on purpose. I’d like us to be family. If you want it.” Elowen laughed.

“We can try,” said Jinx.

“I’ll want the whole story.”

“That’s less reasonable.”

Elowen kissed her cheek before she let her go, and said she’d have the full story out of her eventually, and Jinx believed her completely.

✦ ✦ ✦

They left the bike in a garage round the corner and took a taxi, because it was nearly midnight and she’d had two glasses of wine and she didn’t ride on wine. The city went past in streaks of yellow. He’d been quiet for a block or two, turning the washer on his finger.

He said, “Zhao said something to me. At the back. He said he’d known since your jacket on the chair. Then he told me to look after you.”

“And?”

“I said I intended to. And he said, I wasn’t talking to you, and looked across the room at you.”

“So who was he talking to?”

“I’ve been trying to work it out for two hours.”

Jinx laughed so loudly the driver checked the mirror.

At the first red light he kissed her, enough that the driver probably didn’t notice. She kept her eyes on his face. “That’s one.”

At the next red light she met him halfway, and it went on longer, and she caught his collar when he pulled back. “Two.”

At the third he kissed her cheek. “That doesn’t count.”

“Why not?”

“Because you didn’t do it properly.”

So he did it properly, and the driver cleared his throat, and Jinx said “Sorry” to the front of the car without meaning it.

At the fourth light she kissed him first. “Four.”

“You’re counting.”

“Someone has to. You’re going to keep doing it.”

His hand found hers on the seat between them and the two washers clicked together, metal on metal. No string. No pocket. No hiding place under a shirt. She looked down at their hands. Then the lights went red again, and she turned her face up to him and said “Last one,” and when the lights changed neither of them moved, and the driver waited, and then laughed and said, “You can finish at home.”

Jinx put her hand over her face.

“Yes. That’s the plan,” said Raiden, entirely unhelpfully, delighted.

chapters.title: Her Father Calls After Five Years
chapters.desc: Six weeks of building a taxi called Nobody at night. Then a phone call from under the flyover, a photograph of her childhood camp bed with her husband’s face above it, and a note under his keys.
chapters.epigraph: “Gone to see my father. Don’t come.”
chapters.content:
The second time Jinx met the quiet one, he stood in her shop for eleven minutes without saying a word.

The first time had been ten days earlier, in Serafina’s garage under the railway bridge. Now it was the third Saturday in September, and he was standing by her roll-up door with a paper bag of buns while she and Serafina argued over a silver-grey 2006 saloon that had been a taxi for eleven years and that Serafina had found that morning behind a fleet yard on the docks road. It had a dent over the back wheel, a crack in the dash, a meter still bolted under it, and a back seat that smelt of cigarettes and lemon cleaner. Serafina thought it was perfect.

“Fine, one order. No questions. I don’t want to know where it’s going, or who’s chasing it, or your name,” she said in the end.

That was to him.

“And nobody lies to me about what it has to do. And you never bring it back here with a hole in it,” she said.

“Agreed,” said the quiet one. It was the first thing he’d said.

“And you. Wash my floor. Every night. Good soap.” A black-nailed finger at Serafina.

So that was how the nights began.

✦ ✦ ✦

They worked on it for six weeks with the shutter down and only the bench lamps on. Jinx stripped it to the shell and did the body and the paint and every part that wasn’t optional if a Song was going to drive it. Serafina did the mechanical work and drank too much coffee. The quiet one helped where he could and stood where he wasn’t in the way, which took some doing in her shop. Twice a girl with a ring through her nose came in after ten, pulled the old dispatch terminal and satellite box out from behind the dash, went through every wire with a meter looking for anything else that talked, and left. Serafina washed the floor every night. Jinx checked it every morning and found nothing to complain about, which annoyed her.

From the outside it stayed a tired taxi nobody would hail twice. Underneath it was a bigger saloon’s drivetrain, brakes off something much faster, dampers she and Serafina argued about for two days, and a cabin set up for two people who might have to sit in it a long time. “You’ll test it properly. Not your definition of properly,” she told Serafina.

Raiden was upstairs. He texted her anyway.

Raiden: Still working?

Jinx: No. Asleep.

Raiden: Have you eaten?

Jinx: Food.

He didn’t come down. He didn’t ask whose car it was. He left a bowl covered on the stove every night and told her which one, and she never told him how much she noticed.

On the fourth Saturday in September, at twenty-six minutes to three, he came down with a drawing tube under his arm, looked at the dent over the wheel arch, and said, “I was thinking how much work you’ve given me.” He touched the back of Jinx’s neck as he went past and spread a cutaway of the whole car across her bench in pencil and ink, every part they’d renewed in small clear notes. The quiet one looked at the two seats on the drawing. When Raiden asked what they were calling it, he said “Nobody,” and Raiden wrote it in the corner in his neat capitals. “I want it recorded that I objected,” said Jinx, and an hour later she was strapping a cake tier into her sidecar and forgot about taxis for a day.

One night in October he did come down. It was seven minutes past two. She was on her back under the car, reaching past a support for something she couldn’t see.

“Don’t step there,” she called.

“Good evening to you too.”

She slid out. He was standing by the door with a thermos in one hand and a paper bag in the other, in the dark green jumper she liked, hair everywhere. Serafina looked up from a stool. “Hello, Raiden.”

“Soup. Enough for everyone.”
