Jinx unscrewed the thermos and smelt it. Chicken and mushroom, and ginger, a little, not too much, the amount that settled her stomach after hours of coffee and stubbornness. He’d remembered. She looked at him over the rim. “Thank you.”

He sat at the far end of the bench with a pencil and a scrap of paper while she ate, and didn’t look at the car, which must have taken every ounce of self-control he had. When she went to see what he was drawing, it wasn’t the car. It was her, upside down, half under it, one arm reaching, with 2:07 in the corner. She folded it once and put it in the lid of her toolbox, and he noticed and said nothing.

“Don’t work till sunrise,” he said, and kissed her temple, and went up.

Serafina waited till the door shut. “He didn’t ask anything.”

“No.”

“He’s very nice.”

“Unfortunately,” said Jinx, and threw a rag at her.

Nobody was finished on the last Saturday in October. Not perfect, not new, finished enough. The car stayed in her yard another fortnight while Serafina fussed over it. On the evening of the seventh of November the quiet one walked in, looked at Raiden on the sofa and Jinx by the door, and showed Serafina something on his phone, which was the marriage register with Lin Raiden. Cao Jia. on it and the first of September beside it, and Serafina shouted at them both for twenty minutes, and then hugged them. “Your fiancé is terrifying,” Jinx told her.

“He’s thorough,” said Serafina. A week later the two of them took a train south, and Nobody sat under a cover in the corner of her yard, and the shop was quiet, and the drawing of her under it was still in the lid of her toolbox.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her phone rang on a Thursday afternoon in the middle of November, an unknown number, while she was checking a parts order. She almost let it go.

“Jia.”

Her hand stopped on the screen. She hadn’t heard that voice in five years. It came with engine oil and cigarettes and the smell of the back room.

“Dad?”

“You still have this number.”

“Yes.”

“How are you?”

“Fine.”

“Good. I need to talk to you. There’s trouble. Money.” A long breath. Her father could talk for an hour about a cracked head or a customer who’d tried to cheat him, but anything else made him go quiet.

“Your debts?”

“They’ve been bought. All of them. In September. A man called Guo. He buys debts.”

“What does he want?”

“Bikes. Twelve. Not ours. He says you can do it. He knows about your work. He’s been asking about you, Jia. I told him you don’t come here. He knows anyway.” He meant stolen.

“Where are you?”

“The shop.”

“Don’t go anywhere. I’ll ring you back.”

She put the phone down on the bench and washed her hands. Then she washed them again. The phone buzzed.

Unknown: [a photograph]

A narrow room. A stained wall. An old camp bed with a thin mattress and one bent leg, a faded blanket, a plastic table with a cup on it. She’d slept in that bed when she was small, in the room behind her father’s shop, before the blue suitcase went out of the door and didn’t come back. Above it, on the wall, someone had hung a small cheap frame. She enlarged it.

It was Raiden. Standing outside her roll-up door beside ARCHITECT with his helmet in his hand, taken from across the street.

Unknown: Sunday. Twelve bikes. No questions. Nothing that leads back to us.

Unknown: Your father owes a great deal. You can clear it.

Unknown: You still remember your old room, don’t you?

She turned the phone off and went upstairs and didn’t tell him.

He was at the stove with his sleeves pushed up, stirring something and reading on his phone. “Long day?”

“Mm.”

“Wash your hands. It’s nearly ready.”

She washed them. Twice. He put out bowls behind her, and then he stood at her back with his hands at her waist, and kissed the side of her head. “You’re cold.”

“I’m fine.”

He didn’t argue. He reached past her and turned off the tap and gave her the towel.

At the table he told her his father wanted to know whether to have the fish she liked on Saturday. She answered when she had to. Her phone lay face down by her bowl the whole time, and he saw it, and didn’t touch it. She watched his ring catch the light while he washed up and was more frightened than she’d ever been of anything, not of Guo or twelve bikes but of a photograph of her husband’s face hung over the bed she’d slept in as a child.

“I need to go down to the shop. Something I forgot,” she said.

“Do you want me to come?”

“No.”

He looked at her. Then he nodded. She kissed his cheek, too quickly, and he caught her hand before she could go. “Come back before you’re too tired. Love you.”

“I know,” she said, and left before he could see her face.

She wrote it on the back of a parts receipt in the shop office. Gone to see my father. Don’t come. Then, under it: I’m safe. I’ll call you. It was a lie, and she left it in. She went up the back stairs while he was in the shower and put it on the kitchen table under his keys. She took her old black jacket and her helmet and the pouch with her papers in it, and she took Carp, because she wasn’t putting ARCHITECT anywhere near that photograph.

✦ ✦ ✦

Raiden found the note at 10:46.

He read it twice. He rang her. It went to voicemail. He sent Where are you? and nothing came back. He rang again. Her helmet was gone from the hook. Her jacket. Her spare gloves. Downstairs, ARCHITECT was in its place and Carp wasn’t. In the wardrobe, the pouch where she kept her papers had gone.

He knew what Don’t come meant when she was angry, and when she needed space, and when she was frightened and didn’t want him to see.

He went to his drafting table and opened the bottom drawer and took out a folder from under a pile of old invoices. Six printed pages, two years old. WORKSHOP UNDER THE FLYOVER. Every road and door he’d been able to see from a roof, the open drain, the three ways out from under the flyover, which lamps worked. At the bottom: DO NOT GO IN WITHOUT HER KNOWING. DO NOT GO NEAR HER FATHER.

It wasn’t in the safe. He’d moved everything else into the safe in June and left this in a drawer under invoices, and he stood there and looked at what that made him for about as long as he could bear to.

Then he put the folder inside his coat and went down into the street and got a taxi.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her father was in a plastic chair outside the shop under a strip of yellow light, smoking. He’d got old. His shoulders had narrowed and his hair had gone grey at the sides, and there were lines round his mouth that hadn’t been there five years ago. He stood up when he saw her.

“You still ride that?”

“Yes.”

“Good.” It was the closest he’d ever come to telling her he’d been proud of anything.

Inside it smelt exactly as it always had, oil and damp concrete and smoke. And on the wall over the bench, someone had hung the photograph.

“I didn’t put it there,” he said.

“Who did?”

“Guo’s people. Yesterday. They asked if you still came. If you’d come back. If you had a husband.”

“Did you tell them his name?”

“No. They knew it. He showed me, Jia. When he bought the debt. He had it on his phone. The marriage book, your name in it next to the Lin boy’s. That’s how he found you.” He looked at the floor.

She took the frame off the wall. It was cheap plastic, taped at the back. Under the tape was a folded slip. Twelve bikes. Sunday. And a number. She put it in her pocket.

“Why didn’t you go to the police?”

“You think I didn’t try?”

“Lin Jian, then. You worked for his people for twenty years.”

“And owe the Lins too? Your mother left debts. Then the shop. I borrowed to pay off the borrowing.” He sat down on an upturned crate.

The camp bed was still in the back room. Same frame, same bent leg, a blanket folded at the foot. She went and stood in the doorway.

“Why did you keep this?”

“Because it was yours.”

“You didn’t keep anything else. You didn’t keep me on paper. You never registered me. Do you know what that was like, at the registry? With him standing next to me? I had to swear in front of a commissioner that I’d been born. Mrs. Tong had to swear she’d fed me. Your account books did more for me than you did. Milk, Jia, in the margin of a parts order.” She heard her voice go hard and let it.

His face folded. “I meant to.”

“You didn’t call. You didn’t look for me.”

“I did. Not enough,” he said honestly.

There was no yellow lamp in that room, and nobody telling her nobody was coming back. Only a narrow bed, and a photograph of the man she loved.

Her phone buzzed. Sunday. Don’t make us ask twice. She deleted it.

“What are you going to do?” said her father.

“Find out who Guo is. And you’re going to tell me everything.”

He told her: the three lenders, the visits, the list of bikes. He didn’t tell her how much, or whether he’d already said yes. She wrote down names and promised him nothing.

“You look like your mother,” he said at the end.

“Don’t,” said Jinx.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was twenty to midnight when she looked at her phone properly. Six missed calls. Three from Raiden. She typed I’m with my father. I’m safe. Don’t come and sent it before she could think.

Raiden: I know where you are.

She went to the window.

He was across the street under the flyover, his coat dark against the concrete, his face turned towards the light in her father’s shop. He lifted one hand. Not waving. Just letting her know.

Anger came first, then fear, then something much worse, which was relief.

Raiden: I won’t come closer unless you ask me to.

Jinx: How did you find me?

Raiden: I had a map.

Of course he did.

She crossed the street and stopped just out of his reach.

“You made a map.”

“Yes.”

“Of my father’s street. Two years ago. Without telling me.”

“Yes.”

“It wasn’t in the safe.”

“No.”

She let out a long breath. “I’m going to be furious about that later. Why are you here?”

“Because you left me a note telling me not to come. You’d never have written it unless you were frightened. I won’t go in. I won’t go near your father. But I needed to see you were alive.”

“I’m fine.”

He didn’t argue. She hated how gently he let her lie. She touched the washer on his finger, and then she told him about the photograph, and the bed, and the slip behind the frame, and the marriage book on Guo’s phone, and watched his face go completely still.

“Are you hurt?”

“No.”

“I’m sorry for the note.”

“I’m not angry about the note. I’m worried about you.”

“That’s worse.”

“I know. I brought the map.” He touched her cheek, slowly enough for her to pull away, and she leaned into his hand instead.

“Of course you did. You’re not allowed to make any more maps of my life. And you’re not allowed to follow me like this again. And if I tell you not to come—”

“I’ll ask why. And if you still say don’t, I’ll stay away unless I think you’re in danger.”

“That’s not what I asked.”

“I know,” he said.

She put her forehead against his chest, and his arms came round her, not tight, not as if she might vanish, just enough to hold her, and for a few seconds under the flyover she stopped being the girl who had to sort everything out on her own.

Then she stepped back and took his hand. “Come in. I’m asking.”

Her father was standing just inside the door. He looked at Raiden, and at their hands, and at the rings.

“I’m Raiden.”

“I know who you are.”

“It’s good to meet you.”

“He shouldn’t be here,” her father said to Jinx.

“He’s my husband. I’m not giving Guo twelve bikes. And I’m not letting him use you to get to me. Tomorrow we find out exactly what he thinks he owns.” She put the photograph face down on the bench.

Her phone buzzed on the bench. Sunday’s getting closer. She turned it so Raiden could read it.

“Do you want my family in this?” he said.

“No. Not your father. Not Zhao. Nobody who’ll do it for us. You and me. And I want to know everything before either of us does anything. And no secret arrangements.” She looked at him.

“No secret arrangements,” said Raiden.

He picked up the photograph and put it inside his coat with the map, and didn’t look at it again, and followed his wife out of her father’s shop.

chapters.title: The Men Who Own Her Father
chapters.desc: Under the flyover a polite man in reading glasses swaps twelve stolen bikes for his dead brother’s two-stroke triple, running by seven. Her husband wanders in lost with dumplings, and finds a passage behind her father’s shelves.
chapters.epigraph: “I’m terribly sorry. I think I’m lost. Is this the right flyover?”
chapters.content:
Her father had started sitting down to work.

Jinx saw it the moment she came in under the half-raised shutter on Friday afternoon. He had a stool pulled up to the bench where she’d learned to strip a carburettor at eight, and he was sitting on it to file a key blank, with his elbows close to his body the way old men held themselves when their backs had started to argue. He used to stand all day. He used to shout at the radio and kick tyres to see if they’d kick back and lift a gearbox with one other man while telling him he was useless. Now his hair was nearly all grey and his hands shook a little at the start of every stroke and steadied by the end of it.

“You came back,” he said.

“I said I would.”

He nodded at the file. There was nothing else to say yet, so neither of them said it.

Raiden had gone to the city archive at nine that morning. He’d told her at breakfast, standing at the stove in his socks: “I’m going to look at the drawings for this street. The old ones. I’ll tell you what I find. That’s me telling you.” She’d said fine, and thrown a tea towel at him, and that was the first time since Thursday she’d felt like laughing.

✦ ✦ ✦

Guo came at seven, when the light under the flyover had gone orange and then brown.

Two of his men carried a chair in ahead of him, dark leather, too clean for the place, and set it down where her father’s stool had been. Her father moved the stool without being asked. Guo sat. He was a narrow man in a charcoal suit with reading glasses low on his nose, and he looked like someone who spent his afternoons reading contracts for small mistakes, which as far as she could tell was exactly what he did. One of the men put a cup of tea in his hand. He hadn’t brought one for anyone else.

“Cao Jia, I’ve been looking forward to this,” he said.

“You’re in my father’s place.”

He looked down at the chair as if he’d only just noticed it. “So I am.”

He didn’t get up. He took the photograph out of his inside pocket, the one that had hung over her camp bed, Raiden on the pavement beside ARCHITECT with his hand on the brass plate, and laid it face up on the bench beside his tea.

“Your husband draws for a living. A good family. I made it my business to find out,” he said.

“Then you know I don’t have twelve bikes.”

“I know you could find them by Sunday.”

“I won’t.”

“No, I didn’t think you would. So I have something else for you to do. My younger brother had a motorcycle. A seven-hundred-and-fifty two-stroke triple from 1973. You’ll know the kind,” Guo said, quite pleasantly. He drank some tea.

She did. Everybody who had grown up with a spanner knew the kind. Three cylinders, a frame that had never quite been asked whether it could cope, and power that arrived all at once at the top of the rev range like a door kicked in. Men had called them widowmakers in the seventies, and not as a joke. Her father had shown her one in a magazine when she was eleven and told her the man who designed it was either a genius or a lunatic.

Guo said, “He was arrested on it. Nine years ago. The bike went into the police pound and he went into remand, and he died there before his trial. A heart thing. He was twenty-six. The pound sells what nobody claims. I bought it at their auction last month. It hasn’t turned since the day they wheeled it in.” He said it the way he’d said good family.

“And you want it running.”

“By seven tomorrow morning.”

“That’s not a deadline, that’s a joke.”

“My brother would have liked to hear it. Run it by seven, and you don’t owe me twelve motorcycles. We’ll discuss your father’s account after.” He set the cup down.

“We discuss it now.”

“You’re not in a position to discuss anything now.”

“Then you don’t need me. Running by seven replaces the twelve bikes. Nobody touches it while I work. Nobody tells me to hurry. And when it runs, we talk about the debt with my father in the room.” She looked at him until he looked back.

Guo considered her for some time. Behind his glasses he had a careful, tidy face that gave nothing away, and it occurred to her that a man could miss his brother and still be exactly what he looked like.

“Seven. Dou stays with you,” he said.

The man by the shutter came forward. He was broad and shaven-headed with a heavy jaw and thick forearms, and he looked at her bench the way some men looked at a kitchen, as a place other people worked.

“He doesn’t touch my tools,” said Jinx.

“I’ll see that he behaves,” said Guo, and she didn’t believe a word of it.

✦ ✦ ✦

The van came at nine. Raiden came at twenty to.

She heard him before she saw him. Dou had gone out to smoke at the shutter, and a voice she’d have known through a wall said, apologetically, “I’m terribly sorry. I think I’m lost. Is this the right flyover?”

Jinx shut her eyes.

When she opened them he was ducking under the shutter with a paper bag in one hand and a cardboard tube under his arm, glasses slightly crooked, in the dark green jumper and his old coat, looking like a junior draftsman who’d been sent to the wrong address with the wrong drawings and would be apologising for it all week. Dou had let him in without even looking at the bag. Dou had already decided what he was.

Guo hadn’t. He watched Raiden come across the floor and said, “Mr. Lin. You found us.”

“Eventually. Prawn and chive. And some with cabbage, because I didn’t know what anyone liked.” Raiden put the bag down on the clean end of the bench. He came and stood beside her. Not behind her: beside. She’d asked for that on the street on Thursday night, and he’d remembered.

“You were at the archive,” she said, low.

“Until it shut. Then the dumpling place by the station. I’ll tell you about the archive later. Have you eaten?” He looked at her face.

“No.”

“Then eat first,” he said, and opened the bag.

✦ ✦ ✦

The bike came in on its side in the back of a white van, and when the men stood it up in the work lamps it was worse than she’d hoped and better than she’d feared. Under nine years of pound dust the tank was a dark blue nobody would choose any more, and the chrome had gone the colour of an old spoon. One mirror was missing. Somebody had put the front wheel back on with the spacers the wrong way round. The intake rubbers had gone hard as bone, and when she put a breaker bar on the crank nut and leaned on it, nothing in the engine moved at all.

“It’s seized,” said Dou.

“Thank you. It’s been sitting with water inside it. They pressure-washed it in the pound, probably. Or it sat out in the rain before anybody bothered with a tarp.” She pulled the plugs. Brown, crusted. She put a torch down a plug hole and looked at the top of a piston through a rind of rust.

“Can you fix it?”

“I can tell you when it’s open.”

She was reaching for the tool roll when her father got up off his stool. He went into the little office without a word and was gone long enough that she’d stopped thinking about him, and then he came back with a plastic carrier bag and put it on the bench beside the bike.

Inside was the factory workshop manual. Not a copy: the real one, the cover soft with handling, the spine mended twice with brown tape. She’d forgotten it existed. She opened it and saw her father’s handwriting in the margins, clearances and torque figures crossed out and corrected in blue biro, and on the page for the carburettors, in a round careful hand that wasn’t his, middle one runs hotter with a line under hotter.

She’d written that. She’d been twelve.

She didn’t look at him. He sat back down on his stool. “It was in the cabinet,” he said, to nobody in particular, and went back to his key.

✦ ✦ ✦

By half past eleven the top end was off. Three heads in a row on a clean rag. Three barrels lifted, slowly, with penetrating oil and a soft mallet and a great deal of patience, and the pistons underneath them speckled orange where the rings had rusted into their grooves. The bores were scored but not ruined. The crank, once the pistons were off it, turned. Stiffly, roughly, with a dry complaining sound in the bearings she didn’t like, but it turned.

Raiden held the torch. She hadn’t asked him to; at some point he had been holding it, wherever she needed it, and moving it before she’d finished saying left. He didn’t talk. He didn’t tell her to be careful. Once he fed her a dumpling off the end of a chopstick because both her hands were inside a barrel, and she ate it without looking and said “Thank you” with her mouth full and heard him smile.

Dou didn’t like it. Dou didn’t like any of it. He’d been told to stand in a workshop all night watching a woman take an engine to pieces, and as far as he could see she was only making more pieces. At 1:43 by the clock over the office door he came off the wall.

“Enough. It’s in bits.”

“That’s how you fix it.”

“He wants it running, not on a rag.” He reached past her for the kickstart lever to give the bare crank a shove, and she caught his wrist.

“Don’t.”

He looked down at her hand. Then he pulled free, and his other hand came out of his jacket with a knife in it, short and narrow, and the work lamp found the edge and ran down it.

Her father stood up so fast his stool went over. “Dou—”

“Sit down.”

Raiden had stood up too. He hadn’t moved towards them. He’d only put the torch down on the bench, carefully, with the beam still pointing at the crankcase where she’d need it, and the mild, lost, apologetic face he’d worn under the shutter had gone somewhere and not come back.

“I’d rather you didn’t bring that near my wife,” he said.

Dou laughed. “Or what?”

Raiden didn’t answer. He looked at the knife and then at Dou’s feet and then at Dou’s face, the way he looked at a building he’d been asked to survey, and something about the quality of the looking made Dou stop laughing.

“Dou. Put it away. She’s working.” Guo hadn’t got out of his chair.

It went away. Dou went back to his wall and leaned on it and watched Raiden instead, which was worse. Guo turned a page of the newspaper he’d been reading and said, without looking up, “Perhaps Mr. Lin would be more comfortable on the other side of the room,” and two men walked Raiden to a crate by the storage-room door and stood near him without appearing to stand near anyone.

He let them. On the way he took off his coat and put it round her shoulders, and nobody stopped him, because it was a coat.

“You’ll be cold,” she said.

“You’re colder. Your hands are white. I’m only over there.” He did up the top button for her because hers were full of piston.

It smelled of him, soap and pencil shavings and the station dumplings. She pulled it closer and went back to the rings, and every few minutes she looked up, and every time she did he was looking back.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was the wall that kept Raiden awake, more than the men.

He’d seen it as soon as he came in. The storage room ran deeper on the plan in his head than it did on the floor in front of him. Its back wall was a slightly different grey from the rest, and the floor stepped down two or three centimetres just in front of it, under the shelving, where nobody would notice unless they had spent their whole life noticing that sort of thing.

He’d sat in the archive that morning with the old municipal drawings for the street: nine sheets from 1974, when the flyover went up and the row of workshops underneath it was rebuilt in its shadow. Behind the row, on the 1974 sheets, a narrow service passage ran the length of the block to a door on the next lane, so that the council’s men could reach the drains without going through anyone’s shop. A drawing from 1981 showed it sealed. The dimensions on the two sheets didn’t agree by eighty centimetres. He’d spent an hour of the afternoon wondering where eighty centimetres of passage had gone.

It hadn’t gone anywhere. It was behind Cao Tiehan’s shelves.

At twenty-six minutes past three she came over for the bag of honing stones in her kit by his crate, and he said without moving his lips, “Jia. There’s a passage behind that wall.”

Her hands stopped on the bag.

“The 1974 drawings. It runs to the next lane. Somebody bricked the front of it and put shelves up and left the rest.”

She didn’t look surprised. That was what frightened him. She looked as if he’d said something she’d been waiting a long time for somebody to say, and had hoped nobody ever would.

“I know. Don’t,” she said.

“All right.”

“Not to anyone. Not tonight, not after. I’ll tell you about it. Not here.” She looked at him then, properly, with a hard flat steadiness he’d seen once before, on the morning she’d walked out of the back of Harbourside General.

“Not here,” he agreed, and she took the stones and went back to her bike, and he sat on his crate with his cold hands between his knees and understood that the girl who’d grown up in this building knew exactly where a person could come and go in it without being seen, and had never once said so.

✦ ✦ ✦

At eleven minutes past four Guo folded his newspaper and came over to look.

He looked at the three bare barrels and the pistons laid out in a row and the crank with its rods standing up like two fingers and a thumb, and he said nothing about any of it. Then he turned his head and looked at Raiden across the room.

“You draw buildings, Mr. Lin.”

“I draw what other people design, mostly.”

“Modest. Have you ever drawn a secure room? The kind people pay for.” Guo smiled.

Jinx’s hands stopped.

“A few,” said Raiden.

“Rooms that keep people safe.”

“Yes.”

“And rooms that keep people in?”

Raiden thought about it, or appeared to. “Those are different rooms.”

“Are they? They seem to me to be the same room with the lock on the other side.”

“Then they’re different rooms. I only draw the kind people can leave,” said Raiden.

Guo looked at him longer, with something like interest and something like a man pricing a lot at auction, and then he looked back at her. “You married an idealist.”

“I married a draftsman,” said Jinx, and fitted the first stone into the hone.

Three bores. Two hours and forty-nine minutes. Her father had stopped pretending to file the key. She could feel him watching her hands, and she let him watch, and didn’t look round.

chapters.title: She Builds Her Way Out
chapters.desc: Three bores honed, nine rings freed, and a cracked crank seal that will seize the left cylinder at speed. “Lie to it.” Her father points at the wrong jet, Raiden kisses her for luck, and at 5:40 the widowmaker starts. Then Guo decides she’s too useful to let go.
chapters.epigraph: “Lie to it. Just this once. We’ll fix it properly after.”
chapters.content:
A hone doesn’t care how tired you are. It only cares that you keep it moving.

Jinx put the drill on slow, oiled the bore, and ran the stones up and down the first cylinder in long, even strokes, never stopping in one place long enough to cut a step into the wall. Up, down. Up, down. Every twenty strokes she pulled it out, wiped the bore and put the torch down it to look at the pattern the stones had left. She wanted fine lines crossing each other at an angle, like the weave of a cheap shirt. The angle was where the oil would sit. Without it the rings would scrape a dry wall the first time the engine got hot, and the engine would seize, and some fool would go over the handlebars at a hundred and forty.

Raiden had been allowed back to the bench at half past four, because Guo had decided that a man holding a torch was a man whose hands were accounted for. He held it now at the angle she liked without being told what the angle was.

“You’re thinking about the floor,” she said, without looking up.

“I’m thinking about the drain in the corner. It’s blocked. There’s a slope on this slab of about one in sixty towards it and it’s been holding water since before you were born.”

“Don’t.”

“I’m only thinking it.”

“Think it more quietly.”

He did. She felt him do it. Up, down. Up, down. The first bore came clean under the light with its fine grey crosshatch, and one scratch at the bottom of the stroke that she’d known would still be there and decided she could live with. She moved the hone to the second.

✦ ✦ ✦

The rings were the slowest part. She’d soaked the pistons in penetrating oil since one o’clock, and the first ring came out of its groove under a thin pick with a sound like a fingernail on a tooth. The second one fought. The third she worked round a millimetre at a time, swearing in a steady undertone in three dialects and a little bit of the Italian Serafina had taught her, and when it came free she held it up to the lamp and checked the gap at its ends with her feelers and let out a breath she’d been holding since the pound.

“How many?” said Raiden.

“Nine. That’s three done.”

“Is that good?”

“It’s three.”

He didn’t ask again. By ten to five there were nine rings sitting in their grooves, gapped and staggered, and three honed bores, and three pistons back on their rods with new clips her father had found in a tin in the cabinet without being asked. She hadn’t thanked him for the clips. She’d thanked him for nothing all night. He’d gone back to his stool and his file and his key, and he’d filed that key until it must have been worn down to a pin.

She found the seal when she was cleaning the crankcase to put the barrels back.

Left side, behind the alternator cover, where the end of the crank came out of the cases into open air. It was supposed to be soft and black. It was hard and grey and cracked at one edge like the rind on old cheese, and when she pressed a thumb against the lip it didn’t press back.

She sat back on her heels.

“What?” said Raiden.

“Crank seal. On a four-stroke you’d get a drip. On one of these, the left side runs dry, and when the piston comes up it sucks. It’ll pull air in through that crack straight into the left cylinder. Too much air, not enough petrol. The cylinder runs lean and hot, and somewhere at the top of third gear it seizes, and the back wheel locks.”

“Can you replace it?”

“Not without splitting the cases, and not without a seal, and I don’t have one, and it’s five o’clock. He’ll ride it. You know he’ll ride it.” She looked at it.

Raiden looked at the seal in the light of his own torch. Then he said, so the men by the door couldn’t hear him, “Lie to it.”

She looked up.

“Just this once. We’ll fix it properly after,” he said.

She almost laughed at him, because after and we and properly were three words that didn’t belong to this bike or to anyone in this building who owned it. And then she didn’t laugh, because he was right. A lie was what the night needed. She took a smear of grey sealant from her own kit and worked it into the lip of the old seal with a fingertip, filling the crack from the outside so that it would hold vacuum at idle for an hour, perhaps two, perhaps a day if nobody did anything stupid. Then she took the left carburettor off the rack, unscrewed its main jet and went one size richer than the book said, so that when the seal began to leak again the left cylinder would have a little extra petrol to drown in before it got hot enough to tear itself apart.

“That’s two lies,” said Raiden.

“The second one’s for whoever’s on it. He won’t know the difference. Nobody does, until the day they do.” She screwed the jet home.

✦ ✦ ✦

At five past five her father came off his stool for the second time that night.

He came round the bench and stood at her shoulder and looked at the three carburettors sitting on their rag in a row. His hands were in his pockets. She knew he was going to say something, and she wanted him not to, and she wanted him to, and she kept her eyes on the float bowl in her fingers.

“Middle one,” he said.

“What about it?”

“You’ve given it the same jet as the right.”

She looked. She had. Left one richer for the seal, right one as the book said, and the middle one as the book said too, because she’d been thinking about the seal and the clock and the knife in Dou’s jacket and not about the middle cylinder, which sat between the other two with no cold air on either side of it and always, always ran hotter.

“It wants one up. You wrote it in the book,” her father said.

“I know I wrote it in the book.”

“Then why didn’t you do it?”

“Because I was busy making sure the rings could move.”

He nodded as if that were a reasonable thing to say, which it was. He took the middle carburettor out of her hands, carefully, as if it might be hot, and turned it under the lamp. The tremor in his fingers was worse close up. It stopped when he was holding something.

“You’re Lin Jian’s son,” he said to the carburettor.

Raiden lowered the torch an inch. “Yes.”

“I saw it in the book. Guo showed me the book. Both your names on the same line. I thought it was another one of his tricks. Then I thought, no, she would. She’d find the only boy in this city with a family like that and walk into a registry with him in work boots. One up. And check the float height while you’re in there.” Her father turned the float bowl over, looked at the needle and set it straight with a fingernail. He handed the carburettor back to her.

He went back to his stool. She didn’t watch him go. She changed the jet in the middle carburettor and checked the float height and found it a millimetre low and set it right, and only when all three were back on the rack did she let herself look at Raiden, who was looking at the place where her father had stood with an expression she couldn’t read.

“Don’t,” she said.

“I wasn’t going to say anything.”

“Your face was.”

He put the torch down. Then, before she could say anything else, he leaned in across the bench and kissed her: lightly a kiss for a door you’re about to walk out of. “For luck,” he said.

“That’s not luck. That’s barely a kiss.”

She caught him by the front of his jumper and pulled him back down to her and kissed him properly, with grease on her hands and the night in her shoulders and her father four metres away pretending to file a key. He made a small surprised sound against her mouth and then didn’t make any sound at all. When she let him go his glasses were crooked.

“Better?” he said.

“It’ll do. Barrels.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The barrels went back on at quarter past five, the heads at half past, the carburettors on their new rubbers at twenty to six. She filled the injection tank with two-stroke oil and bled the pump until the oil came up clear in the little lines, one, two, three, because a two-stroke without oil going into it doesn’t run for long and doesn’t stop politely. She put fresh petrol in the tank. She checked that the throttle snapped shut when she let it go. Then she swung a leg over and put her weight on the kickstart and brought it down.

Nothing. A wheeze of air through three cold carburettors.

Again. Something caught for half a stroke and died. Dou made a noise against the wall. She ignored him. She pulled the middle plug and it was wet, and she dried it and put it back, and closed the choke a fraction, and kicked again, and again, and on the seventh kick one cylinder fired with a crack that jumped off the concrete and the flyover above it and came back down on them, and then a second, and then, unwillingly, like a man dragged out of bed at an hour he considered beneath him, the third.

5:40.

It didn’t sound good. It sounded like three angry old men arguing about money. Blue smoke boiled out of three pipes and hung under the lamps. The whole bike shook. But it was running, and it was the middle cylinder she could hear steadiest of all, the one with the extra jet, the one she’d written about in her father’s book at twelve.

She sat on it and let it warm, and kept her hand on the throttle, and for one breath she forgot Guo, and Dou’s knife, and the photograph on the bench, and the twelve bikes and the debt and the five years. There was only the noise and the shake and the heat coming up through the tank into her knees. She looked up. Raiden was smiling at her with his whole face. Behind him her father had stopped filing. He had his eyes shut.

“Beautiful,” said Guo.

✦ ✦ ✦

He wanted to ride it. Of course he did.

She said, “It’s not tested. The crank seal’s a patch. It’ll do round the yard in first and second, it won’t do the expressway. Don’t give it more than half throttle. If it starts to sound different, pull the clutch in and stop.”

“You’re very protective of your work.”

“I’m protective of idiots.”

He laughed, because nobody had called him that in some time and he found it charming. One of his men brought him a helmet. He put it on and swung a leg over and took the bike out under the half-raised shutter into the grey under the flyover, and rode it up and down the length of the concrete between the pillars with the exhaust cracking off them like gunshots. He didn’t give it more than half throttle. Twice. The third time he wound it on, and the rear tyre stepped out on a slick of old oil, and her heart came up into her throat, and he caught it and straightened and came back laughing inside the helmet.

He killed it in front of her. In the silence afterwards the engine ticked.

“Magnificent.”

He took the helmet off and handed it to Dou. He didn’t hand her anything.

“My brother would have ridden it into the harbour,” he said.

“So that’s done. No twelve bikes. Now we talk about my father,” said Jinx.

Guo said, “Yes. We should. Your father told me you were difficult. He didn’t tell me you could do that in eleven hours with a seized engine and a patch. You see my problem.” He looked at the bike again, at the oil starting to bead on the left case already, and at her hands.

“No.”

“You’re too useful to let go.”

The words went round the workshop and settled on everything. Two men at the shutter. Dou with his hand inside his jacket. Her father on his stool with the key in his fingers, not filing it. Raiden beside her, still, his torch switched off in his hand.

“That wasn’t what we agreed,” she said.

“Agreements change. I have your father. I have your husband in my workshop. And now I have a motorcycle only you can keep alive. Stay for breakfast.” Guo smiled.

He went back to his leather chair and called for tea.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was just after six. Somewhere above them the first lorries were starting over the flyover, a low steady rumble that came down through the concrete like weather.

She crouched by the bike with a rag, wiping the left case where the oil had started, for something to do with her hands. Raiden crouched beside her.

“Are you all right?”

“No.”

He didn’t ask her to pretend. She liked him for that more than she could say just then.

Her father’s boots stopped on the other side of the bike. He didn’t crouch; his knees wouldn’t let him. He stood looking down at the engine with the key still in his hand.

“Your mother liked the sound of these,” he said.

Jinx stopped wiping.

“There was one in the window of a shop on the old market road. Red. She used to make me walk her past it on a Sunday so she could hear the man start it. She’d have liked that.” He turned the key in his fingers.

He went back to the office before she could say anything, and shut the door.

She sat on her heels by the bike for a while. Raiden didn’t touch her. He waited, and when she held out her hand without looking, he took it.

“You have that face,” she said eventually.

“Which face?”

“The one you get when you’re drawing a floor plan in your head.”

He looked round the workshop. The shutter, the two men, Dou, the office door, the storage room and the wall behind it, the lamps, the clock. Then back at her.

“I’m thinking how many ways there are to leave a room.”

“Not without me.”

“No.”

“Not with a plan you don’t tell me about.”

“No secret arrangements. I meant it on Thursday,” he said.

She took his hand and pressed his palm flat to the front of her shirt, over her heart, where he could feel how fast it was going and how much she wanted it to slow down.

“Then tell me. We’ve got fifty minutes,” she said.

“An exit,” said Raiden.

chapters.title: He Stops Playing Dumb
chapters.desc: Guo breaks the deal and Dou draws a knife. Raiden steps in front of her, tells Dou where his mother lives and why he won’t use it, and tells Guo which beam in his building is cracked. She writes the settlement on a job card. At home his hands won’t stop shaking.
chapters.epigraph: “I know every building in this district. I know yours. You added two floors in 2019 on a frame drawn for four. Shall I tell you which beam?”
chapters.content:
He told her everything in fifty minutes, crouched beside a two-stroke that was slowly sweating oil, with his voice no louder than the lorries overhead.

She listened without interrupting, which wasn’t like her. When he’d finished she asked him three questions, and he answered them, and she changed one thing, and he said “Yes, that’s better,” and meant it. Then she wiped her hands and stood up, and he stood up beside her, and it was half past six on Saturday morning under the flyover.

“We’re going. My father’s account is settled. You’ve got your brother’s bike,” Jinx said.

Guo looked up from his tea. “I don’t think so.”

“Dou,” he said, and Dou came off the wall.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came slowly, because he’d been waiting all night for someone to give him a reason, and he wanted to enjoy it. The knife was out before he was halfway across the floor. Her weight went back onto one foot and her right hand found the long tyre lever on the bench without her eyes leaving the blade, and she was ready, she had been ready since she was seventeen, and then Raiden stepped in front of her.

He didn’t hurry. He put himself between her and the knife the way you’d put a hand over a cup someone was about to knock off a table, and he held his left arm a little out behind him with the palm open towards her. Wait. She hated it. She waited.

“Put that away,” said Raiden.

“Move, pretty boy.”

“No.”

Dou stopped a metre short of him and grinned. Raiden didn’t look at the knife. He looked at Dou.

He said, “You rang your mother at eleven minutes past twelve. From by the shutter. You told her you’d fix the light on the stairs tomorrow, because she’s frightened of the dark between the third floor and the fourth since she fell. Building twelve, north block. You’re on the fourth floor and she’s on the third, under you, so you can hear her if she calls. The lift’s been out since October. You say your mother’s name very gently. I noticed.” His voice was perfectly level.

Dou’s grin went.

Raiden said, “I’m not threatening her. I’d never do that. I’m telling you that I listen, and that you’ve spent twelve hours in this room thinking nobody was looking at you. Put it away and go home and fix her light.”

Nobody moved. Jinx could see the knife over Raiden’s shoulder, and Dou’s knuckles round the handle going white and then, a little at a time, not.

The knife went back inside the jacket. Dou looked at Guo. Guo was looking at Raiden.

“Thank you,” said Raiden, and the courtesy was worse than anything else he’d said.

✦ ✦ ✦

She had seen him make himself small in rooms full of men like Guo. She’d watched him apologise for being in doorways, and let his glasses slide down his nose, and get lost in buildings he’d drawn himself, and smile vaguely when people talked about him as if he weren’t there. She’d known some of it was an act. She hadn’t known all of it was a choice, made fresh every time, by a man who could have stopped making it whenever he liked.

He stopped now.

“You’ve been asking me all night what kind of rooms I draw, Mr. Guo. I’ll tell you about yours,” he said.

Guo didn’t move. “Mine.”

“The building on the old market road with the pawn shop on the ground floor and your office on the fifth. I spent yesterday in the city archive. I spend a great many days there. I know every building in this district. I know yours. You added two floors in 2019 on a frame drawn for four. Shall I tell you which beam?” He said it with no emphasis at all.

The tea had stopped halfway to Guo’s mouth.

“It’s on the second floor, over the service corridor, carrying a column that was moved eighty centimetres to make room for a lift nobody wanted. Somebody’s put a steel plate under it and painted the plate the same colour as the ceiling. The crack’s still there. It’s on the drawing your builder submitted, because he was honest enough to draw it and frightened enough not to mention it, and it’s in the inspection the city never did. This is a report to the Buildings Department’s dangerous-structures line, with the drawings attached. Section, plans and the builder’s own note. It has my name on it, and the practice’s address, and a request for an emergency inspection on Monday morning. If they agree with me, they’ll close the top four floors until it’s fixed. They’ll be right to.” Raiden took his phone out of his pocket and turned it so Guo could see the screen.

“You’re bluffing.”

“No, I’m a draftsman. I don’t know how,” said Raiden.

Guo set the cup down. When he spoke again, his voice was softer and a good deal more dangerous.

“You think I don’t know whose son you are. This is your father talking.”

“My father doesn’t know I’m here. Nobody does except the woman behind me. I’m not going to say his name to you, Mr. Guo. You’d like me to. Then it would be a family matter, and you know how to price those. This has my name on it. Only mine.” Raiden put the phone away.

It went quiet. Above them a lorry went over the expansion joint with a sound like a door slamming a long way off.

Jinx came out from behind him. She didn’t need to stand behind anyone now, and he stepped aside for her as if he’d known that before she did.

She took one of her father’s old job cards off the nail by the bench, the yellow ones with the shop’s name stamped crooked at the top, and turned it face down and wrote on the back of it with the carpenter’s pencil from behind Raiden’s ear.

Account of Cao Tiehan with Mr. Guo settled in full against one 1973 750 triple, running. Saturday 18 November 2023.

She held it out with the pencil. “Sign it. He doesn’t send the report. You don’t come back here, and nobody you own does either. That’s the deal.”

“And if I don’t?”

“Then he sends it, and I take my lie off your bike.”

Guo looked at her.

She said, “There’s a crack in the left crank seal. I filled it from the outside and put the left cylinder one jet rich to cover it. It’ll idle all day. Take it up the expressway past the top of third gear and the patch goes, and the left cylinder runs lean and hot and seizes, and the back wheel locks at whatever speed you’re doing when it happens. I’m the only one who knows exactly what I did. Sign it and I’ll write it down for whoever you get to fix it properly. I’m not going to let you die on your brother’s bike. I’m not that kind of person. But I could stop you riding it.” She put the pencil in his hand.

Guo looked down at the card. Then he signed it on his knee, a small neat signature, and gave it back.

She turned it over and wrote on the front, under the crooked stamp, in block capitals: LEFT CRANK SEAL CRACKED, PATCHED, NOT FIXED. LEFT MAIN ONE SIZE RICH, PUT BACK WHEN SEAL’S DONE. MIDDLE ONE SIZE RICH, LEAVE IT. NOTHING OVER SECOND UNTIL THEN. DON’T FORGET THE OIL. She tore the card along the old perforation the shop had stopped using in 1990 and gave him the front half and kept the back.

He read it. Something happened behind his glasses that she wouldn’t have called softening, quite.

“My brother never read instructions either,” he said.

The van came round at ten to seven. His men pushed the bike up the ramp. Guo walked out behind it without looking at her father once, and the chair went last, carried by Dou, who stopped in the shutter and looked back at Raiden as if he wanted to say something, and didn’t, and went.

✦ ✦ ✦

Carp was where she’d left her on Thursday night, in the corner under a dust sheet, black and low and cold. Jinx pulled the sheet off. Her father came out of the office while she was checking the tyres.

He stood by the bench with the half of the job card she’d left there, the signed half, and read Guo’s signature, and then read it again.

“You’ll want this,” he said.

“Keep it. It’s your account.”

He nodded. He put it in his shirt pocket and buttoned the pocket. He looked older in the grey light coming under the shutter than he had under the lamps. “Jia.”

She stopped with her hand on Carp’s bars.

“Don’t forget the oil,” he said.

It was such a stupid thing to say. It was the thing he used to shout across the shop at her when she was ten, wheeling some wreck she’d brought back to life out into the lane. It was the most ordinary thing in the world, and she found she couldn’t answer it.

“I won’t,” she managed, and pulled her helmet on.

✦ ✦ ✦

Raiden got on behind her. He hadn’t ridden pillion since the sidecar came; before that, the last time had been the August his wrist came out of plaster, when she’d taken him the long way round the harbour so he could tell her about the farm. He put his arms round her waist and she rode out under the flyover into the morning, past the market road and the pawn shop with its top four floors full of somebody’s sleeping tenants, along the docks road with the cranes coming out of the fog, and the whole way home his hands were shaking against her stomach and he didn’t seem to know it.

She took him up the back stairs of Tai Hing and into the kitchen and turned the kettle on, and he stood by the table in his coat, and she saw it then in the light. His right hand. He was holding it with his left to keep it still.

“Raiden.”

“I’m all right.”

“Sit down.”

He sat. She knelt in front of the chair and took both his hands, and they were cold and they were shaking, quite badly now that there was nothing left in the room to hold them still for.

“It was the note,” he said.

She waited.

“Gone to see my father. Don’t come. I read it about forty times. On the bus, at the flyover, under the lamp across the road. I kept thinking: I’ve asked her a hundred times to tell me when something’s wrong, and she left me a note. And then I thought about Harbourside.” He laughed, slightly, at nothing.

Her hands went still round his.

He said, “I sent you out the back. Do you remember? Ten to five in the morning. You’d sat by that bed all night, and you’d put your jacket over me, and I told you to go out the back before my family came. I told myself I was protecting you. I’ve told myself that for two and a half years. Last night I stood across the road from your father’s shop with your note in my pocket, and somebody I loved had decided I’d be safer not knowing where she was. Now I know what I did to you. I’m sorry. I’m so sorry, Jia. It was a terrible thing to do to someone.” He looked down at their hands.

She couldn’t speak. Then she could.

“I left the note because I thought if Guo only had me, he’d stop there.”

“I know.”

“I was wrong. I was frightened and I wanted to deal with it on my own, the way I always have. It wasn’t fair. I won’t do it again. If I have to go somewhere, I’ll tell you where, even if I tell you not to follow.” She held his hands harder.

“And I’ll ask why.”

“And if I still say don’t?”

“I’ll stay away unless I think you’re in danger. And then I’ll come and stand across the road.”

“That’s not what I asked for.”

“I know,” he said, and that was what made her cry, finally, in her own kitchen at half past seven on a Saturday with the kettle boiling and nobody turning it off.

He slid off the chair onto the floor with her and held her, the way he had under the flyover on Thursday, not tight, not as if she might vanish, just enough. Then his hands came up to her face and he kissed her, the kiss of a man who’d spent twelve hours not shaking for her sake and had nothing left to hold it in with. She kissed him back with both fists in his jumper.

“You were magnificent. You were terrifying. Don’t ever do that again,” she said into his mouth.

“Which part?”

“Any of it. All of it. Do it again if you have to. You told me the plan.” She pulled back to look at him.

“You told me to.”

“I know. I’m just saying you did.”

Her phone buzzed on the table above them. The same unsaved number that had rung her on Thursday afternoon. She’d deleted it on the third of November 2018 in the back of a taxi, and she still knew it by heart.

Drain in the corner was blocked. Cleared it. Tell him.

She held it out so Raiden could read it. He read it twice, and for the first time since the flyover his hands were nearly still.

“He was listening,” he said.

“He’s always listening. He just never says. Bed. You’re asleep on the floor.” She put the phone away.

“I’m not.”

“You’re a terrible liar.”

“Only when you’re looking,” said Raiden, and let her pull him up.

They’d begun at the old-town registry, two years ago in September, with Mrs. Tong for a witness and a napkin in chilli oil and nobody else in the world knowing. She lay beside him with the curtains shut against the morning and the washer on his finger against her collarbone, and counted his breathing down from a hundred, and he was asleep before she got to sixty.

chapters.title: Her Father Says Sorry
chapters.desc: Her father sits on the black step and says sorry for the night she was seventeen. Raiden asks her before he raises the land. A pigeon loft on a river flat, a red door in daylight, and a no in Lin Jian’s kitchen. At New Year: thirty napkins, and “Ask me in March.”
chapters.epigraph: “Nobody has said no to me in my own kitchen since 1987. Sit down. Eat. You’re my daughter-in-law.”
chapters.content:
The first time her father came to see her after the flyover, he brought a bag of oranges and left them on the step without knocking. The second time he knocked and stood on the pavement and asked whether the compressor had always made that noise, and went away again before she could tell him to mind his own business. The third time was the second Saturday in December, and he sat down on the black step outside Tai Hing with his hands between his knees and said, through the open door, “I don’t know how to do this.”

She was at the bench with a carburettor in pieces. She didn’t look up. “Do what?”

“Talk to you.”

“You’re doing it.”

He looked at his hands. The step was a slab of old painted timber gone black with oil and weather, and it had come with the building. She’d sat on one like it outside his shop as a girl, sorting nuts into jam jars while he worked inside and the radio played opera he pretended not to like. She’d stopped sitting there at about fourteen. At seventeen she’d stopped going downstairs at all after dark.

“I owe you an apology,” he said.

She put the float bowl down.

“When you were seventeen. That night. I was in the office. I heard him. I heard you tell him to get out, and I heard something fall. I knew you were on your own with him. I knew, Jia. And I didn’t come out.” He said it to the pavement. His mouth worked.

For a moment she was back there: the smell of rain on concrete, the iron cold in her hand, the office door with the light under it, and waiting, and waiting, and the silence going on so long it had turned into an answer.

“Why?”

“He was buying from me. He had men. I told myself if I went out it would be worse. I was afraid. That’s all. There isn’t anything better than that to say.” He shut his eyes.

“So was I,” said Jinx.

“I know.”

“You don’t know.”

He didn’t argue. That was new. He sat on her step and let it be true.

“You were ten steps away,” she said.

“Yes.”

“You should have come out.”

“Yes.”

“You should have been my father.”

He put a hand over his mouth and his shoulders went, and she turned back to the bench, because she wasn’t going to comfort him. Not today. Possibly not ever. She picked up the float bowl and put it down again and picked up a rag instead.

“I’m not asking you to forgive me. I only wanted you to hear me say it,” he said eventually. His voice had gone thick.

“I heard you.”

He got up. His knees cracked. At the door he stopped. “Can I come again?”

She thought about it honestly. “Ring first.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Raiden came home at seven with the shopping and found her sitting on the kitchen floor with her back against the cupboard and her boots still on and a bowl of noodles gone cold beside her.

He put the bags down. “Your father came.”

“How do you know?”

“Your boots.”

She looked at them. She hadn’t noticed. He sat down on the floor beside her, which he did more easily than any man she’d ever met, as if floors were where the important conversations had always happened.

“He said sorry. For something that happened when I was seventeen,” she said.

He waited.

“I’ll tell you. I want to tell you. Not tonight.” She turned her ring round on her finger.

“All right.”

“Don’t be patient at me.”

“I’m not being patient. I’m sitting on the floor. Did you eat any of that?” He took the bowl of cold noodles off the tiles, looked at it, and put it on the counter above their heads.

“Some.”

“Some isn’t a quantity.”

She leaned into his shoulder, and he didn’t ask her anything else that night.

✦ ✦ ✦

By January her father had started coming on Saturday mornings. He rang first. He never stayed above an hour. He fixed the compressor’s pressure switch without asking and she let him, and once he brought her a cigar box of old carburettor jets he’d been keeping since the eighties, each in a twist of paper with its size on it in his writing, and she didn’t say thank you, and used three of them that week.

Nobody would have called it forgiveness: two people learning to stand in the same room again without pretending nothing had happened in it.

Raiden raised the land with her first.

He did it over dinner, which was the only time she could be made to sit still, and he put the planning notice down beside her bowl rather than talking about it. The block under the flyover, eleven workshops from the tyre place on the corner to the scrapyard at the far end, was to be redeveloped. Two developers had written to the owners. Most of them had already sold. Her father had put both letters in the drawer with the job cards and not answered either.

“How do you know about the drawer?”

“He told me. Last Saturday, while you were on the phone to Serafina. He said it like a man saying he’s got a lump he hasn’t shown anyone. He’s sixty-one, Jia. He lives in the back room of a building that floods every typhoon, with a stove he lights with a match. The land’s worth more than everything he’s ever made in that shop. If he doesn’t sell, the developer will build round him until he does.” Raiden turned his cup.

“He won’t leave.”

“Probably not. I’d like to give him the choice anyway. But it’s your father. If you’d rather I didn’t, I won’t say a word to him.” He looked at her.

She put her chopsticks down. Two years ago he’d have done it first and told her after, and been gentle and sorry and right. She watched him not do it.

“Ask him. With me there,” she said.

It took four Saturdays. Her father was suspicious of the price, then of the solicitor, then of Raiden. “Why is he doing this?” he asked her in the kitchen, where Raiden could hear perfectly well.

“Because he’s my husband.”

“That doesn’t explain anything.”

“It explains enough.”

Raiden found the flat. Ground floor and first, in an old walk-up by the river, ten minutes from the flyover so her father could still go and drink tea with the men he’d shouted at for thirty years. On the third Saturday he spread a drawing of it on the kitchen table, and her father looked at it, and then put his finger on the roof.

“What’s that?”

“A loft. For pigeons. Jia said you kept them. Before the shop.” Raiden didn’t look up.

Her father went still. Jinx hadn’t known Raiden had remembered that. She’d told him once, in the dark, on the night of the walk home: that there’d been a loft on the roof of her grandmother’s building, and her father had kept birds there as a boy, and the shop had eaten them like it ate everything.

“This beam,” her father said, after a while.

“Reinforced.”

“How much?”

“Enough.”

“Enough isn’t a measurement.”

Raiden smiled. “No. I’ll show you the calculation.”

They spent an hour on a pigeon loft. She sat at the end of the table and watched her father argue about drainage falls and the spacing of perches with a man he’d once called the Lin boy, as if it were the most natural thing in the world. At the end he sat back and took his reading glasses off.

“I want it finished before I move. And I choose the birds,” he said.

“Of course.”

“And nobody tells me what to feed them.”

“I wouldn’t dare,” said Raiden.

On the way down the stairs she put her hand in his coat pocket with his. “You built him a pigeon loft.”

“I drew one. A builder in Ms. Bok’s office will build it. In the summer, if the sale goes through.”

“You remembered the birds.”

“You told me about them,” he said, as if that were the end of the matter.

It didn’t make up for anything. It wasn’t meant to. But it seemed to her, walking home along the docks road in the cold, that a life wasn’t built out of things undone. It was built out of what people chose to do after.

✦ ✦ ✦

Since September Lin Jian had come to them for dinner on Saturday nights. He climbed the back stairs at Tai Hing in the black suit with Uncle Mok waiting in the car below, and sat at their kitchen table with his reading glasses in his breast pocket, and ate what Raiden cooked in the wok, and asked her about gear ratios. She’d said nothing in the Walled City, a long time ago, on a napkin. He’d heard. He never once asked her to come.

So on the last Sunday in January she asked Raiden to take her.

They went the back way, through the narrow lanes, past the man who smoked under his awning and the television that was always on somewhere, to a red door in a high wall with three steps up to it and a crack beside the lock. She’d stood here once before, at two in the morning, and knocked three times and walked away. In daylight the paint was peeling at the bottom where rain came off the step.

“Ready?” said Raiden.

“No.”

“All right.” He didn’t tell her it would be fine. He reached for the handle.

The door opened before he touched it. A small woman with silver hair in a knot and an apron over a grey cardigan stood on the other side. She looked at Raiden. Then she looked at Jinx, and at Jinx’s hand, and at the ring on it that had been a washer in a box of washers.

“Ah Sim,” said Raiden.

Ah Sim didn’t say anything. Then she put out both hands and took Jinx’s in them, oil and all.

“You’re the one who taught him to cook properly. Come in. You’re letting the cold into my kitchen,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

It wasn’t a grand house, inside. That surprised her. Old wood and old tiles, a narrow hall with photographs, slippers in a row by the stairs. It smelled of tea and ginger and something slow in a clay pot. Raiden’s father met them in the kitchen doorway, in a cardigan instead of the black suit, holding his reading glasses, and he looked at his son and then at her and then at the two of them standing in his house, and the man who frightened most of the city looked as if he didn’t trust his own face.

“Jia, sit,” he said.

She sat. They had lunch at the kitchen table, because Ah Sim said the dining room was for people she didn’t like, and Lin Jian put fish in Jinx’s bowl and chicken in Raiden’s and asked whether the developer had made her father an offer yet.

She looked at Raiden. He hadn’t told his father. He shook his head, slightly.

Lin Jian said, “I hear things. That block’s been for sale in pieces since the summer. The man buying it is called Sheung, and he’s a thief, and he’ll pay your father less than the pigeon loft costs if nobody stops him. I’ll have my lawyer handle it. Sheung will pay what he’s told.” He set down his chopsticks.

“No,” said Jinx.

Ah Sim, at the stove, stopped stirring.

Jinx said, “Thank you. But no. My father’s selling his own land, with his own solicitor, and he’ll get his own price or he’ll stay where he is. It’s his. And it’s mine to sort out with him. That was one of the conditions.”

“I know the conditions. I’ve read the napkin,” said Lin Jian.

Raiden put his hand over his eyes.

“Mrs. Tong showed me. It’s on her wall.” Lin Jian looked at her over the table, with that heavy unreadable face, and she looked back and didn’t drop her eyes, because she’d never in her life dropped her eyes for anyone and she wasn’t going to start in his kitchen.

Then he laughed. It came up out of him unexpectedly, as if it had been a long time down there.

“Nobody has said no to me in my own kitchen since 1987. Sit down. Eat. You’re my daughter-in-law.”

“I am sitting down.”

“Then eat.”

Ah Sim had turned round from the stove. “Madam said no to him in 1987. In that chair. He wanted a bigger house. She said this one had a good kitchen,” she told Jinx.

“It does have a good kitchen,” said Lin Jian, and put more fish in her bowl.

✦ ✦ ✦

Lunar New Year’s Eve fell on a Friday. The house was full of everybody, which was more people than Jinx had ever eaten a meal with in her life: Elowen and Zhao, Evangeline, Elara and her husband, Eliana, who wanted to know what Jinx’s lathe could cut and wrote the answers on a napkin. Ah Sim fed them all until they couldn’t move and said nobody was eating. At the end of dinner Lin Jian lifted his glass and said, “To the ones who came home,” and looked at Raiden, and then at her, and drank.

Later Raiden disappeared upstairs. She found him in his old room, a narrow box at the top of the house with a desk under the window and drawings of buildings pinned to the walls by a boy of eleven who’d already known exactly how stairs worked. He had a shoebox open on the desk.

Inside were napkins. Paper ones, cloth ones, one from a train, one with a coffee ring on it, folded flat and dated in his small neat capitals. The ship. The treehouse. The crane. The house with CAO JIA’S HOME in the title block. The red door. A yellow lamp and a tin of peaches. A pair of hands holding a torch, drawn three months ago, two days after the flyover.

“Twenty-nine, the first one’s on Mrs. Tong’s wall,” he said.

“Thirty.”

“Thirty. Every one of them was a way of asking the same thing. I know you keep saying not yet. I’m not going to ask tonight, in this house, with my father downstairs and everybody full of fish. I don’t want you to say yes because my family’s been kind, or because of the flyover, or because you’ve met Ah Sim. I want you to stand up in front of everyone with me because you want to. Only that.” He didn’t touch them.

She picked up the napkin with the torch on it. He’d drawn her hands too, at the edge of the light, holding a hone.

“Ask me in March,” she said.

He looked up.

“Not every day. No speech. Nothing you’ve bought. Nobody you’ve invited. March.” She put the napkin back on top of the others and put the lid on the box.

“March,” said Raiden, and it was the first time she’d ever seen him not know what to do with his own face.

At four minutes to midnight they went up onto the roof with everybody else. The city below them was all lanterns and windows, and somewhere a dog was barking at the first crackers. He put his coat round her shoulders, and she told him he’d be cold, and he said, “I have a warm wife,” which was a terrible thing to say, and when the sky over the harbour broke open in red and gold she turned and kissed him before the count got to one.

“WE CAN SEE YOU,” shouted Eliana from the stairwell.

“Your family,” said Jinx into his collar.

“Ours,” said Raiden, and kept his arms where they were.

chapters.title: She Lets Him In
chapters.desc: In the bath she tells him what happened at seventeen. She gives him the code to her cabinet, the day she left. The thirty-first napkin is two creepers under Carp, and on a Thursday at Mrs. Tong’s she puts on a steel ring she turned herself.
chapters.epigraph: “Oh-three-one-one. The day I left. It’s the code to everything I own that’s mine.”
chapters.content:
“You don’t have to look at me,” she said.

They were in the bath. It was the second Saturday in March, late, with the window fogged and the yellow lamp on in the bedroom beyond the half-open door. He was sitting behind her with his knees either side of hers and one arm loose across her waist, and he’d been working the grease out of her hair with his fingers for a quarter of an hour while she said nothing at all. The water had started to cool.

“All right,” said Raiden. He didn’t move.

“I mean it. Stay there. Don’t turn me round.”

“I’m staying here.”

She looked at the water. Her knees came out of it like two islands with scars on them.

“When I was seventeen, there was a man who bought from my father. Parts, mostly. Sometimes whole bikes, the ones that came in at night. He came with other men who weren’t mechanics and didn’t want to be, and they stood around the shop as if everything in it was theirs to pick up. I slept in the back room on a camp bed. The one in the photograph. There’s a door behind the shelves in the storage room that goes out to the next lane. The council forgot about it in 1981. My father didn’t. He let them use it, so nobody saw them come and go.” She was surprised how level her voice came out.

His arm didn’t tighten. She felt him decide not to let it.

“One night he came in through it on his own. My father was in the office doing the books. I woke up and he was standing by the bed. He hurt me. I’m not going to tell you how. Not because I can’t. Because it’s mine, and he doesn’t get to be in this room any more than that.”

“All right,” Raiden said.

“I kept a tyre iron under the bed. I’d kept it there since I was fifteen, because of the way they looked at me. When he turned away I got hold of it and I hit his hand, the one he’d had on me, on the edge of the bench. I heard it go. He screamed. I hit him again when he came back at me, on the arm, and he went out the way he came. My father stayed in the office. In the morning he told me I had to say sorry. To him. Because the man was a good customer and he’d lose the stock.” She turned her ring under the water.

Behind her, Raiden had gone so still that she could hear the tap drip.

She said, “I said it. Sorry. I stood in the shop and said it to his face with his hand in plaster. Then I cleaned the floor of the back room and washed everything and went to school. I didn’t tell anybody. For five years I slept with a tyre iron where I could reach it without sitting up. Under the pillow, against the wall. In every room I lived in. And then one night I forgot to put it there, and I didn’t notice for a week. That’s what happened at seventeen. That’s what my father said sorry for.”

The water had gone cool. She waited for him to say something clever, or kind, or furious, so that she could know what to do with it.

“Thank you for telling me,” he said.

“That’s all?”

“No. I’d like to find him. I’d like to find him and stand across the road from wherever he lives until he understands that somebody knows. I’m not going to, because that’s about me and not you. You didn’t do anything wrong. Not that night, and not in the morning when you said sorry. You were seventeen, and you got yourself out. May I hold you?” His voice was perfectly even, which was how she knew. He was quiet a moment.

She turned round in the bath, which slopped water over the side, and he looked at her face, only her face, as if there were nothing else in the room worth looking at.

“Yes,” she said.

He put his arms round her. She put her forehead on his collarbone. Neither of them said anything. The water got cold and neither of them did anything about it.

“I thought you’d look at me differently,” she said finally.

“I do. I know something about you I didn’t know an hour ago. I understand why you sleep with your back to the wall, and why you need to know where the door is before you’ll lie down. But when I look at you I see the woman who brought a dead triple back to life at five in the morning with three men watching her, and argued with me about drainage while she did it. He doesn’t come into it.” He moved his hand slowly down her spine.

She laughed, wetly, against his skin.

“Come to bed. Leave the lamp on,” she said.

“Always,” said Raiden.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Sunday morning she took him into the small room behind the office, where the grey-blue cabinet stood against the wall.

It had come with her from under the flyover. It was the only thing she’d taken except Carp and a bag of clothes: a narrow steel cabinet with a dent near the bottom and a rust bloom beside the handle and a keypad she’d fitted herself at sixteen. He’d never asked what was in it. She’d been waiting four months to see whether he would.

She crouched and put in the code. 0, 3, 1, 1. The lock clicked.

Inside there wasn’t much. Service manuals with soft covers. A tin of brass screws. Her school certificate, the one with her name typed on it by a clerk who’d assumed she existed. A photograph of her mother in a red jacket on the old market road. A notebook of wiring diagrams in a hand that had got neater year by year. And at the bottom, wrapped in an oily cloth, a tyre iron.

He looked at it. He didn’t touch it.

“I don’t know why I kept it,” she said.

“Maybe it kept you.”

She looked at him, and he didn’t say it as though he knew better. He said it as though he were offering it to her in case it was any use. She shut the door and opened it again, so he could see the code go in.

“Oh-three-one-one. The day I left. It’s the code to everything I own that’s mine.”

He was quiet. “Third of November.”

“2018. A Saturday. I went out of the front with Carp and a bag at six in the morning, and he was asleep, and I didn’t leave a note. I’m not very good at notes.” She almost smiled.

“Jia. You don’t have to give me this because you told me the rest.”

“I know. You gave me your safe. This is mine. Don’t open it unless you have to.” She put his hand on the keypad.

“I won’t.”

“But you can.”

He knelt there beside her with his hand on the steel, and then she took him by the front of his shirt and pulled him over and kissed him on the floor of the cabinet room, for no reason, and he laughed against her mouth and asked what that was for, and she said, “For not opening it for four months.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On Monday he came home at six with a paper bag from the dumpling place by the station and put it on the table and didn’t open it.

There was a napkin on top of it, folded once.

She unfolded it. He’d drawn Carp from underneath, exactly, the way you’d see her if you were lying on the floor of the shop looking up: the sump, the exhaust, the swingarm, the back of the gearbox and every bolt on it. Under the bike, side by side, two mechanic’s creepers. Two pairs of boots stuck out from under the bike at one end, a big pair and a smaller pair, crossed at the ankles. At the other end, two heads, close together.

The creepers had measurements on them. Of course they did.

“Thirty-one,” she said.

“Thirty-one napkins. Twenty-seven times I’ve asked. You said March. It’s the eleventh. I’ve got nothing in my pocket. I haven’t booked anything. I haven’t told anyone. I’d like to marry you again, in front of people, at Mrs. Tong’s, because that’s where it started and that’s where she walked in on us on the floor. Thursday the fourth of April. She’s already said she’ll close.” He stood on the other side of the table with his hands in his coat pockets and didn’t come round it.

“You said you hadn’t told anyone.”

“I asked her if she’d close on a Thursday in April. I didn’t say why. She knew why.” He looked guilty.

Jinx looked at the two heads drawn close together under the bike. She’d kissed him first on those creepers, on a Friday in May three years ago, with a wrench going over somewhere and Mrs. Tong in the doorway. She’d kissed him first more or less every time since, and he’d never once seemed to mind.

“Yes,” she said.

He didn’t move. It was as if the word had gone past him and he was waiting for it to come back.

“Yes, idiot. Thursday. Mrs. Tong’s. No speech.”

His face did something she’d only seen once before, on the forty-third floor of Meridian the first time she’d stayed the night. Then he came round the table.

✦ ✦ ✦

She made her own ring.

She didn’t tell him, and she didn’t let anyone else near it. She took a short length of stainless bar that had come off the dyno mount when Ms. Bok’s man cut it to fit, and on two evenings after closing, with the shutter down, she turned it on the lathe and parted it off and bored it and dressed the edges, and took it down by hand with wet paper from coarse to fine until it was the colour of rain on a window. It fitted over the washer. It was meant to. She wasn’t taking the washer off.

He saw it for the first time at Mrs. Tong’s on the fourth of April, when she took it out of her pocket and put it in his hand and said, “This one. Over the other.”

Mrs. Tong had closed. She’d put a sign on the door in her own writing, CLOSED TODAY FOR FAMILY, and pushed three tables together and put spring flowers in jam jars and the framed napkin from 2021 in the middle of them. Elowen was there, and Zhao, who stood at the back by the fish tank with his hands in his pockets and said nothing at all, and Eliana, and Xiao Pan, who’d bought a new shirt. Ms. Bok came, and the man from the tyre place on the corner, and Serafina, who’d driven back from testing in the south overnight and fell asleep in a chair by the window halfway through the soup.

Her father came. He wore a white shirt buttoned to the neck and stood by the door, and when she came out of Mrs. Tong’s back room in a dark green dress she could walk in and the boots she’d chosen, he didn’t offer to walk her anywhere. She’d told him on the phone she’d walk herself. He’d said, “Yes. You always did.”

Lin Jian didn’t come. He’d rung on Sunday night. “Her father should be the one in the room, not me. I’ll have you both on Saturday,” he’d said to Raiden. And that morning a message, which Raiden showed her in the back room while Elowen pinned her hair: Tell my daughter-in-law the fish will be steamed. Ah Sim says ginger, not too much.

There was no officiant. They’d done the legal part two and a half years ago in a registry office with a clerk who’d yawned. Mrs. Tong stood between them by the counter where she’d taken their order for brisket noodles on the first Sunday, and said, “Well. Go on, then,” and blew her nose.

“I married you on a napkin. I’d do it on anything. That’s all,” said Raiden.

“That was a speech.”

“It was two sentences.”

“I’m keeping you. That’s mine,” said Jinx.

She put the steel ring on her own finger, over the washer, because she’d made it and that was the point. He watched her do it. Then he took her hand and kissed both rings, and she pulled him down by the lapel and kissed him in front of everyone, and Mrs. Tong said, “Not in front of the fish,” and the whole room laughed, and her father, by the door, put his hand over his eyes.

✦ ✦ ✦

They left at five in their wedding clothes. Jinx had her boots on under the dress and the dress hitched over her knees, and Raiden had his jacket folded on the sidecar seat and his tie in his pocket, and they took ARCHITECT north up the coast road with the light going gold and then rose and then grey over the water, past the turning for the custom show and the petrol station where he’d told a stranger about her, to the small hotel on the headland where they’d stayed with the trophy in a box under the bed.
