The room was the same. The window looked over the sea. She’d thought she’d be tired. She wasn’t.

He closed the door and stood with his back against it, looking at her, the way he’d looked at her across Mrs. Tong’s in front of the fish tank.

“Still all right?” he said.

“Come here and find out.”

He came. He undid the buttons down the back of the green dress one at a time, slowly, the way he did everything he cared about, and kissed the place between her shoulder blades where each one had been. She stood at the window with her hands on the cold sill and the sea going dark below her and let him, and felt every one. When the dress went to the floor she turned round. He was looking at her face. He was always looking at her face.

“Tell me, if you want anything to stop,” he said.

“I will.”

“Or slow.”

“Raiden.”

“I know. I’m asking anyway.”

She pulled his shirt out of his trousers herself and put her hands flat on his stomach, on the warm skin over his ribs where they’d been cracked once, and pushed him back towards the bed, and he went. She liked that he went. She liked that he lay down and let her come down over him and that his hands stayed where she put them until she moved them somewhere else. She kissed his mouth and his throat and the inside of the wrist the van had broken, and he said her name, the name only he used, in a voice that had come apart at the edges.

It was slow. She hadn’t known it could be slow and still be this much. The sea was in the window behind her and the lamp was on, because he’d switched it on without being asked, and every time she opened her eyes he was there, watching her with his glasses off and an expression she’d have died rather than describe to anyone. When she took him inside her she held still with her palms on his chest and felt him breathe, and he didn’t move, and he didn’t ask, and he waited for her as if waiting were the whole point and not the price of it. Then she moved, and he moved with her, and the bed creaked in a way that made her laugh into his neck, and then she wasn’t laughing.

He turned them over after a while, carefully, still asking with his eyes, and she wrapped her legs round him and pulled him closer, and the two rings on her hand caught on his shoulder. She came apart under him with her face in his neck and his name in her mouth, and he followed her with a sound she felt more than heard, and held himself up on his forearms afterwards so as not to put his weight on her, until she pulled him down anyway.

They lay in the lamplight with the window open and the sea doing what it did.

“Mrs. Lin,” he said, into her hair.

“Don’t.”

“Mrs. Lin. In front of people.”

“Mrs. Tong’s fish saw it. I’m keeping you,” she said again, because it was true, and because he seemed to need to hear it twice, and he fell asleep before she’d finished saying it. She found his hand in the dark and laced her fingers through his, washer and steel and washer.

chapters.title: The Masterpiece He Could Never Draw
chapters.desc: Jinx in a wig drives Nonna north while Serafina and Haozhen take Nobody the other way. Eighteen days. Two bullet holes in her taxi, a hug instead of a punch, and behind her own shutter she finally cries. He finishes her face.
chapters.epigraph: “I don’t have to wait till you’re happy to draw your face.”
chapters.content:
The wig itched.

Jinx stood in the second bay of a car wash that had closed with the rest of the service station a year ago, on the old coast road, in Serafina’s own black jacket and a short dark wig that Mouse had bought from a theatre shop and cut with kitchen scissors, holding a paper cup of coffee she hadn’t drunk. The pumps outside were gone. The shop was boarded. The sign over the forecourt still promised hot food and clean facilities to nobody. Above bay three the camera had been broken since the autumn, and Haozhen had made sure of that personally, and hadn’t said how.

In the third bay Raiden sat at the wheel of the ugliest taxi in the city with the engine idling and his hands at ten and two, like a man in a driving test.

It was a quarter to ten on Saturday night, the thirteenth of April. Serafina had won the opening round of the season that afternoon by four seconds, round the outside of the Needle, and somebody in the paddock had decided she shouldn’t drive home. Jinx didn’t know who. She’d been told not to ask. She was surprisingly good at not asking when it mattered.

Nonna came in fast and the shutter came down behind her with a clatter, and for a second there was nothing in the bay but dripping pipes and two people breathing.

“You’re late,” said Jinx.

“Traffic,” said Serafina, getting out.

“Three cars of it. Is this the part where I ask what’s going on?” Jinx held out her hand for the keys.

“No,” said Haozhen.

“Excellent. I hate the answers. If they scratch her I’m coming after them myself.” She looked at the little red car, at the white seven on her flank and the dust from the circuit still on her sills.

“Take her north on the expressway. Lights on. Don’t speed. Let them keep you in sight for forty minutes, then go to your father’s yard under the flyover and put her inside.”

“Yes, Dad,” said Jinx, and got in.

She didn’t look at the third bay. She didn’t look at Raiden. If she’d looked at him she’d have got out again. Nonna’s engine caught on the first turn with that uneven bark Serafina loved, and the shutter went up, and she rolled out onto the coast road with someone else’s seat moulded to her back, and turned north.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first car picked her up before the slip road. A saloon, dark, sitting four lengths back with its lights dipped. Then a hatchback, closer. Then, a long way behind, a silver estate that didn’t seem to care whether she saw it. She kept to the speed limit and her lane and her lights, and let them keep her in sight, and didn’t think about the third bay at all.

She’d driven Nonna twice before, both times with Serafina in the passenger seat shouting. The car pulled a fraction left under braking and the clutch bit high, and the steering was so alive in her hands that she could feel the paint lines under the front tyres. On the long straight past the reservoir the hatchback came up close enough for her to see the shape of a man’s head in it, and she thought about the wig and the jacket and how far she’d get on foot from the hard shoulder in Serafina’s boots, which were a size too big. Then it dropped back.

Forty minutes. She took the flyover exit with her indicator on like a good citizen. Under the flyover the lights were orange and the shops were shut, and her father’s shutter was already up a metre, because she’d rung him from the car wash and said, I need the yard tonight. Don’t ask.

He’d said, I wasn’t going to.

She drove Nonna under the shutter into the shop where she’d learned to read, and he brought it down behind her, and by the time she’d switched off the engine the three cars had gone past on the road outside without stopping. Her father stood in the dark with his hand on the shutter chain, listening, until the last engine had faded. Then he turned the light on and looked at the car.

“Whose is she?”

“A friend’s.”

He walked round Nonna once, slowly, the way he’d walked round every car that ever came in under that shutter. He touched the white seven. “She’s been looked after.”

“She has.”

He went into the back room, the one with the camp bed in it, and came out with a dust sheet, and they covered Nonna together without a word, and then he made tea on the stove he lit with a match, and they sat on two stools and drank it.

Raiden came at ten past one in a taxi. He’d left the car wash by the back, he said, after Nobody went out onto the coast road the other way with Serafina at the wheel. He’d walked to the next village and found a taxi rank and told the driver he’d had a fight with his girlfriend, and the driver had been sympathetic all the way into town.

He came under the shutter and stopped. She’d taken the wig off. Her hair was flat and damp and she looked, she knew, like a wet cat. He didn’t say anything about it. He crossed the shop and put his arms round her, standing between the stools, and held on. Her father looked at the dust sheet.

“They went the other way. Nobody had a full tank. She was driving,” Raiden said into her hair.

“Good.”

“Haozhen had the envelope.”

“Good.”

He held her tighter. “That’s all I know.”

✦ ✦ ✦

That was all anyone knew.

On Sunday morning the radio in the shop said that a driver had been injured overnight in a collision on the old coast road, near the salt pans, and was in hospital with a broken leg and burns to one hand, and police were asking for witnesses. It didn’t say who. It didn’t say how many cars. Jinx stood at the bench with a wrench in her hand and listened to the weather afterwards and the price of rice and the traffic on the harbour bridge, and then she turned it off and didn’t turn it on again for a fortnight.

Serafina’s phone went to a voice that said the number was unavailable. Haozhen didn’t have a phone. Mouse didn’t know, and said so, and went white when she said it.

The first week Jinx slept with her phone under her pillow. The second week she stopped sleeping properly. She worked. She rebuilt a gearbox for a man who’d been waiting two months and a set of forks for a man who’d been waiting two days, and she stripped and painted a fuel tank that didn’t need painting. Raiden didn’t tell her to stop waiting. He didn’t tell her they were fine, either, because he didn’t know they were fine. He made enough dinner for two and put half of it away when she didn’t eat it, and left the kitchen light on, and when she came up the stairs at three in the morning he was at the table with a book on concrete open in front of him, and he never pretended he hadn’t been waiting for her.

On the fourteenth day, a Saturday, a message came from a number she didn’t know.

Alive. Both. Somewhere safe. Don’t ask. — A.

She read it standing in the middle of the shop. Then she sat down on the floor with her back against Carp’s front wheel, which was where Raiden found her an hour later, and she showed it to him, and he read it and sat down next to her and didn’t say I told you so, because he hadn’t.

Four more days.

✦ ✦ ✦

They came home on the first of May.

Jinx had brought Nonna back to the garage under the railway bridge on the Monday, under her dust sheet on a trailer behind her father’s van, because her father had insisted on driving and wouldn’t say why. Now she sat on the little car’s bonnet with her arms folded, in Serafina’s garage with the trains going over every eleven minutes, and Raiden stood beside her with a box of pastries from the bakery on the corner. They’d been there since seven. It was getting on for four.

The shutter went up and Nobody came in under it with a brown dog’s head out of the back window, ears flying.

Jinx got down off the bonnet. She didn’t say anything. She walked round the taxi once, slowly, the way her father walked round a car, and stopped at the front passenger door.

Two holes. Neat as punched paper. One below the window and one through the pillar.

“Two,” she said.

“I know,” said Haozhen. His left arm was in a sling under a coat that wasn’t his.

“In my car.”

“I know.”

“I built her to be invisible. Somebody looked at her anyway.” She put her finger into the lower hole. It went in to the knuckle.

“She was invisible. Until I put my arm out of the window,” said Haozhen.

She turned away from them and walked three steps towards the workbench and stood with her back to everyone. She could feel her shoulders going and she couldn’t stop them.

“Oh, Jinx,” said Serafina.

“I’m not crying. I’m angry. It’s different.” She wiped her face on her sleeve, hard, and turned round and walked straight into Haozhen and put her arms round him so hard he grunted, and let go of his left side as if it had burned her, and grabbed Serafina instead and held on.

“Don’t. Either of you. Ever again,” she said into Serafina’s hair.

“We’ll try.”

“Try harder. I’m not filling them. The holes. I’ll paint round them. People should know she’s been shot at and kept going.” She stepped back.

Raiden opened the pastry box. The dog ate one before anyone saw him move.

✦ ✦ ✦

She held it together all the way home.

She held it together while Raiden parked ARCHITECT in its place and while she checked the shutter and the alarm and the back door. She held it together while he went up to put the kettle on. And then she was alone in the shop with the lights off except the one over the bench, and she reached up and pulled the shutter down the last metre to the ground, and turned the radio on and turned it up, loud, some old song she’d always said she hated, and slid down the inside of the shutter until she was sitting on the concrete, and it came out of her.

She hadn’t cried like that since she was eight. Not when her mother went, not at seventeen, not at Harbourside, or under the flyover, or in the bath. She cried until her ribs hurt and her face was a mess and she couldn’t breathe through her nose, with her back against the cold slats and her knees up and the radio playing love songs to nobody.

Upstairs Raiden heard the radio and the shutter, and understood both. He came down the outside stairs and sat on the black step on the pavement with his back against the brick, a metre from the shutter, where he could hear the radio and she could hear him if she needed to, and he didn’t knock.

He sat there an hour. A man walked past with a dog and looked at him. A taxi slowed and went on. At ten past ten the song changed. At twenty past, something inside moved, a stool scraping. At half past he heard her blow her nose, loudly, and laugh at herself, and he put his head back against the bricks and shut his eyes.

At 10:41 the shutter rose thirty centimetres and a hand came out under it, black at the fingertips.

“Get in.”

He lay down on the pavement on his stomach, took his glasses off and put them in his pocket, and slid in under the shutter. His shirt caught on the bottom slat and tore. He didn’t care. She was sitting on the floor with her face swollen and wet and a streak of grease across one cheek where she’d wiped it, and she looked at him.

“You were on the step.”

“Yes.”

“For an hour.”

“I didn’t know if you wanted me inside. I wanted to be where you’d find me if you did.”

She leaned forward and put her forehead on his shoulder. He put his arms round her, and they sat on the floor of her shop with the radio still going.

“She came back,” she said.

“She came back.”

“They both did.”

“They both did. And you drove a car you love up the expressway in a wig with three men following you, so that they could.”

She laughed into his shoulder, a wet, broken, real sound.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later, she sat up on the bench with one boot on a crate, drinking the tea he’d brought down, and he sat on the stool opposite her with his sketchbook.

She thought he was drawing the shop. Then she saw where his eyes kept going.

He’d drawn her a hundred times. Her hands round a spanner. Her back bent over an engine. Her boots under the kitchen table. Her silhouette in a doorway, upside down under Nobody at seven minutes past two. The first week he’d known her he’d drawn her mouth and her eyes on a page with two creepers on it, and stopped, and written that it was closer. He’d been getting closer for three years. He’d never once finished her face. He’d always rubbed it out.

“Look at me,” he said.

“I am.”

“Not at the page. At me.”

She looked at him. He drew.

He didn’t hurry. She’d never seen him hurry with a pencil. He looked at her and down and at her again, and the pencil made its small dry sound, and she sat there with swollen eyes and grease on her cheek and a cold mug in her hands and let him look. At some point she stopped feeling looked at and started feeling seen, and she didn’t know the difference until it had happened.

At a quarter past midnight he stopped.

“It isn’t perfect,” he said.

“Show me.”

He turned the book round.

It was her, no prettier and no softer than she was, and not the face she wore for customers or the one she wore for men like Guo. Tired eyes, swollen at the lids. The smudge of grease on the cheekbone. The small scar under her chin from a bike stand at fourteen that she’d forgotten anybody could see. Her mouth almost, not quite, smiling. And under all of it something she’d never let anybody see on purpose, and he’d seen it anyway, and put it down in pencil, and not rubbed it out.

“Why now?” she said. Her voice didn’t work well.

“Because I finally understood that I don’t have to wait till you’re happy to draw your face. Or safe. Or smiling. I kept waiting for the right day. This is the right day. This is you.” He looked at the page and then at her.

She put the mug down. She reached for him across the bench with both black hands and took his face between them and kissed him, and got grease on him, and didn’t care.

“I’ll ruin your shirt,” she said.

“It’s torn. You’ve ruined it already.”

She took it off him. She took it off him on the floor of the shop on the old blanket she kept for lying under bikes, beside Carp, under the one light, with the radio still playing because neither of them could be bothered to cross the floor and turn it off. She was tired, and wrung out, and greedy for him in a way that surprised her, and he let her be all three. She pushed him down onto his back and he went. She put her mouth on his throat and felt his pulse jump under it. When she sank down onto him she was slow and then not slow, with her hands flat on his chest, and he held her hips and looked up at her as if he were still drawing her, as if he wanted every line of it.

“I love you,” he said, afterwards, with her lying on him and her hair in his mouth and the concrete cold under his back.

“I love you too,” said Jinx, and fell asleep there, and he lay on the floor of her shop for the rest of the night and let her.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the first Saturday in June, Elowen came by with a box of hydrangeas Xiao Pan’s bike couldn’t carry and stayed for tea. Jinx went up to put the kettle on and came back down and found her in the little office, standing in front of the wall.

Raiden had pinned the drawing there, beside the trophy from the custom show and the napkin with the creepers on it. Elowen was standing with her arms folded, quite still, looking at it.

“He’s never drawn a face. Not one of us. Not Baba. Not me. He used to say he could never get it right. He got you,” she said, without turning round. She looked a moment longer.

chapters.title: Her Name Over the Door
chapters.desc: He asks before he buys anything. She buys the chandler’s warehouse herself and he draws it for a dinner. Builders call her Boss, her father brings a pigeon named Jia, and a man in a good jacket wants a bike nobody can catch.
chapters.epigraph: “I named her Jia. Because she won’t go where she’s put.”
chapters.content:
The old chandler’s warehouse three doors down from Tai Hing had been empty for eleven years, and in August a man in a short-sleeved shirt came and put a board up on it.

Raiden saw it on his way to the tram. He stood on the pavement in front of it for long enough that the tram came and went. Then he walked to work, and drew a hospital extension all day, and came home and found her at the bench and didn’t mention it. He didn’t mention it the next day either. On the third evening he put a single sheet of paper down beside her bowl at dinner.

It was the agent’s particulars. Long and narrow, brick, a loading bay at the front and a door onto the service lane at the back. Roof poor. Drainage poor. One steel column patched by somebody who’d used more optimism than steel.

He said, “It’s for sale. I’d like to buy it for you. I’ve got enough left from my mother’s money and what I’ve saved. Or you can buy it, and I’ll draw it. Or neither, and I’ll stop walking past it. I wanted to ask before I did anything. That’s all.” He picked up his chopsticks.

She looked at the sheet.

Three years ago he’d bought the building she was sitting in, and the one next door, with his dead mother’s money, and put them in her name, and told her afterwards in a lawyer’s letter. She’d been so angry she’d thrown a gearbox cover at the wall. She’d also kept the building. She’d thought about that a good deal since.

“How much?”

He told her.

“I’ll buy it. Not you. Me. The bank will lend against this place. It’s mine, so I can borrow on it. You draw it,” she said. She put her finger on the patched column in the photograph.

“All right.”

“And you send me a bill.”

Raiden said gravely that he’d send her a bill, and he did, three weeks later, folded under her coffee cup: To drawings, structural checks and one argument about the dyno room: dinner, cooked by the client, at a time of her choosing. Payment terms: whenever. She paid it the following Friday. He said it was the best fee he’d ever been paid. She said it was rice and fish. He said, “Exactly.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He drew it in the evenings at the kitchen table. She would come up the stairs and find another sheet: the section through the roof, the new slab at the back for the dyno, the extraction run, a separate supply for the machines so that the lights didn’t dip every time the compressor kicked in. He’d put the office at the front, by the window, small, with a door that shut. He’d put a wash bay where the old chandler had stored lamp oil. He’d allowed for a proper lathe, a big one, the kind she’d stood in front of at a dealer’s in the industrial estate with her hands in her pockets and walked away from.

“I can’t afford that lathe,” she said.

“Then the floor will hold one when you can. I’ve checked the load.”

“Of course you have.”

“Twice,” said Raiden.

The title came through on the second Friday in September, in one name, hers, and she took it out of the envelope at the bench and read it three times and put it in the grey-blue cabinet, behind the code.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first builder lasted eleven minutes.

He looked at the floor, and the roof, and the patched column, and her, and then he turned to Raiden and said, “Are you sure about all this?”

Raiden said, “I’m not the client.”

The builder looked back at her. “The dyno slab alone is going to—”

“I know what it’s going to cost. I’ve read the drawings.”

“It’s a lot for a little shop.”

“Then it’s a good thing it’s my money,” said Jinx, and pointed at the door, and he went through it.

The second wanted to shrink the dyno room. The third asked whether she’d thought about moving the office to the back to save on glazing. She asked whether he’d read the plans. He said he had. She asked him to read them again. The fourth was a broad man with a pencil behind each ear who walked round the building in silence with the drawings under his arm, put his hand flat on the bad column, and said, “Who patched this? I’d like to have a word with his mother.” She hired him on the spot.

By the fourth week the builders had stopped looking at Raiden when they had a question. They looked at her.

“Boss, the concrete’s here.”

“Boss, the man from the electricity board wants a signature.”

“Boss, where do you want the spare duct?”

“Don’t call me that,” she told the foreman.

“All right, Boss,” he said, and Raiden had to go and stand outside in the lane for a while.

The roof came off and went back on. The drains went in. The old brick came up clean under the pressure washer, the colour of strong tea. The loading doors were rehung on new tracks and ran so smoothly she opened and shut them six times in a row for no reason. The dyno went onto its slab in a crate that took four men and a forklift and more patience than she had, and she stood next to the forklift with her hands on her hips telling the driver to be careful until he stopped and looked at her and said, with great dignity, “Boss, I have been careful since 1991.”

The paint booth was Raiden’s favourite part. He didn’t know anything about paint. But he’d watched her spray tanks for three years in the corner of a shop with the shutter half up and a fan in the window, holding her breath, and he’d drawn her a booth with its own air and lights down both walls so that she’d never again have to guess what colour something really was. On the first day it was ready she stood in it with a spray gun and a primed panel, and he stood at the door checking the extraction with a strip of tissue on a pencil, and she said, “Don’t breathe near it.”

“I’m in the doorway.”

“You’re breathing in the doorway.”

“Would you like me to stop?”

She put the gun down and came over and kissed him, and backed him into the booth wall, and when she let him go there was a white handprint on the front of his shirt and a smear of primer along his jaw where her thumb had been. He looked down at himself. He put his hand up deliberately and touched her temple, and it came away white too.

The foreman opened the booth door, looked at them both, and closed it again.

“Take your time, Boss,” he called through it.

✦ ✦ ✦

In October her father sold the land under the flyover.

He did it with his own solicitor and at his own price, which was more than Sheung had wanted to pay and less than Lin Jian could have made him pay, and he signed the contract on a Tuesday afternoon in an office with a pot plant and came out and stood on the pavement for a minute with his hands in his pockets. She’d gone with him. He hadn’t asked her to. He hadn’t told her not to.

“That’s that,” he said.

“That’s that.”

The flat by the river was ready by the end of the month. The loft on the roof had been finished in September by Ms. Bok’s builder, with a sloped floor that drained to one corner, perches spaced by her father’s own measurements, and a landing board facing south-east, which he said was the only direction a sensible bird would come home from. He moved in on the last Saturday in October with two vans of things, one of which turned out to be entirely tools. She carried the boxes up. He carried the tools. Raiden fixed the kitchen tap, which had been dripping since the drawings were done, and her father watched him do it with deep suspicion and then said, “Good,” which Jinx had heard him say about perhaps four people’s work in her whole life.

The last thing he moved was the camp bed from the back room. He took it out to the lane and folded it up and leaned it against the skip, and stood looking at it.

“I should have thrown that out a long time ago,” he said.

She didn’t answer. She took his arm, which she hadn’t done since she was nine, and they walked back to the van.

✦ ✦ ✦

She made the sign herself, because she wasn’t going to let anyone else make it.

A sheet of stainless off the offcut rack, the letters drawn on in chalk and cut with the plasma torch on four evenings in November, the edges dressed by hand with a file and then with paper, the face brushed in one direction until it took the light like water. Four letters. No wings. No chequered flags. No skull. Raiden came down at midnight on the Thursday before the opening and found her sitting on the floor beside it with a cloth in her hand.

“Too plain?” she said.

“No.”

“Too small?”

“No.”

“Too much like a name on a shop?”

“That’s what it is. It doesn’t have to explain itself.” He crouched beside her and touched the edge of one letter.

They put it up on Friday morning. The foreman brought a ladder. Raiden checked the fixings. She checked the level. They argued about the height for seven minutes while the foreman took a deep interest in an electrical box, and when it was up she stood in the lane and looked at it with her hands in her pockets.

JINX.

The men in her father’s shop had called her that at nine, after the first car she’d stripped, because the police had found every single part. She’d kept it for twenty years to remind herself what people expected. It was on a sheet of steel now, over a door she’d paid for.

Raiden took her hand. She let him.

“Good morning, Boss,” he said.

“Don’t you start.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The opening was on Saturday the sixteenth of November. She’d refused a ribbon, a photographer, and a speech. She’d agreed to food, because Elowen had said that if Jinx didn’t organise something Elowen would organise it for her, and Jinx had seen Elowen organise a wedding.

By eleven the shop was full. Mrs. Tong brought a pot of brisket the size of a wheel and set up at the end of a bench as if she’d been asked. Xiao Pan brought his red bike in for a service and stayed. Ms. Bok came and looked at the slab and the column and said nothing and then said, “Acceptable,” which made Raiden go pink. Serafina and Haozhen came at noon. His arm was out of the sling now, though he still carried it a little carefully, and Serafina hugged Jinx in the doorway, and this time Jinx could just hug her back, and let go when it was done.

“You did it,” said Serafina.

“It’s a building.”

“It’s your building.”

Lin Jian came a little after one, with Uncle Mok waiting in the car. He stood under the sign and looked up at it for some time.

“Good name,” he said.

“Thank you.”

“I hear you bought it yourself.”

“I did.”

“With a bank. You could have—” He said bank the way other men said rat.

“I could have,” said Jinx.

He looked at her over his reading glasses, and then he laughed the way he had in his kitchen in January, and went inside to tell Ms. Bok what was wrong with her column.

Her father came last. He came on foot from the tram, in his white shirt, carrying a small wicker basket with a cloth over it. He stood in the loading bay and looked at the dyno room and the booth and the benches, and at the sign through the open doors, and then he held the basket out.

She lifted the cloth. A pigeon looked up at her, grey with a sheen of green at the neck and an expression of profound grievance.

“It’s yours,” her father said.

“I don’t want a pigeon.”

“It’s a good bird. Good line. She’ll come home to you from anywhere north of the river. I’ve trained her to this roof since September. I named her Jia.” He set the basket down on the bench.

Behind her Raiden made a sound like a man swallowing a fishbone.

“Why, is it called Jia?” said Jinx.

Her father considered the question seriously. “Because she won’t go where she’s put.”

He’d brought the little loft too, in the van: a box with a landing board, which he and Raiden fixed to the wall of the yard at the back between them, arguing about the bracket, while she stood with the basket in her arms and the pigeon glared at her through the wicker. When it was up her father checked the latch three times.

“Fresh water every day. Don’t overfeed her. She’ll sulk for a week, then she’ll be fine. Good shop.” He looked at the yard, and the back of the building, and the lane.

“Thank you.”

“Your husband drew it well.”

“He did.”

He nodded at the latch. “You built it, though.”

He left before she could answer that. The pigeon watched him go with one orange eye, and Jinx stood in the yard with her arms full of basket, and Raiden came and stood behind her and rested his chin on her head and didn’t say a single word about pigeons, which was the kindest thing he’d done all year.

✦ ✦ ✦

The man in the good jacket came at twenty-six minutes past three.

It was a well-cut jacket, dark, nothing on it that announced anything. Clean shoes, clean hands, no watch. He stood in the loading bay, not quite in and not quite out, and looked at the machines before he looked at her. That was the first thing she didn’t like.

“You’re Jinx.”

“Yes.”

“I’d like a bike built. Something quick and quiet that looks like nothing. Something that can cross the city at night without being stopped.”

“Stopped by who?”

“Anybody. I was told you don’t ask a lot of questions.” He smiled.

“You were told wrong. What’s it for?”

“Transport.”

“Of what?”

“Does that matter?”

“Yes,” said Jinx.

He put a business card on the bench. A name, a number, a logistics company with Global in its title. “If you change your mind.”

“I won’t.”

“You haven’t heard what I’d pay.”

“I don’t need to.”

He looked at her a moment longer, then at the sign over the door, and said, “Shame,” quite pleasantly, and walked out into the lane.

Raiden came over. He’d seen the whole thing from beside Mrs. Tong’s pot. He didn’t touch the card.

“May I?”

“It’s a business card.”

He photographed it. “I’d like Eliana to look at him. Quietly. She can find out who someone is without them ever knowing she’s asked. If you’d rather I didn’t—” He looked at her.

“It’s my shop. I decide what I build. You decide what you worry about. Ask her.” She picked the card up and turned it over. Nothing on the back.

By Monday afternoon Eliana had a page. The company on the card was a shell registered to a director who’d never been to a meeting, at an address that was a rented room with no one in it. The man himself had been questioned twice about stolen motorcycles that had turned up again in the south with new frame numbers. One of his partners had been charged with moving untaxed goods and had the case dropped. Another had left a police inquiry two years ago under one name and come back under a different one.

Raiden read it at the kitchen table and passed her the phone.

She read it twice. Then she put it face down by her cup.

“Stolen bikes. New frame numbers,” she said.

“Yes.”

“That’s what my father did. For men like that. For twenty years.”

“Yes.”

“I’m not building it.”

“I know.” He didn’t say anything else. He didn’t need to. She got up and went round the table and sat in his lap, which she never did, and put her face in his neck, and stayed there until the rice went cold.

✦ ✦ ✦

At the end of the opening, after the last of them had gone, she stood in the lane in the gold light with a rag and wiped the dust off one of the letters with her thumb.

“Do you think it’s strange? Me. With a shop like this,” she said.

“No.”

“Why not?”

“Because you’ve been building it for years. Out of whatever space anybody let you have, and whatever anyone threw away. This is just the first building that’s caught up with you.” He leaned on the door frame.

She didn’t have anything sharp to say to that, so she didn’t say anything. She kissed him under the sign instead, slowly, in full view of the lane, and up on the roof of the yard the pigeon named Jia watched them, and didn’t go anywhere she was put.

chapters.title: The Fire at the Shop
chapters.desc: A delivery rider’s battery goes at 2:09. Raiden runs barefoot and burns both palms on the shutter; she comes down the stair he insisted on, carrying a fuel tank. He sends the beam report to the city because people sleep above it, and tells Guo first.
chapters.epigraph: “You drew the stair, too.”
chapters.content:
At 1:18 on Thursday morning she texted him: Going to close my eyes for ten minutes.

Raiden texted back Come home, and lay looking at the ceiling for a while, and fell asleep with the phone on his chest.

She was at the new shop, three doors down, finishing a fuel tank for a restoration that should have been done a week ago: an old-fashioned shape, long and low with a dip for the rider’s knees, beaten out of a flat sheet over a sandbag and a wooden buck and checked against the frame so many times that she’d stopped counting. She put her head down on the office desk at twenty past one with her arms folded under it and the tank on the bench outside the door, where she could see it, and she slept.

She’d let a delivery rider charge his bike that afternoon. He’d asked at the loading bay, polite, sweating through his shirt, battery flashing red. She’d said fine, by the back bench, away from the work, and he’d plugged it in and gone across to Mrs. Tong’s for noodles and come back and been called away to a job in a hurry, and he’d said he’d come back for it, and she’d said fine, and forgotten.

At 2:09 the camera Eliana had put over the back lane in March saw smoke.

✦ ✦ ✦

Eliana rang him. He answered on the first ring.

“It’s the shop. The back. There’s smoke on the lane camera and the alarm’s gone. Her bike’s outside.”

He didn’t remember getting down the stairs. He remembered the pavement under his bare feet, and the shutter of the new shop at the end of it with grey smoke pushing out through the gap at the top of the long back window and curling up the brick, and the four steel letters over the door catching the streetlight. He remembered thinking quite clearly that the shutter was locked from the inside, because he’d drawn the lock.

“Jia!”

He got his hands under the bottom of the shutter and pulled. It was hot. He pulled anyway. It moved two centimetres and jammed in its tracks, and he pulled again, and the heat went into his palms like teeth.

“JIA!”

Someone had him round the waist. The man from the tyre place on the corner, in a vest and shorts, shouting at him to let go. He didn’t let go. He wasn’t a big man, but he’d never wanted anything in his life as much as he wanted that shutter up, and it took the tyre man and his son together to drag him back off it onto the pavement, where he went on fighting them with his hands held out in front of him like something he’d forgotten he was carrying.

And then, through the noise, from the back lane, a steel door banged open.

He’d drawn that door. When he’d drawn the shop he’d found an old service stair on the 1974 sheets behind the warehouse wall, blocked in the sixties, and he’d opened it up and lined it and put a fire door at the bottom onto the lane, and she’d said it was dramatic and expensive and that nobody was going to need it. He’d said he’d rather be dramatic before.

She came round the corner out of the lane in the orange light, black with soot to the elbows, coughing, with her hair coming down, carrying the fuel tank against her chest in both arms.

He stopped fighting.

She saw him. She saw the tyre man and his son, and Raiden’s bare feet, and his hands.

“Raiden?”

He got loose and crossed the distance so fast she nearly dropped the tank. He took her face in his burnt hands and held it and kissed her, hard, and she tasted of smoke, and he didn’t care, and his hands hurt more than anything had ever hurt him, and he didn’t care about that either.

“Are you hurt?”

“I’m fine. I’m—your hands. What did you do to your hands?” She coughed.

“The shutter.”

“You pulled on a hot shutter? You’re barefoot.” She stared at him.

“I was asleep.”

“You ran down the street barefoot and tried to pull a hot shutter up with your hands?”

“Yes.”

“Are you mad?”

“Yes, you carried a fuel tank out of a fire,” said Raiden, and started to laugh, or something like it, and couldn’t stop. He looked down at the thing between them.

“It’s a commission.”

“Jia.”

“It’s not finished,” she said, and then her face crumpled, and she let the tank go. It hit the pavement with a dull hollow clang and rolled into the gutter, and neither of them looked at it again.

✦ ✦ ✦

Mrs. Tong got to him before the fire engine did.

She came out of her shop in a dressing gown with a towel round her hair and took one look at his hands and marched him into her kitchen by the elbow, and put them under the cold tap, and held them there.

“Twenty minutes. Not ice. Not butter. My mother put butter on my brother and he screamed for a week. Twenty minutes of water. Count,” she said.

He counted. Jinx stood beside him at the sink with soot running off her in grey streams onto Mrs. Tong’s floor, and her hand flat on his back between his shoulder blades, and every few minutes she coughed until she had to bend over. The fire engine came. Through the window he saw them break the shutter and go in with a hose and a man with a mask, and he saw the smoke go white, and then thin, and then stop.

At twenty minutes Mrs. Tong turned off the tap and took a roll of cling film out of the drawer, and tore off the first two turns and threw them away, and laid a fresh piece over each palm, flat, not wrapped round. “So it can swell. I’ve run a kitchen for forty years. You think nobody’s burnt themselves in here?” she said, when Jinx looked at her.

✦ ✦ ✦

At Harbourside General, at a quarter past three, Elara came through the curtain in her scrubs with her hair pinned up from a night shift, looked at her brother on one trolley with his hands in dressings like two white boxing gloves, and at Jinx on the next one with an oxygen tube under her nose and a blanket round her shoulders, and stopped dead.

“Again?” she said.

“It’s a different hospital bed,” said Raiden.

“It’s the same hospital.”

“It’s a different incident.”

“I’m thrilled for you both. Chest?” She sat down on the end of Jinx’s trolley.

“Fine.”

“Don’t. They’ve got your saturation on the screen, I can read it from here. You’re staying till lunchtime. Partial thickness, both palms, base of both thumbs. Whoever cooled them did it properly. You’ll keep the skin.” She turned her head.

“Mrs. Tong,” said Jinx.

“Of course it was. He pulled on a burning shutter.” Elara looked at Raiden’s hands, and then at Jinx’s face.

“Yes.”

“For you.”

“I didn’t ask him to.”

Elara said, “No, you never have to ask him for anything. That’s rather the problem with my brother. I’m not going to shout at either of you tonight. I reserve the right to do it on Saturday.” She stood up and pulled Jinx’s blanket straight.

✦ ✦ ✦

The investigator came to the shop on Friday morning with a clipboard and a face that had seen a great many burnt buildings and expected to see more.

The back of the workshop was black to the roof. The extraction ducting had sagged and split. Half the wiring along the back wall had melted in its trays. The lathe was scorched down one side and the parts store was ruined. The front was sooty but sound. The dyno had survived, sitting on its slab in its own room behind its own wall, because Raiden had drawn it that way so the neighbours wouldn’t complain about the noise.

“Started here. Lithium cells. One goes, it heats the next, the next heats the next. They don’t burn like a normal fire. They go all at once and they make a lot of very bad smoke. Was it yours?” the investigator said, at the back bench. He showed them what was left of a battery pack, a black swollen block with its casing split open like a seed. He looked at Jinx.

“No. A rider’s. I let him charge it.”

“You were asleep in the building?”

“In the office.”

“You’re lucky. Most people don’t wake up for these. You’ve got a good back stair,” he said, writing.

She didn’t look at Raiden. She didn’t need to.

Eliana had the lane footage on her tablet by the afternoon: the rider at four o’clock with his cable, the rider leaving at six, nothing all evening, the first grey haze at 2:07 in the light over the back door. Nobody came. Nobody tried the shutter. There wasn’t anybody to blame but a cheap battery and a tired woman who’d said fine.

She sat on the step of Tai Hing that evening with her arms round her knees and said, “I keep looking for someone.”

Raiden sat down beside her, with his hands on his knees in their dressings. “I know.”

“There’s always been someone. Guo. My father’s buyers. That van. Men who want things. This was a battery.” She looked at the street.

“Yes.”

“I could have died because of a battery and a man who wanted noodles.”

“You didn’t. You went down the stair.” He leaned his shoulder against hers.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the third evening she found him at the kitchen table with the old report open on his laptop, the one from November 2023: the beam over the service corridor on the old market road, the moved column, the steel plate painted to match the ceiling. He was sitting still, with his bandaged hands either side of the keyboard. He’d typed a message to the Buildings Department with two fingers. He hadn’t sent it.

She put a cup of tea down by his elbow and read the screen over his shoulder.

“Is this about the fire?”

“No. There’s nothing to connect him to the fire. I know that. I’ve been sitting here for an hour knowing it. I keep thinking about my photograph over your bed. I keep thinking I could make one thing happen to him, finally, that he can’t sign his way out of.” He didn’t look round. His jaw was tight.

She pulled out the chair opposite and sat down.

“Is the beam still dangerous?”

“Yes.”

“Are there people above it?”

“Four floors. Families on two of them. He rents them out. I know what you’re going to say.” He closed his eyes.

“Then I’ll say it anyway. We made a deal. You don’t send it, he doesn’t come back. He hasn’t come back. But the deal was about us. It didn’t make his beam safe, and the people on the fourth floor never agreed to anything. Send it because it’s dangerous. Not because you want him to hurt. And tell him first. That’s what I’d want, if it was me.” She put her hand flat on the table near his, careful of the dressing. She looked at him.

He looked at her. Then he deleted every word he’d typed and started again, slowly, two-fingered.

To Guo, at the address on the job card: I’m reporting the transfer beam at your building on the old market road to the Buildings Department today. It isn’t about you or about us. There are families above it. You’ll want to have your engineer there when they come. — Lin Raiden.

To the Buildings Department: the drawings, the builder’s note, the measurements, his name. Nothing else.

He sent them both. He sat back and looked at his hands. She took the laptop away and shut it.

“I’m not finished being angry,” he said.

“I know.”

“I don’t know when I will be.”

“That’s all right. You don’t have to make it into anything.” She stood up and came round the table and put her arms round his head and held it against her stomach.

Guo’s reply came at eleven that night, from a number they didn’t have. One word. Understood. The inspectors closed the top four floors on the Monday and his builder had a new beam in by the end of the month, and the families came home, and nobody fell through a ceiling.

✦ ✦ ✦

She washed his hair that weekend because he couldn’t. He sat on the edge of the bath with his hands held up out of the way in their dressings like a surgeon waiting to be gloved, and she stood between his knees with the shower head and her sleeves rolled up and worked the shampoo through with her fingers, slowly, the way he’d washed the grease out of hers in March. He shut his eyes. When she rinsed it he leaned his forehead against her stomach and didn’t move, and she put the shower head down and held him there with the water running into the drain.

“I couldn’t get the shutter up,” he said into her shirt.

“I know.”

“I drew the lock. I knew it locked from inside. I knew before I got there, and I pulled on it anyway.”

“I know. You drew the stair, too.” She bent and kissed the top of his wet head.

✦ ✦ ✦

They rebuilt it in six weeks.

Eliana came on the first Saturday with her laptop and her tool roll and a box of cable, and rewired the back wall herself with the electrician from Ms. Bok’s office checking behind her, and put in new detectors, and a second camera, and a fire alarm that rang on all three of their phones and on Mrs. Tong’s. She wouldn’t take money. “You put the camera up. I complained about it,” Jinx said.

“I know. I’ve been waiting three months to say I told you so,” said Eliana.

Elara came on her day off and stood on a ladder holding new shelf brackets against the back wall while Jinx drilled, and her hands didn’t move a millimetre. Jinx had machined the brace that made those hands steady again, in a back room in 2021, and neither of them had ever said a word about it to anyone. They didn’t now. Elara held the brackets. Jinx drilled. When the last one was up Elara came down the ladder and looked at her hands and then at Jinx and said, “Good,” and that was all.

Her father came on the fourth day with a broom. Lin Jian was already there, in shirtsleeves, which Jinx had never seen, shovelling wet ash into a skip with a borrowed shovel. The two men nodded at each other. They worked side by side for an hour without speaking. Then her father said the floor drain at the back was blocked, and Lin Jian asked whether he knew how to clear it, and her father said he’d been clearing drains since before Lin Jian could walk, and they cleared it together, on their knees, arguing.

“Your father and mine,” said Raiden, from the crate she’d made him sit on.

“Don’t look at them. They’ll stop.”

The lathe came back from the fitter’s with a new cross-slide and a certificate. She measured the bed herself before she’d let anyone bolt it down. The dyno control box was rebuilt. The foreman came back with his crew and stood in the loading bay and looked at the black wall and said, “Good to have you back, Boss,” and she told him not to start, and let him.

His hands healed slowly. The dressings got smaller. The skin under them came up pink and new and shiny across both palms and the soft pad at the base of his thumbs, and the doctor said it would fade, but not all the way. On the night before the reopening she took his hands in the lamplight and turned them over and looked at them.

“You’ll have marks.”

“Probably.”

“Does it hurt?”

“Sometimes. When I hold a pencil too long.”

“Why didn’t you say?”

“I’m saying now. I’ll tell you. I promised.” He watched her face.

She lifted one hand and kissed the middle of his palm, where it was newest. He shut his eyes.

✦ ✦ ✦

They opened again on the last Saturday in July. No ribbon. No speeches. The people who’d swept the floor and pulled the wire and held the brackets, and Mrs. Tong with the brisket pot, and her father with the pigeon in its basket because he said the bird had been fretting at the river flat and wanted to see the roof.

Jinx stood in the loading bay with a coffee and looked at the back wall, new block and new paint and new ducting, and at the steel door at the bottom of the old stair with a green sign over it that said EXIT, which hadn’t been there before because she hadn’t thought she needed one.

Raiden came and stood beside her with his own coffee in his marked hand.

“You drew that stair,” she said.

“You went down it.”

“With a fuel tank.”

“With a fuel tank. I’m still not over the fuel tank,” he agreed.

She took his coffee off him and drank half of it, and gave it back, and he looked at it and then at her with enormous patience, and she kissed him in the loading bay with the doors open and the whole lane watching, and up on the roof the pigeon came home.

chapters.title: “Is That a Racetrack?”
chapters.desc: Serafina crashes at the Needle and Jinx spends two nights in a corridor she isn’t family enough to pass. Then a drawing on his desk: a house on a hill with a 1.2-kilometre driveway, and an option, not a purchase. A Saturday in the long grass.
chapters.epigraph: “Is that a racetrack?”
chapters.content:
The oil came from a green car two laps down.

Jinx saw it on the big screen opposite the main stand, because she’d been watching Serafina on the big screen for thirty laps instead of the track, the way she always did at the home round: a black car with a white seven and gold across the bonnet, a long way ahead of the next one, coming down towards the Needle at the end of the back straight on lap thirty-one in the low September sun. The green car had dropped something. She saw a faint dark shine on the braking zone that nobody else in the stand seemed to see. She was on her feet before Serafina’s front wheels found it.

The black car didn’t turn. It went straight on at the apex, quite slowly it seemed, the way things go in the moments before you understand them, across the gravel and into the barrier, and the screen cut away to a wide shot, and then to a car three corners back, and then to nothing at all.

Raiden had her hand. She didn’t remember him taking it. The stand had gone quiet in the way that crowds go quiet, all at once and from the edges in.

“Jia.”

“She’ll get out. She always gets out. Watch,” said Jinx.

On the far side of the circuit a helicopter started its rotors.

✦ ✦ ✦

The ninth floor of the big hospital on the hill had windows that didn’t open, and plastic chairs in a row by the fire door, and two sets of doors at the end of a corridor that only opened for a card.

Jinx wasn’t family. She found that out at the desk, from a tired nurse who was sorry about it. Serafina’s mother and father were family. Haozhen, by the end of the first night, was family too, because Vittoria Song had put both hands flat on the nurses’ desk and told them so in a voice nobody on that floor was going to argue with. Jinx was a friend. Friends sat in the corridor.

So she sat in the corridor. Raiden sat beside her.

They’d put Serafina to sleep. That was how Haozhen said it, when he came out the first time at three in the morning with his face grey and his tie gone and his voice even: her collarbone was broken in two places and there was a plate in it now; three ribs; a bruised lung that wasn’t doing its job, so a machine was doing it for her; a concussion they were watching. They were keeping her asleep so the lung could rest. He said it all twice. Jinx listened both times, because she could tell he needed to say it to someone who wasn’t a doctor.

“Did you eat?” she said.

He looked at her as if she’d spoken another language.

“Raiden,” she said, and Raiden got up without a word and went to find something from the machine round the corner that could be eaten by a man who wasn’t going to taste it, and came back with three packets of crackers and a tea, and Haozhen held the tea in both hands and didn’t drink it and went back through the doors.

She didn’t sleep that night. She didn’t sleep on Monday either. She sat on a plastic chair with her boots up on the next one and her jacket over her knees and counted the times the doors opened. Raiden went home once, at noon on Monday, and came back with clean clothes for both of them and a flask of congee, and didn’t tell her to go home, and didn’t tell her Serafina would be fine. At four on Monday afternoon he fell asleep sitting up with his head on her shoulder, and she let him, and watched the doors over the top of his hair.

At 2:14 on Tuesday morning the doors opened and Haozhen came through them, and stopped, and stood in the corridor looking at the two of them with an expression Jinx had never seen on his face.

“She woke up. They took the tube out. She looked at me. She said Car?” he said. His voice cracked straight down the middle.

Jinx put both hands over her face and laughed into them until it turned into something else, and Raiden put his arm round her and held on, and Haozhen stood there in the corridor in his ruined shirt and laughed with her, helplessly, wiping his eyes with the heel of his hand.

✦ ✦ ✦

Serafina went home on the twenty-fifth with her arm in a red sling and a list of things she wasn’t allowed to do that was longer than the race regulations. Haozhen moved onto the sofa under the railway bridge and wrote every dose of every tablet in his small square handwriting in his black notebook, and Serafina complained about it, and he went on doing it.

Jinx went twice. The first time she took food. The second time she took a box of brake parts Serafina had been asking about since August.

“I’m injured,” said Serafina, looking at them.

“The car isn’t.”

Serafina laughed and then held her ribs and swore, and Haozhen came out of the kitchen and said, “Don’t laugh,” and Serafina said she’d laugh if she wanted to, and, watching them, something in Jinx’s chest that had been clenched for eleven days let go a little.

Only a little. At home she still couldn’t sleep. She’d wake at three and pick up her phone and look at it. When Serafina didn’t answer a message for an hour on the Saturday, because she was asleep, Jinx went cold from her scalp to her feet and rang Haozhen, who said, kindly, “She’s asleep. I’m watching her breathe. I’ll ring you when she wakes up,” and did.

Raiden found her at the kitchen table at four in the morning a week later with a glass of water she hadn’t drunk.

He didn’t ask. He sat down opposite.

“I’m tired,” she said.

“I know.”

“I’m so tired of being frightened every time someone doesn’t answer. The flyover. Serafina in April. The shop. Now this. I keep waiting for the next phone call. I’ve been waiting for it since I was seventeen.” She turned the glass round.

He reached across the table and put his marked hand over hers.

“Can we go somewhere? Somewhere quiet. Just for a day. Where nobody’s going to ring,” she said.

His face did something she didn’t expect. It looked almost like relief.

“Yes. There’s somewhere I’d like to show you,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

The drawing was on his desk in the little room off the kitchen the next evening, held flat at the corners with two steel rules and a stone he’d picked up on the headland after the wedding. He’d left it there on purpose. She knew he had. He liked leaving things where she’d find them: a sketch under her coffee cup, a napkin, a cutaway on her bench. He liked watching her find them more than he liked giving them.

It was a house on a hill. Not big. Long and low and set into the slope so that the hill came up to its shoulders at the back, with stone walls and deep windows and a roof that followed the line of the land. A terrace looking down a valley to water. A garden with a long table. An old tree he’d drawn carefully, branch by branch, at the bottom of the slope. And on the roof, behind glass on three sides, a workshop: two benches, a tool wall, an office at one end with a drawing table in it, a room for a dyno with its own floor and its own air.

She leaned closer. A long road wound up the hill from a gate at the bottom to the house at the top. It came round the lower slope in a sweep, climbed through two tight bends, ran up a straight past the house and curled back round behind it. Beside the line, in his neat capitals, it said DRIVEWAY, 1.2 KM.

“Raiden.”

He was in the doorway. Of course he was. “Yes?”

She put her finger on the second bend. “Is that a racetrack?”

He considered the drawing with great seriousness. “It’s a driveway.”

“It’s one point two kilometres long. It’s got a hairpin. It’s got a straight.”

“For the gradient. And deliveries,” he said.

“Raiden that’s a racetrack,” said Jinx, and he smiled at her, the slow crooked smile he’d had on the shipyard road the first night, and she had to look back down at the paper to stop herself.

In the title block, where the client’s name went, it said: HILL HOUSE. CLIENTS: LIN RAIDEN AND CAO JIA.

“Where is this?”

“Forty acres north of the reservoir, an hour up the old road. An orchard once. Nobody’s farmed it for twenty years. I haven’t bought it.” He came in and stood beside her, not touching the drawing.

She looked up.

“I wanted to. I nearly did. I stood in the agent’s office in August with the pen in my hand and then I put it down. I’ve paid for a three-month option. If we want it, it’s ours at the price. If we don’t, I get the money back less the survey, and nobody’s lost anything but an afternoon. I drew it first because I wanted you to see what it could be before you saw what it is, which is a lot of grass and a broken wall and an old tree. But I’m not buying anything with both our names on it unless you ask me to.” He looked at the drawing and then at her.

She sat down on the edge of his desk.

“Why?”

“Because we’ve spent four years making a home out of buildings that weren’t meant to hold us. Your two rooms. The forty-third floor. The flyover. Tai Hing, which floods. The new shop, which burned. I wanted somewhere you could make as much noise as you liked, for as long as you liked, and leave a job half done on the bench, and know it would still be there in the morning. And I wanted somewhere nobody would ring.” He said it.

✦ ✦ ✦

They went on the second Saturday in October. He drove. She sat beside him with the drawings on her knees and a pencil, and by the time they’d passed the reservoir she’d written NOT ENOUGH STORAGE across the roof plan and circled the dyno room twice. He glanced over at a red light and saw it, and wrote Discuss with client in the margin with his left hand, and she drew a small skull next to it.

The gate was rusted open. Beyond it a farm track ran up through long gold grass to a ridge with a line of trees along it, and a stone wall half fallen, and a low shed with no roof. He stopped at the top and they got out.

It was quiet. Not empty. There were birds in the trees, and grasshoppers in the grass, and far below on the old road a single car going somewhere slowly. The valley opened out under them all the way to the water. She stood by the car with the wind in her hair and listened to nothing ringing.

“The house would be there. Against the trees,” he said, pointing.

She walked out into the grass. He followed. She looked at the slope and the ridge and the line of the track, and then she pointed down the hill at the lower bend.

“The road’s wrong.”

“Is it?”

“Your second bend’s blind. Coming up you can’t see what’s coming down until you’re on top of it. Swing it out ten metres towards those rocks and you’ll see all the way to the gate. And it’s a better line.” She looked at him.

He looked at the ground, and at the rocks, and at her. “That’s a good point.”

“I’m not just here to admire the view.”

“I know.”

She went on down the slope to the old tree. It was broad and bent by years of wind off the water, and its lowest branches came down almost to the grass. She put her hand on the bark.

“This stays.”

“It’s on the drawing.”

“I saw. I’m telling you anyway. I’ll buy it with you. Half. The bank’ll lend against the new shop. And the roof workshop’s mine to build. Not draw. Build. I’ll argue with your builders. I’ll check the foundations. I’ll choose the steel.” She turned round.

“All right.”

“Don’t say all right to make me happy.”

“I’m not. I’m saying it because it’s what I want. I’d like to live here with you, Jia. I’d like to come home and hear the dyno from the gate.” He came down the slope to her.

She looked at him. Then she took the pencil out from behind her ear and wrote something on the back of her hand, and held it up. YES.

He laughed. It came out of him like something let go.

✦ ✦ ✦

He’d brought a blanket and food in a basket, and they ate under the tree with the plans spread out between them and weighed down with the basket and her boots. She made him enlarge the workshop by thirty percent. He did it on the spot, in pencil, without arguing. She made him add a bench for electrical work, and a store for the parts she wasn’t allowed to leave on his desk at home, and a bath, a proper one, deep, not one of the beautiful kind that couldn’t be cleaned. She moved the bedroom to face the trees. She put a tap in the garden by the long table.

“Something should grow on that. Something you can eat,” she said, of the pergola he’d drawn along the terrace.

“Peaches. On the slope below the terrace. Six trees. They’d get the morning sun,” said Jinx.

He looked up.

She said, “You’ve only ever had them out of a tin. Off a windowsill, after the soldiers, with a kitchen knife. You’ve never had one off a tree.”

He didn’t say anything for a while. He looked down the slope at the grass where she’d pointed, as if he could already see them there. Then he wrote PEACHES (6) on the drawing in small capitals, and his hand wasn’t quite steady, and she leaned across the plans and kissed him, and the drawings slid off the blanket into the grass, and neither of them went after them.

The sun went low and gold along the ridge. The grass was long enough to close over them when they lay down in it. He looked at her with the light on her face, the way he’d looked at her the night he finally drew it, and she pulled his shirt over his head and pressed her mouth to his chest where his heart was going hard and fast.

“Here?” he said.

“Nobody’s going to ring.”

She unbuttoned her own shirt and let the warm wind have her. He kissed her slowly, her mouth and her throat and the soft skin under her collarbone, and she arched up into him in the grass with the old tree black against the sky above them and the smell of crushed stems everywhere. She took him in her hand and then inside her, and wrapped her legs round him, and held him there, not moving, for a long breath, so she could feel the whole length of him and the ground under her back and the wind going over them both. Then he moved and she moved with him, unhurried, the way you’d climb a long road you knew the end of. She opened her eyes at the end and found him watching her, the way he always did, as if she were the only thing in the valley worth looking at, and that was what took her over the edge, more than anything his body was doing: being looked at like that, here, with nobody ringing. She heard herself cry out and didn’t care who heard it. A bird went up out of the tree. He followed her a moment after, with his face in her neck and her name in his mouth.

They lay in the grass afterwards with their clothes half on and the plans somewhere near their feet.

“Forty acres,” she said, to the sky.

“Forty acres.”

“A racetrack.”

“A driveway.”

“Don’t spoil it,” said Jinx, and he laughed into her hair.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the way home she took the drawings back onto her knees and his pencil out of his shirt pocket, and under the title block, where the conditions usually went, she wrote in her own big untidy capitals:

CLIENT’S CONDITIONS.
1. Workshop thirty percent bigger. Built by client.
2. Two benches. One for him.
3. Bath you can lie down in.
4. Tree stays.
5. Driveway stays a racetrack.

She underlined the fifth one twice. At the red light by the reservoir he read it and said, “That isn’t a condition.”

“It is now.”

He picked up her hand from the drawing and kissed the YES on the back of it, which had begun to smudge.

“Home,” she said.

“Which one?”

She looked out of the window at the water going dark, and the lights coming on along the far shore.

“All of them. Drive,” said Jinx.

chapters.title: The Roof Never Falls
chapters.desc: A summer as her monkey on the driveway. The autumn hill climb on the old pass road with both fathers sharing a flask, and the class by 1.4 seconds. They move into Hill House in March, and on his birthday she says it first.
chapters.epigraph: “You’ve never said that first.”
chapters.content:
The first thing finished at Hill House was the driveway, which told you everything you needed to know about who was building it.

The roof wasn’t on. The walls were still a line of grey blockwork against the trees with the window holes taped over, and the builders ate their lunch on pallets of stone, and the old tree at the bottom of the garden had a ring of orange fence round it that Jinx had put up herself on the first day and checked every morning. But by June there was a road, one point two kilometres of fresh dark tarmac coming up from the gate in a long sweep round the lower slope, through two tight bends, one of them moved ten metres towards the rocks, up a straight past where the front door would be and round behind the house. She’d painted a white line across the bottom of it. She’d put a marker cone at the hairpin. By the garage she’d hung a board: SIDECAR TRAINING. NO EXCUSES.

“I think we should reconsider the wording,” said Raiden.

“You’re alive. That’s encouragement.”

The outfit was new. She’d built it over the winter in the shop, on a long low frame of her own design with a short-stroke engine out of something much faster bolted into it and the chair on the left, like ARCHITECT’s, a flat platform with grab rails and a little screen and nothing else. This one wasn’t for cake deliveries; she’d built it for the sidecar class at the autumn hill climb on the old pass road, which she’d entered in March without telling him and then told him about at dinner the same evening, because she didn’t do that any more.

“The passenger,” she’d said, “is called the monkey.”

“Why?”

“Because he spends all his time hanging off the side of it.”

He’d been a terrible monkey the first week. He’d sat in the chair as if it were furniture, holding on, upright and polite, and she’d come off the throttle at the first bend because she could feel him not moving. The second week he’d moved too much and too early, flinging himself out over the back wheel on right-handers before she’d turned in, so that the chair lifted and she had to shout at him through the helmet. By the third week he’d stopped thinking and started feeling it, the moment when she leaned and the weight wanted to go somewhere, and he’d begun to go there half a second before it asked. By August he was hanging off the outside of the chair on the left-hander with his head a hand’s breadth off the tarmac and his body flat and his knee locked on the rail, and coming back across the platform for the right-hander with his whole weight over the back wheel, and she could feel him through the frame like a second engine.

“Better,” she said, at the end of a run, pulling her helmet off.

“Only better?”

“Much better, Monkey.”

He’d liked that. He hadn’t said so. But she’d seen it, and called him it again, and by the end of the summer he answered to it in the kitchen of the house that didn’t have a roof yet.

He walked the pass road in September with a measuring wheel and drew it: every bend, every change of surface, every place the camber fell away and every drain cover, a long scroll of paper with the road running down the middle of it like a river. Beside the third bend, where the road narrowed and tightened at the same time, he’d written LATER THAN YOU WANT TO. Beside the last hairpin before the finish he’d drawn a small monkey.

“I’ll withdraw you,” she said.

“You can’t. Nobody else will get in that thing with you.”

She looked at him. He had a point.

✦ ✦ ✦

The hill climb was on the first Sunday in October. The road had been closed since six. It went up the side of the mountain in a series of tightening bends through pine trees, with straw bales on the outside of the corners and marshals in orange in every lay-by, and at the top it came out under a ridge into the sky.

Their family came. All of it. Jinx had never had a family to come to anything.

Lin Jian came in the black suit, with Ah Sim and a thermos of tea the size of a fire extinguisher, though there was a catering tent, and sat on a folding chair at the start line as if it had been put there for him. Elowen came with Zhao, who stood behind her chair with his hands in his pockets and looked at the outfit and said “Hm,” which from Zhao, Raiden said, was a review. Eliana came with a camera and a notebook. Mrs. Tong came on the coach with her grandson and a box of buns. Her father came on the tram and then a bus and then a lift from a stranger, with a folding stool and a flask of his own, and set himself up two metres from Lin Jian without saying hello, and after ten minutes Lin Jian offered him tea, and he took it.

Serafina came with Haozhen, two weeks before the last round of her own season. She walked round the outfit twice, the way Jinx’s father walked round a car, and put her hand on the chair.

“You’re letting him ride in this.”

“He asked.”

“I didn’t,” said Raiden.

“He didn’t,” Jinx agreed.

Serafina looked at Jinx’s face, and then at Raiden’s, and laughed. Her left shoulder still sat a fraction lower than her right under her jacket, where the plate was. Jinx caught herself looking at it, and Serafina caught her catching herself, and said, “Stop it,” and Jinx said, “I’m not,” and Haozhen said, “She is,” and Serafina told them both to go and win something.

Raiden brought two coffees from the tent and gave her one. Then he stood beside her and looked at them all: his father and hers sharing a flask, his sisters, Mrs. Tong handing out buns to marshals, the people from the shop, the foreman, who’d brought his wife.

“What?” she said.

“I like seeing you here. With all of them,” he said.

She looked at them too. Then she took his hand.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first run was clean and slow. She’d known it would be. The second was faster and wrong: he went out over the chair a fraction late at the third bend, the narrow one, and the chair came up, and she had to feather the throttle to put it down, and she felt the time go.

“Late,” she said, at the top, with her helmet off.

“I know.”

“Half a second.”

“I know. I’m watching the bend. I should be watching you.” He looked at the scroll.

“Then watch me.”

The last run was in the afternoon, when the road was warm and dry. She sat on the bike with her chest on the tank and her knees tucked in. He knelt on the platform with his hands on the rails. The starter raised the flag, and she looked down at him, and he looked up through his visor and tapped her calf twice, the way they’d agreed: later than you want to.

The flag dropped.

The first bend came at them out of the trees, a long left, and he was out over the chair before she’d finished leaning, flat, his helmet a hand off the road. The chair dug in. They came through. Up the hill through the gears with the engine screaming and the pines going past in a blur. Right, tightening, and he came back across the platform over the back wheel and she felt the rear tyre bite. The narrow bend came up, the third one, the one on the scroll, and she braked later than she wanted to, much later, so late that for a fraction of a second the whole thing hung at the edge of the corner like a held breath, and then he moved, exactly when she did, not after, and the outfit turned as if it had been waiting all its life to turn there, and came out onto the straight a second faster than it had ever gone.

She didn’t remember the rest. She remembered the last hairpin, and him going out so far over the chair that she thought she’d lose him, and the little drawn monkey on the scroll in her head, and the finish line coming down out of the sky at them under the ridge.

They crossed it. She sat up and let the engine fall away to nothing.

Neither of them moved. Then she looked up at the timing board by the marshals’ hut.

SIDECAR. FIRST. BY 1.4 SECONDS.

She stared at it. He climbed off the platform, slowly, as if his legs had been borrowed, and stood beside the bike and pulled his helmet off and looked at the board and then at her.

“We won,” he said.

She got her gloves off. He reached up and undid her helmet strap and lifted it off her, and her hair came down flat and wet, and he held the helmet under one arm and kissed her, there at the finish under the ridge, not carefully at all, with the marshals cheering and somebody’s horn going and half her family coming up the last bend on foot to see. She put her bare hands in his hair and kissed him back until she forgot where she was.

“Monkey,” she said, when she could.

“Driver.”

“You were good.”

He put his forehead against hers. “So were you.”

Behind them Mrs. Tong was crying. Eliana was photographing everything. Lin Jian had got to his feet. Jinx’s father was standing on his folding stool, which wasn’t designed for it, to see over the bales, and Zhao had one hand on the back of his collar in case.

✦ ✦ ✦

They moved in at the end of March. The roof workshop went in last, because she wouldn’t move her tools until the electrics had been tested twice and the dyno room floor had cured for its full twenty-eight days. She’d built it herself, with the foreman and his crew and a crane for the steel, as she’d said she would: two benches under the glass, the one by the window for him; a fabrication bay; an electrical bench; storage enough for every part she’d ever been told not to leave on his desk. The bath downstairs was deep enough to lie down in. The bedroom faced the trees. The six peach trees went in on the slope below the terrace in the first week of April, thin as walking sticks, and she told him she’d be impressed when they fruited and not before.

His birthday was on a Friday. His and Evangeline’s on paper; his alone in truth. They went down to the Walled City for it, in through the red door, and Ah Sim made two cakes, as she’d made two every year since the spring of 2023, and Lin Jian put fish in everybody’s bowl and asked whether the dyno room had proper extraction. Jinx said it did. He asked whether the driveway was still being used for racing. Raiden opened his mouth. Jinx said, “Yes,” and Lin Jian laughed, and said, “Good.”

They drove home at eleven, up the old road past the reservoir with the lights of the far shore lying on the water. She went up to the roof while he locked the doors, onto the little terrace outside the workshop glass, and stood at the rail looking down the valley. He came up with two cups of tea and put them on the ledge and stood beside her.

It was cool. The peaches were black sticks below them. The road wound down the hill in the dark to the gate.

She said, “I used to think that if I had somewhere to go, I’d be safe. Then I thought if I had enough money I could leave whenever I wanted. Then I thought if I could fix enough things, nobody would ever be able to take anything off me. I was wrong about some of that.” She looked at the water.

“Not all of it.”

“Not all of it. Raiden.” She turned round. He had the lights of the house behind him and the night in front, and the scars on his palms showed pale when he lifted his cup.

“Yes?”

“I love you.”

He went still. He put the cup down carefully on the ledge, as if it might go off.

“You’ve never said that first. Not once. Four and a half years. You always say too,” he said.

“I know. I’m saying it first.” She’d known for a while. She’d been saving it.

He looked at her. His face did something slow and quiet that she didn’t think he could have stopped if he’d tried.

“Say it again,” he said.

“I love you.”

“I love you. I’ve loved you since you threw a spanner at my head,” said Raiden.

“I missed on purpose.”

“I know. That’s why.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Later, when she’d gone in, he went to the drawing table at the end of the workshop and switched on the lamp.

She found him there at one in the morning, sitting in front of a clean sheet of paper with a pencil in his hand. He’d ruled the title block in the corner, the way he did on every drawing he’d ever made. The rest of the sheet was blank.

“What are you drawing?”

“I tried to draw tonight. The terrace, and you at the rail, and the house, and the road going down. I’ve been sitting here an hour. I can’t do it.” He didn’t look round.

“You drew my face.”

“That was one night. A face holds still long enough, if you look. This doesn’t. It keeps going. Every time I think I’ve got it, there’s something else. Your father on a stool. The peaches. Tomorrow. It’s the only thing I’ve ever wanted to draw that I can’t. I think it’s the best thing I’ll ever not draw.” He turned the pencil over. He smiled, a little helplessly.

She came and stood behind him and looked at the empty sheet, and the title block he’d filled in, in his small neat capitals.

PROJECT: HOME. CLIENTS: LIN RAIDEN AND CAO JIA. SCALE: 1:1. STATUS: IN PROGRESS. DRAWN BY: —.

There were two boxes left. CHECKED. APPROVED.

She took the pencil out of his hand and leaned over his shoulder and wrote her initial in both, J and J, in her own big untidy hand.

He looked at it.

“That’s not how it works. You can’t approve a drawing that hasn’t been drawn,” he said.

“I just did.”

She put the pencil down and switched off the lamp. Down the hill the road curled away in the dark to the gate. Above them the roof he’d drawn held everything it was meant to hold, and under it, in the bed that faced the trees, he lay awake for a while with his wife asleep against him, and didn’t count the doors once.

chapters.title: Oil on His Cheek
chapters.desc: Six hours under Serafina’s gold bike, with her husband hovering and reading her the welder’s safety notice. She finds the bent selector fork, then draws a stripe of gearbox oil down his face.
