chapters.epigraph: “I’ve been trying to get you to stop talking for six hours.”
chapters.content:
He had been hovering for forty-seven minutes.

Jinx knew because she’d counted, not on purpose. She’d been under Serafina’s gold bike since nine, on her back on the creeper with the gearbox half out above her face, and somewhere around ten she’d become aware of his footsteps: to the bench, to the door, back to the bench, a pause, the small dry rustle of his phone, and then the footsteps again. It was the first Saturday in July. The shutter was up a metre for the air. They’d been married nine months and nobody in the world knew except Mrs. Tong, and he still hadn’t learned how to be in her shop without wanting to be useful in it.

“Jia.”

Nothing.

“Jinx.”

A ratchet clicked.

“I found something.”

“Mm.”

“It’s about a mechanic.”

The ratchet stopped. “If it’s another one about a man who loses a finger because he wasn’t wearing gloves, I’ll lose one of yours.”

He looked at his phone. “It isn’t.”

“Then read it.”

He read it. It was about a mechanic who said a job would take two hours and was found under the car the following Tuesday. She didn’t laugh. She heard him not mind. After that he sat down on the upturned crate by her feet and was quiet for nearly three minutes, which she suspected was a personal best, and then he said, “There’s a safety notice on the welder.”

“I’m not welding.”

“It’s still important. Ensure the work area is adequately ventilated. Remove all flammable materials. Wear appropriate eye protection. Don’t touch recently welded components with bare hands—” He took it off its hook. It was laminated and greasy and had been there since before she bought the welder second-hand.

“I’m going to weld you to the floor.”

He laughed. She heard it above her, warm, in the half-light of the shop, and lying under the gearbox with grease running down her wrist she found she was smiling, and was annoyed about it, and went on smiling.

✦ ✦ ✦

The trouble was third gear. Serafina had ridden the gold bike for three weeks before she’d brought it back, and said it jumped out of third under load, politely, the way people did when they’d paid a lot and didn’t want to sound ungrateful. Jinx had built that box. She’d taken it personally. By two in the afternoon she’d had it apart twice and found nothing, and at a quarter to three she found it: a selector fork a hair out of true, so slight that she could only see it by laying a steel rule along it under the lamp and looking for the light underneath.

She straightened it on the press by eye and feel, a little at a time, checking after each touch. She put it back. She ran the shafts through every gear by hand, then again, then again, with her eyes shut, listening for the click of the dogs going home. Third went in and stayed in like a door shutting.

She lay there with her hands on the cases and let out a breath she’d been holding since nine.

Six hours. She slid out on the creeper into the light.

He was standing over her with a bowl of something from Mrs. Tong’s in one hand and a cup of tea, long cold, in the other.

“Hello,” said Raiden.

She blinked up at him. “Did you eat?”

“Mrs. Tong brought brisket at one. I saved you half.” He put the bowl and the cup on the bench and crouched down beside the creeper and held out his hand, and she took it and let him pull her upright. Her hair had come mostly out of its tie. Her arms were black to the elbow. Her shirt was a disgrace.

He looked at her face. “You’ve got something—”

“I know.”

“Just there.” He reached towards her cheekbone with his thumb.

She caught his wrist. His hand stopped a few centimetres from her face. He looked at her with a faint amused question in his eyes. She looked down at her own hand, at the grease ground into the lines of it. Then, deliberately, she reached up with two fingers and drew a long dark stripe down his cheek from the bone to the corner of his jaw.

He went completely still.

She examined it. “Better.”

He touched his cheek and looked at his fingertips. “That’s gearbox oil.”

“Well spotted.”

“I was trying to clean your face.”

“And I was improving yours. You’ve been hovering for six hours.” She hadn’t let go of his wrist. She could feel his pulse under her thumb, and it had picked up.

“Forty-seven minutes. Then I sat on a crate.”

“You read me the welder.”

“It contained important information.”

“Raiden. I’ve finished. I’ve been under that thing since nine o’clock and the only thing I’ve been thinking about for the last hour, apart from a selector fork, is getting my hands on you.” She pulled on the wrist, and he came closer, still crouching.

His expression changed. Not much. Just enough. His smile went slow and warm and slightly too pleased with itself, and she recognised it, because she was usually the reason for it.

“I’ve been trying not to distract you,” he said.

“You did a terrible job.”

“I noticed,” said Raiden, and she kissed him.

✦ ✦ ✦

It started with her black hands on his face and his clean ones at her waist. Somewhere between the creeper and the bench she remembered the shutter, and broke off, and went and pulled it down to the ground with a crash that made the windows ring, and came back, and he was standing by the bench with oil on his face and his shirt half undone already, by his own hand, looking at her.

“Are you sure? You’ve been working all day,” he said.

“Raiden. I’ve been trying to get you to stop talking for six hours.” She put both hands flat on his chest and pushed him back against the bench.

He laughed, and stopped talking.

She left prints on everything. On his shirt as she pushed it off his shoulders, on his ribs, on the pale skin over his hip where she held him. He didn’t seem to care. He lifted her onto the bench beside the gearbox cases and the steel rule and the tea gone cold, and the bench was hard and warm from the lamp and smelt of oil and old iron, and she wrapped her legs round him and pulled him in and kissed him with her filthy hands in his clean hair.

He undid her overalls slowly, one stud at a time, watching her face, and she let him go slowly because she’d learned that he liked to, and that she liked him to, more than she’d ever have admitted on any day but this one. When he put his mouth to her collarbone she put her head back against the tool wall and a spanner fell off its hook and rang on the floor, and neither of them looked. He said her name against her skin, the name only he used. She pulled him closer by the hips until there was nothing between them, and when he pushed into her she let out a breath she felt all the way down her spine, and held on to his shoulders, and left two black handprints there that he found in the mirror that night and wouldn’t wash off for an hour.

It wasn’t slow, in the end. Six hours was a long time to want someone with your hands full. She moved against him on the edge of the bench with the cases rattling and the lamp swinging on its chain, and he held her steady with one arm round her back, and the shop went bright and narrow and close round the two of them, and she came apart with her face in his neck and her teeth in his shoulder, and he followed her with a sound she would think about for weeks.

Afterwards they stayed where they were. The bench was warm. Her legs were still round him. Somewhere beyond the shutter a delivery van reversed, beeping, and somebody shouted, and it was all a long way off.

“Comfortable?” he said, into her hair.

“No. There’s a gear shaft in my back.”

He laughed and lifted her off the bench and they sat on the floor instead, against the tool wall, on the old blanket she used for lying under things, and she put his clean shirt on because hers was past saving. It came down to her thighs. The sleeves were too long. He looked at her in it and didn’t say anything, which she understood perfectly.

“I’ve got another one,” he said, eventually.

“Another what?”

“A meme. About a woman who threatens her husband with welding equipment.”

She lifted her head off his shoulder. “Show me.”

✦ ✦ ✦

When she came back from washing, he was at the little drawing board by the office door with a pencil.

“What’s that?”

“Nothing.”

“That’s a lie.”

He moved his arm. It was a sketch of her, quick and loose, sitting on the bench in his shirt with one knee up and her hair coming down and a stripe of grease on her cheek where he’d finally put it, at some point she hadn’t noticed, with his thumb. He hadn’t done her face properly. He never did. But he’d got her hands exactly, black to the knuckle, and the shirt, and the knee.

Underneath, in his small neat capitals: SHE STARTED IT.

She looked at it.

“That’s your version,” she said.

“An accurate historical record.”

“You were hovering.”

“I was supporting.”

She took the pencil out of his hand and leaned over his shoulder and drew a small arrow to the stripe of oil on the cheek of the man in the corner of the sketch, who she now saw was him, small, standing by the bench with a phone. Beside the arrow, in her own big untidy capitals, she wrote: HE WAS ASKING FOR IT.

He laughed, delighted. She kissed his cheek, the clean one.

“Third’s fixed. Ring Serafina,” she said.

“Now?”

“Now. Then feed me. You said you’d saved half.”

He’d saved half. She ate it at the bench in his shirt, cold, with her fingers, while he rang Serafina and told her that third gear was fixed and that Jinx had found a selector fork out by less than the thickness of a hair and had straightened it by feel. Serafina said something on the other end that made him look across at Jinx and smile.

“She says you’re a witch,” he reported.

“Tell her she owes me a gearbox.”

“She says she knows.”

The drawing stayed pinned to the board by the office door until the end of the year, two captions and one oil-stained cheek, and when Mrs. Tong came in on the Monday with the bowl to collect and stood in front of it for some time with her reading glasses on, Jinx said, “It’s about the gearbox,” and Mrs. Tong said, “Of course it is,” and took the bowl, and went.

chapters.title: She Tries to Cook
chapters.desc: The day after his birthday at the Walled City, where Ah Sim made two cakes for the first time, she tries his steamed fish. The oil catches. The extinguisher wins. The cake was behind the peaches.
chapters.epigraph: “It’s still mine. That’s what makes it mine.”
chapters.content:
She had a secret, and it was a fish.

It was the Monday after his birthday, the tenth of April, raining since dawn in long grey sheets off the harbour. His birthday had been on the Sunday, and he’d spent it at the Walled City with his family, as he did every year, because it was his sister’s birthday too on paper and his father liked them both at the table. Jinx hadn’t gone. She’d said, on a napkin, a long time ago: nothing in the Walled City. And nobody but Mrs. Tong knew there was anyone to invite.

He’d come home at eleven and kissed her hair in the dark and said, “I’m home,” and she’d pretended to be asleep, because she had a plan.

At breakfast he’d told her about the cakes.

“Two. Ah Sim made two. One for each of us. She’s made one for both of us every April since the paper was signed, since I was ten, and she said yesterday that one cake isn’t enough for two birthdays. Twenty-five, and I nearly cried over a cake in front of my father.” he’d said, buttering toast, with a look on his face she hadn’t seen before. He’d looked down at the toast.

“Did you?”

“Zhao ate the belly of the fish so nobody would notice my face. He’ll deny it.” He’d smiled.

She’d thought about that all morning. About a boy who’d come home at ten to a house that had given him somebody else’s birthday, and had shared it for fifteen years without minding, or without saying he minded, which with him was the same thing until it wasn’t. About Ah Sim, whom she’d never met, standing in a kitchen she’d never been in, deciding one cake wasn’t enough.

He’d gone to work at eight. She’d told him not to come home before six.

“Why?”

“Because I said so.”

“Should I be worried?”

“Yes,” she’d said, and he’d gone off smiling under his umbrella, and she’d shut the shutter and gone up to the kitchen and looked at the fish.

✦ ✦ ✦

He made steamed fish the way she fixed carburettors, without appearing to think about it. He’d choose the fish at the market by its eyes and its gills and the way it lay on the ice, and score it, and lay it on a plate on ginger, and steam it for exactly as long as it needed and not a second more, and then shred the spring onion fine and pile it on top with more ginger, and heat oil in a small pan until it shimmered and pour it over the top so that the whole kitchen hissed and smelled of something that made her want to sit down. She’d watched him do it perhaps thirty times. She’d assumed, the way you do, that watching something thirty times was the same as knowing how to do it.

She’d asked Mrs. Tong for the steps. Mrs. Tong had written them on the back of an order pad in her careful round hand and underlined DO NOT WALK AWAY FROM THE OIL three times, and Jinx had taken that the way she took most warnings, as something meant for other people.

At twenty past four she bought the fish. It was a good fish. It looked at her from the plate with a clear eye. She scored it. She put it on the ginger. She got the steamer going and set the timer on her phone and stood over it like a woman watching a dyno run.

At twelve minutes past five the fish was done, and she put the oil on.

It began to shimmer. She’d been told to wait for the shimmer. She waited for it. Then her phone rang on the counter behind her, and it was a man about a set of forks, and she turned round to answer it for not more than forty seconds, and when she turned back the oil was on fire.

She stared at it. For one long unreasonable moment she thought it might go out if she looked disappointed enough. It didn’t. A sheet of yellow flame stood up out of the little pan to the extractor hood.

She knew what to do. Everyone who’d ever worked in a shop with a parts washer knew what to do. Not water. Never water. Lid, or damp cloth, or the thing on the wall. The lid was in the sink under the steamer pan. The cloth was on the other side of the fire. The thing on the wall was right beside the door, where she’d hung it herself on the day she moved in.

She pulled the pin and squeezed.

The kitchen vanished.

When it came back it was white. The fire was out. So was the stove, the counter, the cupboards, the floor, the window, and the fish, which lay on its plate under a thick soft drift of yellow-white powder like a fish in snow. A small cloud of it was still coming down, slowly, out of the extractor hood.

“Excellent,” said Jinx, to nobody.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came up the stairs just before six, shaking his umbrella, and opened the kitchen door, and stopped.

He looked at the kitchen. He looked at her, in the middle of it, in his old jumper with her hair tied up and powder in her eyelashes and an expression of the deepest personal offence. He looked at the extinguisher on the floor, and at the fish.

He put his keys down carefully on the shelf by the door.

“Are you hurt?”

“No.”

“Did you get burnt?”

“No.”

“Did you breathe any of it?”

“Some. I opened the window. Don’t look at the fish.” She folded her arms.

He crossed the kitchen in three steps, leaving footprints, and checked her hands, turning them over, and her arms, and her face, tilting it up to the light, the way he checked a drawing for errors. She let him. When he’d finished he let out a breath and looked at the stove.

“What happened?”

“Dinner. That’s your birthday dinner.” She pointed at the plate.

He looked at the fish under its powder. The fish looked back.

“You cooked. For me,” he said.

“I tried. Don’t sound so surprised.”

“I’m not surprised. The oil caught?” His mouth had gone soft at one corner.

“I answered the phone. Forty seconds. Mrs. Tong said not to walk away from the oil. She underlined it. The extinguisher’s very efficient.” She heard her own voice go wobbly and hated it.

“Yes. Yes, it is,” said Raiden carefully.

She pointed at him. “Don’t laugh.”

“I’m not.”

“You’re doing it with your eyes.”

He pressed his lips together. He lasted about two seconds. Then it came out of him, helplessly, a laugh that bent him nearly double in the doorway of a kitchen that looked like the inside of a cloud, and she looked at him with total betrayal, and then he reached out and pulled her into his arms, powder and all, and held on, still laughing, into her hair.

“You’re covered in it now,” she said into his shirt.

“I know.”

“It’s going to take hours.”

“I know,” he said, and kissed her, and she tasted extinguisher on his mouth, and he didn’t seem to mind.

✦ ✦ ✦

They sat on the top stair while the kitchen aired, with the rain coming down outside and the window open and a thin white dust still settling on the landing. She’d washed her hands and face. He’d changed into an old shirt. He had his arm round her waist and she was leaning on him, sulking.

“I had everything ready.”

“I know.”

“I watched you do it thirty times.”

“I believe you.”

“The oil wasn’t supposed to do that.”

“No, it usually waits till you’ve turned your back,” he agreed.

She nudged his knee. Then she said, more, “I wanted you to have one here. At home. That wasn’t anyone else’s.”

He went still beside her.

She said, “You have it at the Walled City every year, with her. That’s good. I’m glad Ah Sim made two cakes. But you told me about the cakes like somebody who’s been given something for the first time, and you’re twenty-five. And I can’t go there. I don’t want to. But I wanted you to come home and find something that was only yours.”

He was quiet. He picked up her hand, the one with the washer on it, and turned it over and looked at the palm, where there was still a little white powder in the lines.

“You did,” he said.

“It’s under an inch of fire extinguisher.”

“It’s still mine. That’s what makes it mine.” He kissed her fingers.

✦ ✦ ✦

At seven she remembered the cake.

She got up so fast that he looked at her, and she said, “Stay there,” and went down the stairs to the shop and through to the back, and pulled the tool wall open on its recessed handle, and went into the steel room where the yellow lamp was always on. On the shelf, behind the tin of peaches he kept there, there was a white box.

She brought it up and put it on the stair between them.

“You hid a cake in the steel room,” said Raiden.

“You never look behind the peaches.”

She opened the lid. It was small. White icing, a dark chocolate edge, one candle. On the top, in blue piping that the woman in the bakery on the corner had done while Jinx stood over her, it said ONE CAKE. JUST YOURS.

He looked at it.

“I got the woman to do the writing. I didn’t trust myself after the fish,” said Jinx.

He didn’t answer. He put his hand over his eyes. She waited. She’d never seen him cry, not in the hospital, not ever, and she didn’t now, quite. When he took his hand away his eyes were wet and he was smiling.

She lit the candle with the lighter she kept for the blowtorch. “Make a wish.”

“What if I don’t?”

“Then I’ll set the kitchen on fire again.”

He closed his eyes. She watched him think of something. Then he blew the candle out, and the smoke went up in a thin grey thread into the rain-light on the stairs, and she cut the cake with his pocket knife and they ate it with their fingers, and ordered noodles, because there was nothing else in the house that wasn’t white.

✦ ✦ ✦

At ten she found him in the kitchen with the extinguisher.

He’d wiped it clean and checked the gauge and was holding a marker pen. On the red side of it, in his neat capitals, he’d written: JIA’S COOKING KIT.

“That’s rude.”

He added a line underneath: DO NOT REMOVE.

“I’m cooking you something next year. And I’m not using that.”

“I look forward to it.”

“I’m not. Probably,” she said.

She took the pen out of his hand and wrote beneath his label, in her own capitals: HUSBAND’S EMERGENCY EQUIPMENT. Then she hung it back on its hook by the door, and he put his arms round her from behind, and they stood in the white kitchen with the rain going on outside and the window open and the smell of ginger and powder and noodles.

“Happy birthday. Your own one,” she said.

“Thank you. Jinx,” said Raiden, into her hair.

She turned round in his arms. He almost never called her that.

“It’s a good name. You should hear it from someone who means it kindly,” he said.

chapters.title: The Socialite Act at the Police Gala
chapters.desc: Sent to the police benevolent gala in his partner’s place, he plays the fool and mentions that the evidence store’s hinge pins are on the outside. An inspector sees through him. Jinx walks into a police building for the first time because she wants to.
chapters.epigraph: “Because nobody shoots the boy who can’t find his own coat.”
chapters.content:
The invitation had come to the practice, for the senior partner, who had flu. It was for the police benevolent fund’s winter gala, in the old drill hall behind headquarters, and it said black tie, and the partner had sent it down to the forty-first floor with a note that said Lin, you go. Be charming. They’re thinking about the new forensic wing.

“You hate these things,” said Jinx, watching him do his cufflinks in the bedroom mirror.

“I don’t hate them.”

“You once spent forty minutes telling a hotel manager what was wrong with his ballroom ceiling.”

“It was sagging.”

“It was a decorative ceiling.”

“It was sagging decoratively,” said Raiden, and she looked at him in the mirror until he smiled.

She was on the foot of the bed in her work trousers, doing up her boots. The new shop opened in a week and she’d be at it till midnight, and she’d never been to a police gala in her life and didn’t intend to start. She’d grown up under a flyover in a shop where the police came in twice a year and left with less than they’d come for. She’d never once walked into a police building because she wanted to.

He looked perfectly harmless in the dark suit. That was the part she liked least.

“Don’t do anything stupid.”

“I’ll try.”

“If anyone asks what you do—”

“I draw buildings for a practice on Harbour Road.”

“And nothing else.”

He bent and kissed her. She caught his tie before he could straighten up. “You’re never good.”

“Only with you,” he said, and went.

✦ ✦ ✦

The drill hall was full of men in dinner jackets who stood like men in uniform, and women in silk who stood like the wives of men in uniform, and a few women in dinner jackets of their own who stood like nobody’s wife. There was a string quartet and a lot of bad wine and a raffle for a weekend at a hotel on the islands.

Raiden was good at this. Within twenty minutes he had been introduced to two superintendents, a deputy commissioner, a man from the fund, and a chief inspector who had decided after four sentences that he was either extraordinarily polite or extraordinarily stupid, and was content not to find out which. Raiden helped him along. He admired the flowers. He asked whether the hall had been reroofed recently, and listened with interest to the answer, which was wrong. He listened to a long story about a stolen-car ring that had taken three months to crack, and asked at the end, wide-eyed, how they’d ever known where to look, and the superintendent telling it glowed.

Then, holding his glass, he said, apologetically, “I may be remembering wrong. The door on the car park side of the old block, the steel one with the yellow stripe by the bins. Is that the evidence store?”

The superintendent looked at him. “Why?”

“Nothing. I walked past it from the taxi. It opens outwards. With the hinges on the outside. The pins are just ordinary pins. Somebody with a nail punch and a hammer could have them out in about four minutes, and lift the door off from the car park, and the lock wouldn’t mind at all. It’s quite a nice lock. It’s probably nothing. I draw buildings. I notice doors.” Raiden smiled vaguely. He looked at his wine.

There was a short silence.

“It’s a security door,” said the superintendent.

“Oh, I’m sure.”

“It’s perfectly secure.”

“Yes, it just isn’t attached very well,” said Raiden. He turned to the woman beside them and asked whether the flowers were local.

The superintendent didn’t answer her. He’d taken his phone out and was walking away towards the corridor with it at his ear.

✦ ✦ ✦

Inspector Lui Yan had been watching from the pillar by the bar since the stolen-car story.

She was at the gala because her superintendent had made her come and refusing would have taken more conversation than coming. She was forty-four and had spent nineteen years watching people in rooms. She watched the young man in the plain suit, the one with the round glasses and the hair that wouldn’t stay down and the vague, apologetic face. She watched him ask about the roof. She watched him stand a little back from every group, where he could see the doors. She watched his eyes go to the entrance every time it opened, and come back, and she watched the harmlessness, which was good and a fraction too well kept.

When he went out onto the terrace, she went too, after a minute, with her glass.

He was at the rail, looking down at the car park. He didn’t turn round. “Inspector.”

“You saw me.”

“By the pillar. You’ve been there an hour. You haven’t touched your wine.”

She came and stood beside him at the rail. Below them the steel door with the yellow stripe was lit up by two men with torches, crouched at the hinges.

“Who are you?” she said.

“A draftsman.”

“You’re not stupid.”

“No,” he agreed. He sounded sorry about it.

She looked at him for a while. “I won’t tell anyone. That you’re not. It’ll be more useful if they don’t know,” she said.

“Thank you.”

“Why do you do it?”

He thought about the question honestly, which she hadn’t expected. “Because nobody shoots the boy who can’t find his own coat,” he said, and smiled at her, and went back in.

✦ ✦ ✦

Jinx’s phone went just before eleven. A photograph: him on the terrace with the city behind him, tie loosened, looking pleased with himself.

Raiden: The flowers are nice.

Jinx: Are you drunk?

Raiden: No.

Jinx: Have you annoyed anyone?

Raiden: Not on purpose.

Jinx: Raiden.

Raiden: A superintendent has found out something about his evidence store.

She rang him. “What did you do?”

“I told him his door was hung the wrong way round.”

There was a pause.

“You went to a police gala, and told them how to rob their own evidence store,” said Jinx.

“I told them how somebody else could. It’s different. I thought you’d be proud.”

“I’m not proud.”

“You’re smiling.”

She was. She was on the floor of the new shop with a box of fasteners, sorting them into a tray by size, and she was smiling at a box of screws.

“Come home,” she said.

“I have to say goodbye to people.”

“Then say goodbye fast. And don’t make friends with anyone who has a badge.”

“One. I think I’ve made one,” said Raiden.

✦ ✦ ✦

She was there before he’d finished saying goodbye.

She came through the side gate of headquarters on Carp at quarter past eleven in her jacket and her work boots with grease on her hands, and she stood in the yard with the blue lamp over the door and the windows lit, and felt every hair on her arms stand up, the way it had when she was nine and a patrol car slowed outside her father’s shop. She made herself walk. She went past the man at the door, who looked at her boots and then at her face and decided not to say anything, and through the drill hall full of silk and medals, where a woman by a pillar watched her go by with mild interest, and out onto the terrace.

He was at the rail. He turned round and saw her and his face did something she’d never get tired of.

“What are you doing here?”

“Collecting my husband.”

“You were nearby.”

“I wasn’t.”

She reached up and straightened his tie, which didn’t need it. “You look ridiculous.”

“Thank you.”

“Too handsome. Everybody in there’s going to remember you.”

“Is that a complaint?”

“It’s a problem.” She kissed him. His hand came to her waist, and he leaned into her against the rail, smiling against her mouth, with the whole of the city’s police force a pane of glass away.

The terrace door opened. A young man in a dinner jacket with a detective’s haircut stepped out with a cigarette, saw them, looked at Raiden and then at her, and said “Sorry,” and went straight back inside.

“Good evening, Inspector,” Raiden called after him.

“Don’t,” said Jinx, into his shoulder, and laughed until she had to hold on to the rail.

✦ ✦ ✦

The Commissioner’s wife rang the practice three weeks later.

She’d heard about the door. Everybody had heard about the door. The superintendent had changed every hinge on the old block and then told the story at dinner as his own discovery, and somebody at the dinner had known better. She wanted a room in her house, she said. Not a bunker, not a steel box with a dramatic door and nowhere to sit. Somewhere she could go with her mother, who was eighty-seven and lived with them, if anyone came into the house who shouldn’t. Somewhere with its own air and a telephone and water, and a way out that wasn’t the way in.

He went and looked at the house. He spent an afternoon in the basement with a torch and the original drawings. He designed her a room under the stairs with its own air and its own power and a telephone on a separate line, water for three days, a washroom, a door that locked from inside and could be opened from outside by one code that only she would hold, and a second way out through the old coal store to the garden. He put two proper chairs in it, with arms, because her mother had bad knees. He put a lamp on its own circuit that would stay on.

When the Commissioner asked for the fee, Raiden gave him the cost of the work and nothing else.

“That seems low.”

“It’s what it cost.”

“And your fee?”

“I’m not charging one.”

The Commissioner looked at him across his own dining table. “Why?”

“Because I’d rather it was never used,” said Raiden, which was true, and not the whole of it.

✦ ✦ ✦

He told her the whole of it that night, on the floor of the shop, where she was sorting the last of the fasteners.

“You did it for nothing.”

“For the cost.”

“Why?”

He sat down beside her on the concrete and picked up a bolt and put it in the wrong compartment, and she took it out and put it in the right one without looking.

He said, “When I was nine. I was in a freezer for eleven hours. You know that. It was the only safe place on the farm, and it wasn’t safe, it was just somewhere nobody looked. I counted to four thousand in it. Every one of those rooms I draw, I put a chair in. And a light that stays on. And another way out. It’s the room I didn’t have. I’m not going to charge a woman with an eighty-seven-year-old mother for the room I didn’t have.” He turned another bolt over.

Jinx put the tray down.

She looked at him in the light over the bench. Then she reached up and put her greasy hand against his clean cheek and held it there.

“You’re a strange man, Lin Raiden.”

“I’ve been told.”

“You go to a police gala in a suit, tell a superintendent how to break into his own building, and come home with a job you won’t take money for.”

“An unexpected professional development.”

She kissed him on the concrete floor among the screws. He kissed her back with one hand flat on her spine, and when they stopped she left her forehead against his.

“Did you make any friends?”

“One. An inspector. She told me she knew I wasn’t stupid.”

Jinx laughed. “Finally. Someone in that building with eyes,” she said.

chapters.title: Locked in His Own Safe Room
chapters.desc: At the eighteen-month check on the Peak room he presses the button to test it, and it works. The owner’s code is on a plane and the house copy is in the house safe, inside. She brings the envelope in twenty-six minutes.
chapters.epigraph: “I knew who I’d ring. And I knew she’d come.”
chapters.content:
Every room he drew got a check at eighteen months. He put it in the contract: the architect returns, at his own cost, and makes sure the thing still does what it was drawn to do. Most clients forgot. Some were annoyed. Chen Si had read the clause, looked at him for a long, still moment across the table on the forty-fourth floor, and initialled it.

So on the second Saturday in February, at ten in the morning, Raiden took a taxi up the Peak road with his tool roll and a clipboard, to check the room under the stairs.

Chen Si was in the air to Milan. Aurelia let him in herself, in a pink cashmere jumper with her hair held back in a soft band, and gave him coffee in the kitchen, and asked after Jinx, and said, “You’ll want to be alone with it. Everybody who builds something does.” She took her own cup through to the morning room and left him to it.

The study was as he’d drawn it. Books to the ceiling on three walls. On the fourth, under the stair, a run of shelves that looked exactly like the others and weren’t. He knelt and put his fingers to the release in the bottom rail, the one you’d only find if you knew, and the whole section swung in on its counterweight without a sound.

Inside: six seats, two of them proper chairs. Water for a week. A washroom. Its own air, filtered, from a shaft that came out three gardens away. A telephone on a line that didn’t go through the house. A lamp on its own circuit. A steel door behind the shelves with a seal that would hold against smoke and a lock that, once a certain button was pressed, would answer to nobody on earth but the people it was meant to answer to.

He checked the air first. Then the water, the batteries, the light, the seals on the door. He ran the telephone. He sat in each of the chairs. Then, because it was what he’d come to check and he’d never in his life signed off a thing he hadn’t tested, he pulled the door to behind him and pressed the button.

The room did exactly what he’d designed it to do.

The bolts went home in the frame with a sound like a heavy book shutting. The panel by the door lit up red. The air changed note as the shaft took over. The shelves outside, he knew, had locked themselves into the wall, and would look to anyone in the study like an ordinary run of books.

“Good,” said Raiden, to the room, and put in the code to let himself out.

It didn’t work.

He looked at the panel. He put it in again, slowly. Twelve digits. The panel thought about it and stayed red.

Of course it did. The owner’s code changed itself on the first of every month and went to one telephone, which was at thirty-eight thousand feet over somewhere with its owner asleep beside it. The code he’d just put in was January’s. He’d written it down at the handover himself.

He stood in the middle of the most secure room he’d ever drawn and began, to laugh.

✦ ✦ ✦

There was a second way. There was always a second way; he’d never drawn a room without one. From outside, a maintenance code would open the door, for the day the person inside couldn’t open it themselves. That code didn’t change. It had been sealed in an envelope at the handover, and the envelope was in a folder marked WORK, PRIVATE, in a safe bolted to the concrete in a shop office by the docks, behind a parts cabinet, where he’d put it so that he couldn’t keep anything about his work out of her sight.

The house’s own copy of the owner’s code, for emergencies, was in the house safe.

The house safe was in the room. With him. He’d put it here because this was the safest place in the house.

He picked up the telephone.

✦ ✦ ✦

Jinx was on her back under a customer’s bike at the new shop when her phone went. She looked at the number. It wasn’t one she knew.

“Hello?”

“Hello,” said Raiden.

She slid out. “Why are you ringing me from a number I don’t know?”

“I’m on the safe-room line at the Peak house. I’m in the safe room.”

“Why?”

“I was testing it.”

“And?”

“It works.”

She sat up on the creeper. “Raiden.”

“I pressed the button. It locked. That’s what it’s for. The owner’s code changed on the first, and Chen Si’s on a plane, and the house copy is in the house safe, which is in here, with me. I put it in here. It’s extremely secure.” He sounded, she thought, almost proud.

“You designed that room. You designed the lock. And you’ve locked yourself in it,” said Jinx.

“There’s water for a week. I’m quite comfortable. There’s a very good chair,” said Raiden.

She put her hand over her eyes. “What do you need?”

“The envelope in the safe at Tai Hing. WORK, PRIVATE, at the back. It’s got a code in it for the outside panel. It’s under the bottom shelf in the study, behind a flap, on the left. You’ll have to push the third book from the end on the second shelf to find the flap.”

“I’m coming.”

“There’s no hurry. There’s a lamp. There’s a washroom.”

“Raiden, I’m coming,” said Jinx, and hung up, and went.

✦ ✦ ✦

She opened his safe in the office at Tai Hing with the numbers he’d given her the day he bolted it to the floor, and found the folder, and the envelope at the back of it with C.S. on the front in his small capitals, and put it inside her jacket without opening it. She took Carp. It was forty minutes to the Peak on a Saturday. She did it in twenty-six.

Aurelia met her at the door, white.

“He’s been in there an hour. I only knew when he rang the house line from inside. I’ve been sitting on the floor of the study talking to a bookcase. I’m so sorry. I don’t know the code. It goes to Si’s phone, and Si’s asleep somewhere over the Gulf. He’ll be furious with himself.” She pressed her hands together.

“He’ll be fine. They both will. Where’s the flap?” said Jinx.

It was where Raiden had said. Third book from the end on the second shelf, which wasn’t a book, and behind the flap it opened, a small panel and a keypad. Jinx tore open the envelope and read the code, and put it in, twelve digits, and the panel thought about it.

Nothing happened.

She looked at it. She looked at the envelope again. Under the code, in small capitals: THEN PRESS CONFIRM. RAIDEN, IF THIS IS YOU, YOU ALWAYS FORGET.

There was a small grey button under the keypad. She pressed it. The panel went green, and somewhere inside the wall something heavy drew back, and the run of books swung in on its counterweight without a sound.

He was sitting in the good chair with his clipboard on his knee and his tool roll beside him, and a cup of water from the room’s own supply, and he looked up at her through the gap with an expression of enormous gratitude and no shame at all.

“Thank you for coming.”

“You’re an idiot.”

“Yes.”

“You designed it.”

“It did exactly what I drew it to do. I’d like that noted,” said Raiden.

Aurelia, behind her, had started to laugh, a little hysterically, with her hand over her mouth.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the terrace afterwards, with the city laid out below them and Aurelia gone inside to ring Milan and leave a message for when her husband landed, Jinx stood with her arms folded and looked at him.

“Were you frightened?”

He thought about it honestly. He always did. That was the worst thing about him and the best.

He said, “For about four seconds. When the code didn’t work. Then I remembered I’d put the house copy in the house safe, and I laughed, and then I sat down in the chair and thought about where the envelope was. I was alone in a locked steel room for an hour and a half. I used to think that was the thing I was most afraid of in the world.” He looked at the city.

“And?”

“I wasn’t afraid. Because I knew who I’d ring. And I knew she’d come.” He looked at her.

Her face did something she didn’t let it do often. She unfolded her arms and took his face between her hands, out there on the terrace in front of the whole Peak, and kissed him, slowly, with her thumbs on his cheekbones and his clipboard digging into her ribs.

“Most husbands, ring their wives because they miss them,” she said, when she’d finished.

“I missed you.”

“You rang me because you’d locked yourself in a room.”

“I can miss you for several reasons at once,” said Raiden.

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening he sat at the kitchen table with the room’s documentation, which ran to forty pages, and wrote a new paragraph on page thirty-one in pencil: Testing the internal lockdown from inside when the owner isn’t present isn’t recommended.

She read it over his shoulder. Then she took the pencil out of his hand and turned to the last page, which was blank, and wrote across it in her big untidy capitals:

THE CODE TO GET OUT OF ANYWHERE: RING ME.

She underlined it twice and put the pencil down.

He looked at it.

“That’s not twelve digits,” he said.

“No.”

“It’s not very secure.”

“I’m not a security consultant.”

“Anybody could use it.”

“Good, I’ll answer. And if I’m busy, I’ll come. Don’t overcomplicate it,” said Jinx.

His phone buzzed on the table. A message from a number he’d had for two years and used four times.

Chen Si: I’m told the room has been tested.

Raiden: Thoroughly.

Chen Si: Good.

A minute later, another.

Chen Si: Change the house copy’s location.

“He’s right,” said Raiden.

“He’s always right. It’s very irritating,” said Jinx, and she took the documentation off him and closed it, and turned the lamp out over the table, and took him upstairs.

chapters.title: The Golden Ratio Tattoo
chapters.desc: She’s never let anyone draw on her. At the end of August she asks him to: a spiral of gears below her collarbone with a pencil where the smallest gear goes. He cries at Dot’s. On the third night she’s done being an exhibit.
chapters.epigraph: “I never wanted anybody else’s drawing on me. This would be yours.”
chapters.content:
She’d never had a tattoo. People assumed she had, the way they assumed she smoked and had been to prison. She’d never wanted one. She’d spent her childhood being looked at by men who decided what she was from the outside, and the idea of letting somebody else draw on her for the rest of her life had always seemed to her like giving them the last word.

It was the end of August, two months after the fire, when she changed her mind.

She’d been looking at her right shoulder in the bathroom mirror for three days. The flat place below the collarbone, above the curve of her breast. Nothing there. She’d never noticed it as a place before. On the Saturday morning she came down to the kitchen and found him at the table drawing the roof of a house that didn’t exist yet, with his healing hands round the pencil carefully, the new skin across his palms still pink and shiny.

“I want you to draw something. For me,” she said.

“For the shop?”

“For here. I want a tattoo.” She pulled the neck of her shirt aside and showed him the place.

He put the pencil down slowly.

“You’ve never wanted one.”

“I never wanted anybody else’s drawing on me. This would be yours.” She let the shirt go.

He looked at the place where her collarbone was, under the cotton, and then at her face, for long enough that she started to feel she’d said something she couldn’t take back.

“Not a flower. Not an animal. Not your name. Something that’s a machine but isn’t a gear. And don’t make it sentimental,” she said quickly.

“I wouldn’t dare.”

“About this big.” She showed him with her finger and thumb.

“Does it have to mean something?”

“No. Yes. But don’t tell me what until it’s done.” She thought.

✦ ✦ ✦

He drew all day. She went to the shop and came back and showered and came down, and he was in the same chair with sheets of paper round him on the floor like leaves. Some had been crossed out. A cluster of gears. A crankshaft, beautiful, which he’d decided was too much. A valve spring, which he’d decided was a joke.

The last one was different.

It was a spiral, the kind that opens out from a centre and keeps the same shape however large it grows, like a shell, or a fern uncurling. He’d built it out of gears. Not identical ones: each a little smaller than the one before, each meshing exactly into the next, so that they wound in towards the centre in a long curve of teeth, with plenty of bare space between the lines so the drawing could breathe on skin. The lines were fine. They looked like something that had grown, until you looked closely and saw that every tooth had been drawn to mesh.

At the centre, where the smallest gear should have been, was a pencil. An ordinary wooden one, sharpened to a point, so small she had to lean in to see it.

She stood behind his chair.

“Why the pencil?”

“Because the gears are yours. Everything you’ve ever built, taken apart, put back. The pencil is me. It’s small. I didn’t want to be obvious.” He didn’t look round.

“It’s almost hidden.”

“That’s the point.”

“And the spiral?”

“It’s a proportion. You find it in things that grow. Things that keep getting bigger without losing their shape. I thought it suited you.” He picked up the drawing and turned it a little in the light.

She took it out of his hands and folded it in half, carefully, along a line with nothing on it.

“I’m getting it. That one. Don’t change anything,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

The woman who did it was called Dot, and she had a shop over a herbalist’s near the market with a sign in the window that said NO NAMES OF BOYFRIENDS, and she looked at his drawing under her lamp.

“Who did this?”

“My husband.”

Dot looked at him. “You’re an artist?”

“I draw buildings.”

“Of course you do,” said Dot, and laughed, and went to make the stencil.

She put the stencil on, and took it off, and put it on again, a little higher and turned a few degrees, until the spiral followed the line of Jinx’s collarbone as if the bone had been drawn to fit it. Then she put on her gloves.

Raiden sat on a stool beside the bed. He’d brought a book. He didn’t open it.

It hurt more than Jinx had expected, which she’d expected. A hot, close, scratching pain, like being written on with a needle, which she was. The first hour was the outline. She held his hand and looked at the ceiling. The second hour was the small gears near the centre, where the lines were finest and the skin over the bone was thinnest, and that hurt in a new way, bright and precise, and once or twice she closed her fingers on his hand hard enough to make him take a breath. He moved his thumb over her knuckles. Somewhere in the second hour she noticed he was moving it in time with the needle.

“All right?” he said.

“Fine.”

“Do you want to stop?”

“No.”

“Water?”

“Raiden. Stop looking at me like I’m dying.” She turned her head on the pillow.

“I’m not.”

“You look worse than I do.”

“She’s doing very well. You, on the other hand, are sitting on the very edge of that chair,” said Dot, from her stool.

He looked down. He was.

“Idiot,” said Jinx, with her eyes shut, and smiled.

“Yours,” he said, and kissed her fingers.

✦ ✦ ✦

It took three hours and forty minutes. Dot wiped it clean and held up a mirror.

Jinx looked.

The spiral wound inward from the point of her shoulder along the line of her collarbone, gear into gear, each one smaller, the black lines fine and a little raised and red at the edges where the skin was angry. At the centre, almost lost between two curves, was the pencil.

She turned her shoulder. It moved with her. It looked as if it had always been there and she’d only just noticed.

“It’s beautiful,” she said.

Dot looked pleased. “He did good work.”

Jinx looked at Raiden. He hadn’t said anything. He was looking at her shoulder, not at the mirror, and his mouth had gone soft, and his eyes were wet behind his glasses.

“What’s wrong?”

“Nothing.”

“Don’t lie to me.”

He said, “I drew it. I’ve drawn a thousand things. I’ve never once seen one of them be part of someone. It looks like it was always supposed to be there.” His voice wasn’t steady. He shook his head at himself.

A tear went down his face before he could stop it. He took his glasses off and wiped it with his marked palm, and laughed, embarrassed.

“Oh, husband,” said Jinx.

She sat up carefully on the bed and put her good arm round his neck and kissed his cheek, and then the other one, and then his mouth, lightly, with Dot cleaning her needles and pretending not to be in the room.

“It’s only a tattoo,” she said against his mouth.

“I know.”

“You draw me all the time.”

“I know.”

“But this one’s on me,” said Jinx, and he closed his eyes.

✦ ✦ ✦

Dot covered it with film and gave them a sheet of instructions. Keep it covered tonight. Wash it in the morning with your hands, warm water, no cloth. A thin layer of balm. No bath, no swimming, no sun, for two weeks. Don’t pick it. Don’t let anyone touch it who hasn’t washed their hands.

He read the sheet twice in the taxi and once more at home.

He was careful that night. He helped her out of her shirt and into a loose old one of his that buttoned down the front, and didn’t touch the shoulder at all. He spent a considerable amount of time looking at it, though. She caught him doing it in the bedroom mirror.

“You’re staring.”

“I’m admiring.”

“Same thing.”

“Not quite,” said Raiden.

The second night he brought her tea and sat down on the bed while she washed it at the basin, and asked whether it felt tight, and whether it itched, and whether the balm was the right balm, until she told him to stop fussing, and he kissed her cheek and stopped for about six minutes.

On the third night she’d had enough.

He was by the wardrobe, folding the loose shirt she’d been wearing, as if it were something precious. She was sitting on the bed in a vest with the spiral bare, healing, shiny with balm.

“Raiden.”

“Yes?”

She held out her hand.

He came. She caught the front of his shirt and pulled him in between her knees.

“Careful. Your shoulder—” he said.

“I know where my shoulder is.”

She kissed him. He kissed her back gently, one hand on her waist and the other hovering a few centimetres from her arm, not touching, as if her shoulder were a wet drawing he might smudge.

“You’ve spent three days looking at me like a museum exhibit,” she said.

“It’s a very good exhibit.”

“Then come and appreciate it properly.”

He laughed, and she pulled him down. He went down onto the bed with her carefully, on her left side, so that nothing would press on the right, and she let him be careful, because she knew he needed to be, and then she slid her hand into his hair and made it clear that she was done being looked at.

He undressed her slowly, with his scarred hands, and she watched him do it, the pink new skin across his palms catching the lamplight as he moved, and felt them on her, warm and a little rough at the edges where they were still healing. He kissed her everywhere but the shoulder. Her throat, the inside of her elbow, her ribs, the soft skin of her stomach, the inside of her knee. He was thorough. She’d have teased him for it on any other night. Tonight she lay back on her left side with her right arm flung up out of the way on the pillow and let him, until she couldn’t bear it, and pulled him up by the hair and wrapped her leg over his hip and took him inside her, slowly, the two of them on their sides face to face so that nothing touched the shoulder at all.

They moved together like that, unhurried, foreheads almost touching. He watched her the whole time. She watched him watch her. When she came it was quiet, a long shiver that went through her from the soles of her feet, with her mouth open against his, and his name in it, and he held her through it and followed her with his face in her good shoulder, still, as if he’d been holding his breath for three days.

Afterwards she lay with her head on his chest and his heart under her ear. He moved his fingers in slow circles on her left arm, the unmarked one, carefully, nowhere near the other.

“Do you like it?” he said.

“Of course I like it.”

“Even the pencil?”

“The pencil. You know what I like most?” She traced his jaw with one finger.

“What?”

“You didn’t put yourself in the middle.”

“It’s a pencil.”

“Exactly. You put yourself where the smallest gear goes. The one everything else turns round, but you’d never see it unless you knew to look. You’re the thing that makes it go. Not the thing it’s all about.” She lifted her head to look at him.

He didn’t speak for a while.

“I might draw another one,” he said eventually.

“Where?”

“Your left shoulder.”

“Don’t get ambitious.”

He laughed. She put her head back down on his chest and shut her eyes, and was nearly asleep when she said, “But you can draw it.”

He looked down at her. She was asleep. He didn’t need to draw anything else that night. The pencil was already where he’d wanted it, on her skin, near her heart, in a place she’d chosen to give him, and under his marked hand her breathing went slow and even, and he lay awake and listened to it, and didn’t count anything at all.

chapters.title: He Names Her Bikes
chapters.desc: She gives him an engraving set and regrets it. GERALD on the dyno, MRS. TONG on a scooter, BOSS on a wheelbarrow, SHIPYARD ROAD under Carp’s tank. She cuts MONKEY herself, and NOT BAD LUCK for an apprentice, and MY HUSBAND.
chapters.epigraph: “Somebody gave me a chance once.”
chapters.content:
She gave him the engraving set for Christmas, which was her own fault.

He’d been making the plates by hand for years: the tag on ARCHITECT’s key, in 2022, cut with a borrowed set of punches at the bench while she was out, and one or two since that he wouldn’t show her. He did them slowly, letter by letter with a hammer, and they were always slightly crooked, and she’d watched him do it with his scarred hands that autumn and thought, he should have proper tools. So she bought him a proper engraving set with a fine graver and a vice that tilted, and wrapped it in a sheet of newspaper, and he opened it on Christmas morning and looked at it and then at her, with the expression of a man who’d been handed the keys to a city.

“You realise what you’ve done,” he said.

“It’s a hobby. You need a hobby.”

“Jia. You’ve given me an engraving set.”

She realised what she’d done in the second week of January.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first one was on the dyno at the shop. She came in on a Tuesday morning and found a small polished brass plate on the side of the control cabinet, beautifully cut, perfectly straight.

GERALD.

She went back home along the lane and up the stairs and into the kitchen, where he was making congee.

“What, is Gerald?” she said.

“The dyno.”

“I know it’s the dyno.”

“Then I don’t understand the question. He looks like a Gerald. He sits in his own room and he’s very reliable and he judges everyone.” He stirred.

“I’m taking it off.”

“Of course,” said Raiden.

She took it off. He put it back that evening. She took it off again on Wednesday. On Thursday there was a second plate beside the first, slightly smaller, that said GERALD (AGAIN), and she stood in front of it in the dyno room for a while with her screwdriver in her hand and then went back to work and left them both where they were.

✦ ✦ ✦

By February there were three.

She’d rebuilt Mrs. Tong a little step-through scooter for New Year, an old cream one that had been in the back of the noodle shop since Mrs. Tong’s husband died, and on the Monday after New Year a plate appeared on its front apron, under the headlamp. MRS. TONG.

“She is not a scooter,” Jinx said.

“She approved it.”

“She approves of everything you do.”

“That’s because I’m very good,” said Raiden, and the following week Jinx went into the noodle shop and found Mrs. Tong at a table by the window with the plate off the scooter and a tin of brass polish, rubbing at it with a corner of her apron, and decided not to say anything at all.

In March he did her father’s pigeon basket, the wicker one the bird travelled in from the river flat to the shop roof and back. JIA (THE BIRD). Her father read it, and read it again, and laughed so much that he had to sit down on the step, and after that he carried the basket with the plate turned outwards on the tram so that people would ask.

In April the foreman at Hill House found a plate on his wheelbarrow that said BOSS, and refused to use any other.

✦ ✦ ✦

By June it was a family matter.

Serafina came into the shop with a coffee and said she’d like a plate for Gilded, and Raiden, who happened to be there with a parcel, said that Gilded already had a name and he didn’t rename other people’s children. Eliana asked for one for her laptop. He declined on the grounds that it lacked wheels. Elowen asked whether he’d do one for Xiao Pan’s red bike and he said Xiao Pan would have to ask himself, because a name was a personal thing, and Xiao Pan came round the next day in his grey hoodie and asked, formally, and got one that said FLOWER POWER, which he screwed on himself and photographed from nine angles.

Jinx threatened to confiscate the graver. He bought a second graver. She hid the vice. He found it in under a minute, because he’d watched her hide it, and because she’d hidden it in the steel room behind the peaches.

“You always hide things behind the peaches,” he said.

“Because you never eat them.”

“I’m saving them.”

“For what?”

“For when there’s a tree,” said Raiden, and she didn’t have an answer to that.

✦ ✦ ✦

In August a customer came in to collect his bike off the dyno, a big man in a leather jacket who’d been coming to her since the old days at Tai Hing, and stood in the doorway of the dyno room reading the two plates on the control cabinet.

“Who’s Gerald?”

“The dyno,” said Jinx, without looking up from the printout.

Then she heard herself.

She stood there with the printout in her hand and the customer looking at her. Somewhere behind her, at the bench, Raiden had stopped what he was doing.

“He’s very reliable,” she told the customer, and handed him the printout, and walked straight out of the dyno room past her husband without catching his eye, because if she’d caught his eye he’d have been unbearable for a week, and he was unbearable for a week anyway.

✦ ✦ ✦

In October, she found the one he’d hidden.

She was replacing a fuel line on Carp, which meant the tank had to come off, which it hadn’t for nearly a year. She lifted it clear and set it on the bench on a towel and turned it over to look at the tap, and saw something small and bright fixed flat to the underside, right up under the front where the tank sat over the frame, where nobody would ever see it unless they had the tank off and upside down in their hands.

A narrow brass plate. Two lines, finely cut.

SHIPYARD ROAD.
15.5.21.

She went still.

The shipyard road was where it had started. A Saturday night in May, two kilometres of cracked concrete between the cranes, a new intake singing at nine thousand revs, and a man kneeling in the middle of the road with a sketchbook, right where she’d have hit him. She’d stopped with the back wheel shrieking a metre from his knees. He’d looked up at her, not frightened in the least, and smiled, an annoyingly pleasant smile, and then looked straight past her at the bike. She’d thought about that smile for three days. She’d never told him that.

She sat back on her heels with the tank in her lap.

He was in the doorway. He’d come down with tea. He saw what she was holding, and his face did something careful.

“You put this here,” she said.

“Yes.”

“When?”

“The week after the hill climb.”

“Why under there?”

He came and crouched beside her and looked at the plate. “Because I didn’t want it anywhere anybody else would see it. Only you. Only when you had her in pieces. That’s where you found me. I thought it should be written down somewhere. On something you’d built.” He touched the edge of it with one marked fingertip.

She swallowed. She turned the tank over again and put it back on the frame and did up the bolts, slowly, one at a time, and didn’t look at him.

“Don’t tell anyone,” she said.

“I won’t.”

“Especially not Gerald.”

He laughed, and she let him, and fitted the new fuel line with her hands not quite steady.

✦ ✦ ✦

In November she did one of her own.

She did it at night when he was asleep, with his graver, at his tilting vice, slowly, because she’d never done it before and it was harder than it looked and her letters kept wandering. It took her three plates to get one right. In the morning, when he went down to the yard to clean the racing outfit after its last outing of the year, he found it on the passenger rail of the chair, where his knee went when he was hanging off the side of it.

MONKEY.

He read it twice. He turned round. She was standing at the tool cabinet in the doorway of the yard with her coffee, not looking at him.

“Don’t,” she said.

“You named the chair.”

“It’s not a name. It’s a description.”

“It’s engraved.”

“It’s a job title.”

“Jia.”

She looked up then. He was smiling so much that it looked as if it hurt.

“It’s my favourite one,” he said.

“It’s the only one you’ve got.”

“Still,” said Raiden, and crossed the yard and took the coffee out of her hand and kissed her, and she still had the third spoiled plate in her pocket, with MOKNEY on it, which she never showed him and never threw away.

✦ ✦ ✦

In December an apprentice came to the shop, or rather, he’d been coming since the summer, twice a week after school, and in December she decided he was an apprentice.

His name was Chun. He was sixteen and thin and painfully careful with every tool, and he cleaned parts without being asked and asked questions only when he’d tried to work out the answer first. His mother cleaned offices at night. He’d told Jinx once, that he wanted to be a mechanic, and then gone red as if he’d confessed to something. She’d noticed how long he stood in the back of the shop looking at the old bikes waiting for parts.

On the third Saturday in December she called him over to the dyno room.

There was a small commuter bike by the door. Nothing special. Ten years old, second-hand, a little dented on the tank. But the frame was straight, the engine rebuilt, the brakes new, the chain new, the electrics checked twice, the tyres new and at the right pressure.

He looked at it. Then at her. “Boss?”

“It’s yours.”

“I can’t—”

“You’re not buying it. It’s registered in your name. There are conditions. You service it yourself, here, with me watching. You don’t ride like an idiot. And when anything goes wrong with it, you bring it back here first.” She folded her arms.

“Why?”

She thought about it. “Because the man at the tyre place on the corner let me have a corner of his yard when I was twenty with nothing but a bag and a bike and a set of spanners. He didn’t charge me for eight months. Nobody asked him to. Somebody gave me a chance once.” She looked at the bike.

Chun’s eyes had gone wet. He looked down at the bike so she wouldn’t see, and then he saw the plate on the headstock, small and straight, under the bars.

NOT BAD LUCK.

He read it twice. He laughed, and it came out wet.

“The registration’s got your name on it. That’s just for the bike,” said Jinx gruffly.

“Thank you, Boss.”

“Go on. Take it outside before I change my mind.”

He wheeled it out through the loading doors so carefully that it took him a full minute, grinning so widely that even she had to smile.

Raiden had watched the whole thing from the bench. He came and stood beside her.

“Not bad luck,” he said.

“Don’t.”

“That’s not one of mine.”

“No, I chose that one,” said Jinx.

✦ ✦ ✦

That night he was at the bench in the workshop at Hill House, the one by the window, polishing a blank plate.

“Who’s that for?” she said.

“I haven’t decided.”

She took it out of his hand and turned it over. Then she took the graver from the vice and sat down on the stool beside him, and he watched her cut two words into it, slowly, the way she’d learned, letter by letter, her tongue between her teeth. Her letters wandered. She didn’t care.

She put it in his palm, on the shiny place where the shutter had burned him.

MY HUSBAND.

He looked at it.

“That isn’t a bike,” he said.

“I know.”

“Then what is it?”

She leaned over and kissed him. “Mine,” said Jinx.

For once in his life, he didn’t try to think of a better name for anything. He closed his marked hand round the brass, and held her.

extras.title: Architect
extras.line: He said it once, almost to himself. She remembered. Six weeks at the bench after closing.

extras.title: Four Visits
extras.line: The morning after the Peak drawings. His phone rang beside the peaches, and he never puts drawings away wrong.
